Strengthen immunization system and withdraw oral polio vaccine... 3. Containment and certification... 4. Legacy planning.]

category: Describe the global polio eradication initiative
front: Q: What criteria define 'adequate' stool specimens in Acute Flaccid Paralysis (AFP) surveillance?
back: Two specimens collected 24–48 hours apart, within 14 days of paralysis onset, arriving in the lab via reverse cold chain (4–8°C).
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 210 (Book Page): [‘Adequate’ stool specimens are two stool specimens of sufficient quantity for laboratory analysis, collected at least 24 hours apart, within 14 days after the onset of paralysis, and arriving in the laboratory by reverse cold chain.]

category: Describe the global polio eradication initiative
front: Q: Which three countries remained endemic for wild poliovirus as of 2014?
back:
1. Afghanistan
2. Pakistan
3. Nigeria
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 209 (Book Page): [Since then, implementation of the eradication strategies has reduced the number of polio endemic countries from more than 125 in 1988 to 3 in 2014. These countries are Afghanistan, Pakistan and Nigeria.]

category: Describe the global polio eradication initiative
front: Q: What is the minimum sensitivity indicator for non-polio AFP surveillance for certification?
back: Detection of at least 1 case of non-polio AFP per 100,000 population under 15 years old (2 per 100,000 in endemic regions).
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 210 (Book Page): [A country's surveillance system needs to be sensitive enough to detect at least one case of AFP for every 100,000 children under 15 — even in the absence of polio.]

category: Describe the global polio eradication initiative
front: Q: A 10-year-old child presents with sudden onset of limb limpness. What is the mandatory immediate action under the GPEI?
back: Promptly report as Acute Flaccid Paralysis (AFP) to the district health officer and initiate virological investigation (stool sampling).
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 210 (Book Page): [They must promptly report every case of acute flaccid paralysis (AFP) in any child under 15 years of age... All children with acute flaccid paralysis (AFP) should be reported and tested for wild poliovirus within 48 hours of onset.]

category: Describe the global polio eradication initiative
front: Q: Why is the transition from trivalent OPV (tOPV) to bivalent OPV (bOPV) critical to the eradication endgame?
back: Wild poliovirus Type 2 was eradicated in 1999; its continued presence in tOPV is the main cause of circulating vaccine-derived poliovirus (cVDPV) outbreaks.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 209 (Book Page): [As wild poliovirus type 2 was eradicated in 1999, and the main cause of VDPV outbreaks is currently type 2 component of OPV, this component must be removed... replacing the trivalent OPV with bivalent OPV.]

category: Describe the global polio eradication initiative
front: Q: Differentiate Environmental Surveillance from AFP Surveillance in the context of GPEI.
back:
AFP Surveillance: Clinical detection of paralyzed children. 
Environmental Surveillance: Testing sewage/environmental samples for poliovirus, often detecting circulation before paralysis occurs.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 210 (Book Page): [Environmental surveillance involves testing sewage... Environmental surveillance often confirms wild poliovirus infections in the absence of cases of paralysis.]

category: Describe the global polio eradication initiative
front: Q: When was India officially declared a polio-free country by the WHO?
back: March 27, 2014 (following three years without a reported case since the last case in January 2011).
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 209 (Book Page): [India has not reported any polio case since January 2011, and has been declared polio-free since 27th March 2014.]

category: Describe the global polio eradication initiative
front: Q: In which year did the World Health Assembly resolve to globally eradicate poliomyelitis?
back: A: 1988. This initiative reduced endemic countries from over 125 to only 3 (Afghanistan, Pakistan, Nigeria) by 2014.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 208 (Book Page): In 1988, the World Health Assembly resolved to eradicate poliomyelitis globally. Since then, implementation of the eradication strategies has reduced the number of polio endemic countries from more than 125 in 1988 to 3 in 2014.

category: Describe the global polio eradication initiative
front: Q: How does the immunity induced by OPV differ from IPV regarding the community?
back: A: OPV induces intestinal secretory IgA, preventing gut reinfection and transmission. IPV only protects the individual from paralysis and does not prevent virus excretion.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 213 (Book Page): OPV induces both local and systemic immunity... Intestinal infection stimulates the production of IgA secretory antibodies which prevent subsequent infection of the alimentary tract... IPV induces humoral antibodies but does not induce intestinal or local immunity.

category: Describe the global polio eradication initiative
front: Q: What defines a Vaccine-Derived Poliovirus (VDPV) compared to routine Sabin strains?
back: A: VDPVs are genetically altered Sabin strains showing prolonged replication or transmission (exceeding 4-6 weeks), regaining neurovirulence similar to wild poliovirus.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 212 (Book Page): VDPVs resemble WPVs biologically... they have genetic properties consistent with prolonged replication or transmission, which is substantially longer than the normal period of vaccine virus replication of 4-6 weeks in the OPV recipient.

category: Describe the global polio eradication initiative
front: Q: What are the two mandatory clinical reporting criteria for Acute Flaccid Paralysis (AFP) surveillance?
back: A: 1. Any child under 15 years with acute flaccid paralysis. 2. Any person of any age with suspected polio.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 210 (Book Page): They must promptly report every case of acute flaccid paralysis (AFP) in any child under 15 years of age. In addition... search for AFP cases which may have been overlooked or misdiagnosed.

category: Describe the global polio eradication initiative

back: A: 1. Detect and interrupt transmission. 2. Strengthen immunization and withdraw OPV. 3. Containment and certification. 4. Legacy planning.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 209 (Book Page): The plan has 4 objectives: 1. Detect and interrupt all poliovirus transmission... 2. Strengthen immunization system and withdraw oral polio vaccine... 3. Containment and certification... 4. Legacy planning.

category: Describe the global polio eradication initiative
front: Q: What is the primary non-polio AFP rate indicator for a sensitive surveillance system?
back: A: Detection of at least 1 case of non-polio AFP per 100,000 children under 15 years annually (2 per 100,000 in endemic regions).
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 210 (Book Page): A country's surveillance system needs to be sensitive enough to detect at least one case of AFP for every 100,000 children under 15... In endemic regions... this rate should be two per 100,000.

category: Describe the global polio eradication initiative
front: Q: What defines an "adequate" stool specimen in the context of polio surveillance?
back: A: Two specimens collected 24-48 hours apart, within 14 days of paralysis onset, arriving in the laboratory under reverse cold chain.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 210 (Book Page): Because shedding of the virus is variable, two specimens — taken 24-48 hours apart are required. Speed is essential... during the first two weeks after onset of paralysis.

category: Describe the global polio eradication initiative
front: Q: Why is Genomic Mapping (Sequencing) used in the Global Polio Eradication Initiative?
back: A: It identifies the exact genetic make-up to trace the virus to specific geographic families and pinpoint sources of importation.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 211 (Book Page): By determining the exact genetic make-up of the virus, wild viruses can be compared to others and classified into genetic families which cluster in defined geographical areas... allowing inferences about the geographical origin.

category: Describe the global polio eradication initiative
front: Q: What is the epidemiological significance of the "Zero Dose" of OPV?
back: A: It refers to OPV given at birth (within 15 days) to maximize population immunity before exposure to wild poliovirus or environmental interference.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 129 (Book Page): OPV-0 At birth or as early as possible within the first 15 days... Page 213 (Book Page): It is recommended that a dose of OPV (zero-dose) is required to be given to all children delivered in health institutions.

category: Describe the global polio eradication initiative
front: Q: Which specific wild poliovirus (WPV) types have been eliminated or nearly eradicated?
back: A: Type 2 was eradicated in 1999; Type 3 has not been reported since November 2012. Type 1 remains the current focus.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 209 (Book Page): wild poliovirus type 2 was eradicated in 1999 and case numbers of type 3 are down to the lowest-ever levels with the last case reported in November 2012.

category: Describe the global polio eradication initiative
front: Q: What are the four main objectives of the Polio Eradication and Endgame Strategic Plan 2013-2018?
back: 1. Interrupt all poliovirus transmission. 2. Strengthen immunization systems and withdraw OPV. 3. Containment and certification. 4. Legacy planning.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 209 (Book Page): The plan has 4 objectives : 1. Detect and interrupt all poliovirus transmission... 2. Strengthen immunization system and withdraw oral polio vaccine... 3. Containment and certification... 4. Legacy planning.

category: Describe the global polio eradication initiative
front: Q: Why does the global initiative mandate the withdrawal of the type 2 component from OPV?
back: Wild poliovirus type 2 was eradicated in 1999; current type 2 OPV is the primary cause of Vaccine-Derived Poliovirus (VDPV) outbreaks.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 209 (Book Page): As wild poliovirus type 2 was eradicated in 1999, and the main cause of VDPV outbreaks is currently type 2 component of OPV, this component must be removed from the vaccine by mid-2016.

category: Describe the global polio eradication initiative
front: Q: Contrast the community-level impact of Inactivated Polio Vaccine (IPV) versus Oral Polio Vaccine (OPV).
back: OPV prevents intestinal reinfection and transmission (herd immunity) via local IgA. IPV only protects the individual from paralysis (IgG/IgM) but permits gut transmission.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 213 (Book Page): IPV induces, humoral antibodies... but does not induce intestinal or local immunity... OPV induces both local and systemic immunity.

category: Describe the global polio eradication initiative
front: Q: A 10-year-old child presents with sudden limb weakness. What mandatory surveillance steps must be initiated?
back: 1. Report as Acute Flaccid Paralysis (AFP). 2. Collect two stool samples 24-48 hours apart within 14 days of onset. 3. Maintain reverse cold chain.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 210 (Book Page): They must promptly report every case of acute flaccid paralysis (AFP) in any child under 15 years... To test for polio, faecal specimens are analyzed... two specimens — taken 24-48 hours apart are required.

category: Describe the global polio eradication initiative
front: Q: Which pharmacological agent is used to prepare Inactivated Polio Vaccine (IPV) from harvested viral components?
back: Formaldehyde is used to inactivate wild poliovirus strains grown in Vero or human diploid cell cultures.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 212 (Book Page): Harvested viral components are inactivated with formaldehyde.

category: Describe the global polio eradication initiative
front: Q: What defines an "adequate" stool specimen for certification-standard polio surveillance?
back: Two specimens collected 24 hours apart, within 14 days of paralysis onset, arriving at the laboratory in reverse cold chain.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 212 (Book Page): ‘Adequate’ stool specimens are two stool specimens... collected at least 24 hours apart, within 14 days after the onset of paralysis, and arriving in the laboratory by reverse cold chain.

category: Describe the global polio eradication initiative
front: Q: How is environmental surveillance conceptually applied to identify poliovirus circulation in polio-free regions?
back: Testing sewage or wastewater for poliovirus detects transmission in the community before clinical cases of Acute Flaccid Paralysis appear.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 210 (Book Page): Environmental surveillance often confirms wild poliovirus infections in the absence of cases of paralysis. Systematic environmental sampling... provides important supplementary surveillance data.

category: Describe the global polio eradication initiative
front: Q: Which clinical conditions form the primary differential diagnosis for Acute Flaccid Paralysis (AFP) in children?
back: 1. Guillain-Barr�� Syndrome. 2. Transverse myelitis. 3. Traumatic neuritis.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 210 (Book Page): polio may be difficult to differentiate from other forms of acute flaccid paralysis, such as Guillain-Barre Syndrome, transverse myelitis, or traumatic neuritis.

category: Describe the global polio eradication initiative
front: Q: Describe the physiological immunity loop triggered by the secondary spread of OPV.
back: Vaccinees excrete progeny virus in faeces, which then infects and immunizes susceptible household and community contacts, creating widespread herd immunity.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 214 (Book Page): The vaccine progeny is excreted in the faeces and secondary spread occurs to household contacts and susceptible contacts in the community. Non-immunized persons may therefore, be immunized.

category: Describe the global polio eradication initiative
front: Q: Which three countries remained polio-endemic according to the Global Polio Eradication Initiative in 2014?
back: Afghanistan, Pakistan, and Nigeria.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 209 (Book Page): implementation of the eradication strategies has reduced the number of polio endemic countries from more than 125 in 1988 to 3 in 2014. These countries are Afghanistan, Pakistan and Nigeria.

category: Discuss the historical and current global impact of poliomyelitis vaccination efforts
front: When did the World Health Assembly (WHA) resolve to eradicate polio globally and what was the impact?
back: Resolved in 1988. It reduced endemic countries from over 125 to just 3 (Afghanistan, Pakistan, Nigeria) by 2014, protecting 80% of the global population.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 208 (Book Page): [In 1988, the World Health Assembly resolved to eradicate poliomyelitis globally. Since then, implementation of the eradication strategies has reduced the number of polio endemic countries from more than 125 in 1988 to 3 in 2014.]

category: Discuss the historical and current global impact of poliomyelitis vaccination efforts
front: How does Oral Polio Vaccine (OPV) provide community protection compared to Inactivated Polio Vaccine (IPV)?
back: OPV induces intestinal IgA immunity and vaccine progeny is excreted in faeces, causing secondary spread to contacts. IPV only induces serum IgG/IgM and does not prevent gut reinfection.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 214 (Book Page): [The vaccine progeny is excreted in the faeces and secondary spread occurs to household contacts and susceptible contacts in the community... widespread “herd immunity” results.]

category: Discuss the historical and current global impact of poliomyelitis vaccination efforts
front: Differentiate between Wild Poliovirus (WPV) and Vaccine-Derived Poliovirus (VDPV).
back: WPV are naturally occurring strains. VDPVs are Sabin strains that have regained neurovirulence through prolonged replication or transmission in under-vaccinated populations, posing identical clinical threats.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 212 (Book Page): [VDPVs resemble WPVs biologically... they have genetic properties consistent with prolonged replication or transmission... cVDPVs pose the same public health threat as WPVs.]

category: Discuss the historical and current global impact of poliomyelitis vaccination efforts
front: What are the gold-standard surveillance indicators for a sensitive Acute Flaccid Paralysis (AFP) program?
back: Detection of ≥1 non-polio AFP case per 100,000 children <15 years and ≥80% 'adequate' stool specimens (two samples 24 hours apart within 14 days of onset).
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 210 (Book Page): [A country's surveillance system needs to be sensitive enough to detect at least one case of AFP for every 100,000 children under 15... At least 80% of AFP cases having ‘adequate’ stool specimens.]

category: Discuss the historical and current global impact of poliomyelitis vaccination efforts
front: Why is trivalent OPV being replaced with bivalent OPV in global 'Endgame' strategies?
back: Wild type 2 was eradicated in 1999; trivalent OPV's type 2 component causes most VDPV outbreaks. The switch eliminates VDPV risk while maintaining immunity to types 1 and 3.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 209 (Book Page): [As wild poliovirus type 2 was eradicated in 1999, and the main cause of VDPV outbreaks is currently type 2 component of OPV, this component must be removed... replacing the trivalent OPV with bivalent OPV.]

category: Discuss the historical and current global impact of poliomyelitis vaccination efforts
front: What is the primary clinical case definition for Acute Flaccid Paralysis (AFP) surveillance?
back: Any child under 15 years with acute onset of flaccid (floppy) paralysis, or any person of any age if poliomyelitis is clinically suspected.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 210 (Book Page): [Finding and reporting children with acute flaccid paralysis (AFP) : ...staff in all health facilities... must promptly report every case of acute flaccid paralysis (AFP) in any child under 15 years of age.]

category: Discuss the historical and current global impact of poliomyelitis vaccination efforts
front: What is the strategic utility of environmental surveillance in the Polio Eradication Initiative?
back: Testing sewage/environmental samples confirms poliovirus circulation in a community even in the absence of reported paralytic cases, helping map silent transmission and viral genetic families.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 212 (Book Page): [Environmental surveillance often confirms wild poliovirus infections in the absence of cases of paralysis. Systematic environmental sampling... provides important supplementary surveillance data.]

category: Discuss the historical and current global impact of poliomyelitis vaccination efforts
front: How does Vaccine-Associated Paralytic Poliomyelitis (VAPP) differ clinically and etiologically from Wild Polio?
back: Clinically indistinguishable. VAPP is a rare adverse event (4/1,000,000 births) caused specifically by Sabin strains in OPV, whereas wild polio is caused by WPV transmission.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 212 (Book Page): [Vaccine-associated paralytic poliomyelitis (VAPP) is the most important of these rare adverse events. Cases of VAPP are clinically indistinguishable from poliomyelitis caused by WPV, but can be distinguished by laboratory analysis.]

category: Discuss the historical and current global impact of poliomyelitis vaccination efforts
front: List the four main objectives of the Polio Eradication and Endgame Strategic Plan 2013-2018.
back: 1. Detect/interrupt transmission. 2. Strengthen systems/withdraw OPV. 3. Containment/Certification. 4. Legacy planning (transitioning assets to other health goals).
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 209 (Book Page): [The plan has 4 objectives : 1. Detect and interrupt all poliovirus transmission... 2. Strengthen immunization system and withdraw oral polio vaccine... 3. Containment and certification... 4. Legacy planning.]

category: Discuss the historical and current global impact of poliomyelitis vaccination efforts
front: When was India declared polio-free and what was the milestone for its last recorded case?
back: India was declared polio-free on March 27, 2014. The last case was reported on January 13, 2011, in Howrah, West Bengal.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 215 (Book Page): [The last case of polio in the country was reported from Howrah of West Bengal with date of onset of disease on 13th January 2011... On 27th March 2014, India was declared as non-endemic country for polio.]

category: Discuss the historical and current global impact of poliomyelitis vaccination efforts
front: How many countries were polio-endemic in 1988 compared to 2014?
back: 1988: Over 125 countries. 2014: Reduced to 3 endemic countries (Afghanistan, Pakistan, and Nigeria).
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 208 (Book Page): [implementation of the eradication strategies has reduced the number of polio endemic countries from more than 125 in 1988 to 3 in 2014.]

category: Discuss the historical and current global impact of poliomyelitis vaccination efforts
front: Explain the mechanism by which Oral Polio Vaccine (OPV) provides 'herd immunity' to the community.
back: Vaccinees excrete attenuated virus in faeces; this virus spreads to and immunizes susceptible household and community contacts.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 213 (Book Page): [The vaccine progeny is excreted in the faeces and secondary spread occurs to household contacts and susceptible contacts in the community. Non-immunized persons may therefore, be immunized.]

category: Discuss the historical and current global impact of poliomyelitis vaccination efforts
front: Contrast the mucosal immunity produced by Inactivated Polio Vaccine (IPV) and Oral Polio Vaccine (OPV).
back: OPV: Induces intestinal IgA, preventing gut reinfection. IPV: Induces serum IgG but no local intestinal immunity; cannot prevent wild virus multiplication in the gut.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 212 (Book Page): [IPV induces, humoral antibodies... but does not induce intestinal or local immunity... for the community, it offers nothing because the wild viruses can still multiply in the gut]

category: Discuss the historical and current global impact of poliomyelitis vaccination efforts
front: What is the mandatory protocol if a child spits out the Oral Polio Vaccine (OPV) during administration?
back: The vaccinator must repeat the process immediately to ensure the full dose is received.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 213 (Book Page): [Repeat the process if the child spits out the vaccine.]

category: Discuss the historical and current global impact of poliomyelitis vaccination efforts
front: Under the Polio Endgame Strategic Plan, why is trivalent OPV being replaced with bivalent OPV?
back: To eliminate the risk of Type 2 vaccine-derived polioviruses (VDPV2), as wild Type 2 was eradicated in 1999.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 209 (Book Page): [As wild poliovirus type 2 was eradicated in 1999... this component must be removed from the vaccine by mid-2016... replacing the trivalent OPV with bivalent OPV]

category: Discuss the historical and current global impact of poliomyelitis vaccination efforts
front: Define the criteria for 'adequate' stool specimens in Acute Flaccid Paralysis (AFP) surveillance.
back: Two specimens collected 24–48 hours apart, within 14 days of paralysis onset, arriving at the lab via reverse cold chain.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 210 (Book Page): [‘Adequate’ stool specimens are two stool specimens... collected at least 24 hours apart, within 14 days after the onset of paralysis, and arriving in the laboratory by reverse cold chain]

category: Discuss the historical and current global impact of poliomyelitis vaccination efforts
front: What is the significance of environmental surveillance in the context of a polio-free region?
back: It detects poliovirus in sewage, pinpointing silent wild virus circulation or importation even in the absence of clinical paralysis cases.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 210 (Book Page): [Environmental surveillance often confirms wild poliovirus infections in the absence of cases of paralysis.]

category: Discuss the historical and current global impact of poliomyelitis vaccination efforts
front: A child develops paralysis after OPV. How is Vaccine-Associated Paralytic Poliomyelitis (VAPP) lab-confirmed vs Wild Polio?
back: Molecular analysis (rRT-PCR) of stool isolates differentiates Sabin vaccine strains from naturally occurring wild poliovirus strains.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 210 (Book Page): [Cases of VAPP are clinically indistinguishable from poliomyelitis caused by WPV, but can be distinguished by laboratory analysis.]

category: Discuss the historical and current global impact of poliomyelitis vaccination efforts
front: Describe the epidemiological objective of 'Pulse' Polio Immunization (PPI) campaigns.
back: Sudden, simultaneous administration of OPV to all children <5 years to replace wild viruses with attenuated strains during low-transmission seasons.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 215 (Book Page): [The term "pulse" has been used to describe this sudden, simultaneous, mass administration of OPV... This procedure virtually eliminates the wild polio strains in the community and replaces them by attenuated strains]

category: Discuss the historical and current global impact of poliomyelitis vaccination efforts
front: Which specific wild poliovirus strain has not been recorded globally since 1999?
back: Wild poliovirus Type 2.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 209 (Book Page): [Of the 3 strains of wild poliovirus (type 1, type 2 and type 3), wild poliovirus type 2 was eradicated in 1999]

category: Discuss the historical and current global impact of poliomyelitis vaccination efforts
front: Q: What was the primary goal of the 1988 World Health Assembly resolution regarding poliomyelitis?
back: To eradicate poliomyelitis globally. This initiative reduced the number of endemic countries from over 125 in 1988 to just 3 (Afghanistan, Pakistan, and Nigeria) by 2014.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 208 (Book Page): [In 1988, the World Health Assembly resolved to eradicate poliomyelitis globally. Since then, implementation of the eradication strategies has reduced the number of polio endemic countries from more than 125 in 1988 to 3 in 2014.]

category: Discuss the historical and current global impact of poliomyelitis vaccination efforts
front: Q: Why is OPV considered superior to IPV for community-level polio eradication efforts?
back: OPV induces intestinal (local) IgA immunity, preventing wild virus replication in the gut. IPV only provides humoral protection, meaning vaccinated individuals can still shed and spread wild virus.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 212 (Book Page): [IPV... does not induce intestinal or local immunity... for the community, it offers nothing because the wild viruses can still multiply in the gut and be a source of infection to others.]

category: Discuss the historical and current global impact of poliomyelitis vaccination efforts
front: Q: Distinguish between the eradication status of Wild Poliovirus (WPV) Type 2 and Type 3.
back: WPV Type 2 was globally eradicated in 1999. WPV Type 3 has reached record lows, with the last reported case occurring in Nigeria in November 2012.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 209 (Book Page): [Of the 3 strains of wild poliovirus (type 1, type 2 and type 3), wild poliovirus type 2 was eradicated in 1999 and case numbers of type 3 are down to the lowest-ever levels with the last case reported in November 2012 from Nigeria.]

category: Discuss the historical and current global impact of poliomyelitis vaccination efforts
front: Q: What are the two mandatory criteria for 'adequate' stool specimens in Acute Flaccid Paralysis (AFP) surveillance?
back: Two specimens collected 24–48 hours apart. Must be collected within 14 days of paralysis onset and arrive at the laboratory via reverse cold chain.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 210 (Book Page): [‘Adequate’ stool specimens are two stool specimens of sufficient quantity for laboratory analysis, collected at least 24 hours apart, within 14 days after the onset of paralysis, and arriving in the laboratory by reverse cold chain.]

category: Discuss the historical and current global impact of poliomyelitis vaccination efforts
front: Q: What is the 'Switch' strategy in the Polio Eradication and Endgame Strategic Plan 2013-2018?
back: Replacing trivalent OPV (tOPV) with bivalent OPV (bOPV). This removes the Type 2 component to eliminate the risk of Type 2 Vaccine-Derived Poliovirus (VDPV) outbreaks.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 209 (Book Page): [As wild poliovirus type 2 was eradicated in 1999, and the main cause of VDPV outbreaks is currently type 2 component of OPV... replacing the trivalent OPV with bivalent OPV in all OPV using countries.]

category: Discuss the historical and current global impact of poliomyelitis vaccination efforts
front: Q: Define the minimum sensitivity indicator for certification-standard Non-Polio AFP surveillance.
back: Detection of at least 1 case of non-polio AFP per 100,000 population aged under 15 years. In endemic regions, this rate should be 2 per 100,000.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 210 (Book Page): [At least one case of non-polio AFP should be detected annually per 100,000 population aged less than 15 years. In endemic regions, to ensure even higher sensitivity, this rate should be two per 100,000.]

category: Discuss the historical and current global impact of poliomyelitis vaccination efforts
front: Q: How do Pulse Polio Immunization (PPI) doses interact with the routine National Immunization Schedule?
back: PPI doses are supplementary extra doses. They do not replace routine doses, and there is no minimum required interval between PPI and scheduled OPV doses.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 215 (Book Page): [The dose of OPV during PPIs are extra doses which supplement, and do not replace the doses received during routine immunization services... There is no minimum interval between PPI and scheduled OPV doses.]

category: Discuss the historical and current global impact of poliomyelitis vaccination efforts
front: Q: How does Vaccine-Derived Poliovirus (VDPV) differ from Vaccine-Associated Paralytic Poliomyelitis (VAPP)?
back: VAPP is a rare individual adverse event (mostly Sabin 3). VDPVs involve genetic mutations indicating prolonged replication (>4-6 weeks) and person-to-person transmission threat equivalent to wild virus.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 212 (Book Page): [VDPVs resemble WPVs biologically and differ from the majority of vaccine-related poliovirus (VRPV) isolates in that they have genetic properties consistent with prolonged replication or transmission.]

category: Discuss the historical and current global impact of poliomyelitis vaccination efforts
front: Q: Describe the mechanism by which OPV produces 'herd immunity' in a community.
back: Vaccinated children excrete the vaccine virus progeny in faeces. This secondary spread infects and immunizes susceptible household and community contacts, protecting up to 66% of the population.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 213 (Book Page): [The vaccine progeny is excreted in the faeces and secondary spread occurs to household contacts and susceptible contacts in the community. Non-immunized persons may therefore, be immunized. Thus widespread “herd immunity” results.]

category: Discuss the historical and current global impact of poliomyelitis vaccination efforts
front: Q: Which three countries remained polio-endemic for Wild Poliovirus (WPV) as of 2014?
back:
1. Afghanistan
2. Pakistan
3. Nigeria
(India was declared polio-free on March 27, 2014).
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 209 (Book Page): [These countries are Afghanistan, Pakistan and Nigeria. India has not reported any polio case since January 2011, and has been declared polio-free since 27th March 2014.]

category: Discuss the historical and current global impact of poliomyelitis vaccination efforts
front: Q: What is the historical reduction in the number of polio-endemic countries since 1988?
back: The number of endemic countries decreased from over 125 in 1988 to only 3 by 2014 (Afghanistan, Pakistan, and Nigeria).
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 209 (Book Page): implementation of the eradication strategies has reduced the number of polio endemic countries from more than 125 in 1988 to 3 in 2014. These countries are Afghanistan, Pakistan and Nigeria.

category: Discuss the historical and current global impact of poliomyelitis vaccination efforts
front: Q: Which specific wild poliovirus (WPV) types have been eradicated or reached lowest-ever levels globally?
back:
• Type 2: Eradicated (last case 1999)
• Type 3: Lowest-ever levels (last case November 2012)
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 209 (Book Page): Of the 3 strains of wild poliovirus (type 1, type 2 and type 3), wild poliovirus type 2 was eradicated in 1999 and case numbers of type 3 are down to the lowest-ever levels with the last case reported in November 2012 from Nigeria.

category: Discuss the historical and current global impact of poliomyelitis vaccination efforts
front: Q: Contrast the historical certification years for WHO polio-free regions.
back:
• Americas: 1994
• Western Pacific: 2000
• Europe: 2002
• SEAR (including India): 2014
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 209 (Book Page): Four of the six Regions of WHO have been certified as polio-free : the Americas (1994), Western Pacific (2000), Europe (2002) and SEAR (2014).

category: Discuss the historical and current global impact of poliomyelitis vaccination efforts
front: Q: In a high-risk region, what is the clinical benchmark for sensitive AFP surveillance?
back: Detection of at least 2 non-polio AFP cases per 100,000 children under age 15 annually (1 per 100,000 in non-endemic areas).
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 211 (Book Page): Sensitivity of surveillance: At least one case of non-polio AFP should be detected annually per 100,000 population aged less than 15 years. In endemic regions, to ensure even higher sensitivity, this rate should be two per 100,000.

category: Discuss the historical and current global impact of poliomyelitis vaccination efforts
front: Q: Why is the global withdrawal of the Type 2 component from Oral Polio Vaccine (OPV) critical?
back: Type 2 is the primary cause of Vaccine-Derived Poliovirus (VDPV) outbreaks; removing it minimizes the risk of vaccine-linked paralysis.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 210 (Book Page): As wild poliovirus type 2 was eradicated in 1999, and the main cause of VDPV outbreaks is currently type 2 component of OPV, this component must be removed from the vaccine by mid-2016.

category: Discuss the historical and current global impact of poliomyelitis vaccination efforts
front: Q: What defines 'adequate' stool specimen collection for Acute Flaccid Paralysis (AFP) surveillance?
back: Two specimens collected 24–48 hours apart, within 14 days of paralysis onset, arriving at the lab in a reverse cold chain.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 211 (Book Page): ‘Adequate’ stool specimens are two stool specimens of sufficient quantity... collected at least 24 hours apart, within 14 days after the onset of paralysis, and arriving in the laboratory by reverse cold chain.

category: Discuss the historical and current global impact of poliomyelitis vaccination efforts
front: Q: How does environmental surveillance supplement Acute Flaccid Paralysis (AFP) reporting?
back: It tests sewage samples to detect wild poliovirus circulation in communities even in the absence of reported clinical paralysis cases.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 211 (Book Page): Environmental surveillance often confirms wild poliovirus infections in the absence of cases of paralysis. Systematic environmental sampling... provides important supplementary surveillance data.

category: Discuss the historical and current global impact of poliomyelitis vaccination efforts
front: Q: Differentiate between cVDPV and iVDPV in terms of epidemiological threat.
back:
• cVDPV: Shows community person-to-person transmission (high public threat)
• iVDPV: Prolonged replication in immunocompromised individuals (individual threat with transmission risk)
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 212 (Book Page): (1) cVDPVs, when evidence of person-to-person transmission in the community exists; (2) immunodeficiency-associated VDPVs (iVDPVs), which are isolates from persons with primary immunodeficiencies.

category: Discuss the historical and current global impact of poliomyelitis vaccination efforts
front: Q: What is the physiological limitation of IPV that necessitated the continued historical use of OPV?
back: IPV induces humoral immunity (IgG) but lacks intestinal/local immunity (secretory IgA), allowing wild virus to multiply in the gut and spread.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 213 (Book Page): IPV induces, humoral antibodies (IgM, IgG and IgA serum antibodies) but does not induce intestinal or local immunity... the wild viruses can still multiply in the gut and be a source of infection to others.

category: Discuss the historical and current global impact of poliomyelitis vaccination efforts
front: Q: When was the final case of wild polio reported in India, leading to its current status?
back: January 13, 2011 (Howrah, West Bengal). India was certified polio-free on March 27, 2014.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 216 (Book Page): The last case of polio in the country was reported from Howrah of West Bengal with date of onset of disease on 13th January 2011... On 27th March 2014, India was declared as non-endemic country for polio.

category: Discuss the historical and current global impact of poliomyelitis vaccination efforts
front: Q: How has the Global Polio Eradication Initiative (GPEI) changed the number of endemic countries since 1988?
back: Reduced from over 125 countries in 1988 to only 3 remaining endemic countries by 2014 (Afghanistan, Pakistan, and Nigeria).
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 208 (Book Page): [implementation of the eradication strategies has reduced the number of polio endemic countries from more than 125 in 1988 to 3 in 2014.]

category: Discuss the historical and current global impact of poliomyelitis vaccination efforts
front: Q: Contrast the primary immunological limitation of Inactivated Polio Vaccine (IPV) compared to Oral Polio Vaccine (OPV).
back: IPV induces humoral immunity (IgG) but lacks intestinal/local immunity (IgA); it prevents systemic paralysis but fails to prevent gut reinfection or viral shedding.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 213 (Book Page): [IPV induces, humoral antibodies (IgM, IgG and IgA serum antibodies) but does not induce intestinal or local immunity... for the community, it offers nothing because the wild viruses can still multiply in the gut.]

category: Discuss the historical and current global impact of poliomyelitis vaccination efforts
front: Q: Which specific wild poliovirus (WPV) serotypes have been eradicated or reported at lowest-ever levels as of 2014?
back: Type 2: Eradicated (last case 1999). Type 3: Lowest-ever levels (last case Nov 2012). Type 1: Only remaining circulating wild strain.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 209 (Book Page): [wild poliovirus type 2 was eradicated in 1999 and case numbers of type 3 are down to the lowest-ever levels with the last case reported in November 2012.]

category: Discuss the historical and current global impact of poliomyelitis vaccination efforts
front: Q: In Acute Flaccid Paralysis (AFP) surveillance, what constitutes 'adequate' stool specimens for laboratory analysis?
back: Two specimens collected 24-48 hours apart, within 14 days of paralysis onset, arriving at the laboratory within 72 hours via cold chain.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 210 (Book Page): ['Adequate' stool specimens are two stool specimens of sufficient quantity... collected at least 24 hours apart, within 14 days after the onset of paralysis, and arriving in the laboratory by reverse cold chain.]

category: Discuss the historical and current global impact of poliomyelitis vaccination efforts
front: Q: What is the primary operational challenge regarding the storage and transportation of Oral Polio Vaccine (OPV)?
back: Extreme thermolability; requires strict sub-zero storage (-20°C) and a continuous cold chain until the point of administration to prevent loss of potency.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 214 (Book Page): [A primary problem is the instability of the vaccine at high ambient temperatures. The vaccine has to be kept frozen during storage, and kept cold during transportation.]

category: Discuss the historical and current global impact of poliomyelitis vaccination efforts
front: Q: What is the standard sensitive indicator for a country's non-polio AFP surveillance in children?
back: Detection of at least 1 non-polio Acute Flaccid Paralysis (AFP) case per 100,000 population under age 15 annually.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 210 (Book Page): [A country's surveillance system needs to be sensitive enough to detect at least one case of AFP for every 100,000 children under 15 — even in the absence of polio.]

category: Discuss the historical and current global impact of poliomyelitis vaccination efforts
front: Q: What is the core transition objective of the 'withdrawal' phase in the Polio Eradication and Endgame Strategic Plan 2013-2018?
back: The global cessation of OPV use, starting with the removal of the Type 2 component (switching trivalent OPV to bivalent OPV) to eliminate VDPV risks.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 209 (Book Page): [all OPV must be removed from routine immunization programmes... this component must be removed from the vaccine by mid-2016... replacing the trivalent OPV with bivalent OPV.]

category: Discuss the historical and current global impact of poliomyelitis vaccination efforts
front: Q: Differentiate Vaccine-Associated Paralytic Poliomyelitis (VAPP) from wild-type polio clinically and etiologically.
back: Clinically indistinguishable. Etiologically, VAPP is a rare adverse event (4 cases/million births) of Sabin strains (mostly Type 3) replicating in recipients or contacts.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 212 (Book Page): [Cases of VAPP are clinically indistinguishable from poliomyelitis caused by WPV... most frequently associated with Sabin 3 (60% of cases).]

category: Discuss the historical and current global impact of poliomyelitis vaccination efforts
front: Q: How does the replication mechanism of Oral Polio Vaccine (OPV) contribute to community 'herd immunity'?
back: Vaccine virus replicates in the gut and is excreted in faeces, allowing secondary spread to household and community contacts, passively immunizing them.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 214 (Book Page): [The vaccine progeny is excreted in the faeces and secondary spread occurs to household contacts and susceptible contacts in the community. Non-immunized persons may therefore, be immunized.]

category: Discuss the historical and current global impact of poliomyelitis vaccination efforts
front: Q: Define the 'Pulse' strategy utilized in India's Pulse Polio Immunization (PPI) campaigns.
back: Sudden, simultaneous mass administration of supplemental OPV to all children aged 0-5 years on a single day, regardless of prior vaccination status.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 216 (Book Page): [The term 'pulse' has been used to describe this sudden, simultaneous, mass administration of OPV on a single day to all children 0-5 years of age, regardless to previous immunization.]

category: Discuss the historical and current global impact of poliomyelitis vaccination efforts
front: Q: When did the WHO officially resolve to eradicate poliomyelitis globally and what was the impact?
back: The resolution was made in 1988. It reduced endemic countries from over 125 to just 3 by 2014 (Afghanistan, Pakistan, Nigeria).
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 208 (Book Page): [In 1988, the World Health Assembly resolved to eradicate poliomyelitis globally. Since then... reduced the number of polio endemic countries from more than 125 in 1988 to 3 in 2014.]

category: Discuss the historical and current global impact of poliomyelitis vaccination efforts
front: Q: Why is Oral Polio Vaccine (OPV) superior to IPV for community-wide transmission control?
back: OPV induces intestinal IgA (local immunity), preventing wild virus multiplication in the gut. IPV only provides humoral IgG (systemic immunity).
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 213 (Book Page): [IPV induces humoral antibodies... but does not induce intestinal or local immunity... for the community, it offers nothing because the wild viruses can still multiply in the gut.]

category: Discuss the historical and current global impact of poliomyelitis vaccination efforts
front: Q: Differentiate between Vaccine-Associated Paralytic Polio (VAPP) and Vaccine-Derived Poliovirus (VDPV).
back: VAPP is a rare adverse event in recipients/contacts. VDPV is a mutated strain resulting from prolonged replication and person-to-person transmission.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 212 (Book Page): [VAPP is the most important of these rare adverse events... VDPVs resemble WPVs biologically... they have genetic properties consistent with prolonged replication or transmission.]

category: Discuss the historical and current global impact of poliomyelitis vaccination efforts
front: Q: What are the stool collection criteria for 'adequate' Acute Flaccid Paralysis (AFP) surveillance?
back: Two specimens collected 24-48 hours apart, within 14 days of paralysis onset, arriving at the laboratory via reverse cold chain.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 210 (Book Page): ['Adequate' stool specimens are two stool specimens... collected at least 24 hours apart, within 14 days after the onset of paralysis, and arriving in the laboratory by reverse cold chain.]

category: Discuss the historical and current global impact of poliomyelitis vaccination efforts
front: Q: Why does the Polio Endgame Plan mandate the switch from trivalent to bivalent OPV?
back: Wild Poliovirus Type 2 was eradicated in 1999; the Type 2 component in OPV causes the majority of cVDPV outbreaks.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 209 (Book Page): [As wild poliovirus type 2 was eradicated in 1999, and the main cause of VDPV outbreaks is currently type 2 component of OPV, this component must be removed.]

category: Discuss the historical and current global impact of poliomyelitis vaccination efforts
front: Q: Which three countries remained endemic for Wild Poliovirus (WPV) transmission as of 2014?
back: Afghanistan, Pakistan, and Nigeria. India was declared polio-free on March 27, 2014.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 209 (Book Page): [These countries are Afghanistan, Pakistan and Nigeria. India has not reported any polio case since January 2011, and has been declared polio-free since 27th March 2014.]

category: Discuss the historical and current global impact of poliomyelitis vaccination efforts
front: Q: Define the 'Pulse' strategy in Pulse Polio Immunization (PPI) campaigns.
back: Simultaneous mass administration of OPV to all children 0-5 years on a single day, regardless of prior vaccination status.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 216 (Book Page): [The term "pulse" has been used to describe this sudden, simultaneous, mass administration of OPV on a single day to all children 0-5 years of age, regardless to previous immunization.]

category: Discuss the historical and current global impact of poliomyelitis vaccination efforts
front: Q: How does environmental surveillance provide a sensitive supplement to clinical AFP monitoring?
back: It detects wild or vaccine-derived poliovirus in sewage/water samples, identifying viral circulation even in the absence of paralytic cases.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 210 (Book Page): [Environmental surveillance involves testing sewage... Environmental surveillance often confirms wild poliovirus infections in the absence of cases of paralysis.]

category: Discuss the historical and current global impact of poliomyelitis vaccination efforts
front: Q: What is the clinical significance of the 'Zero Dose' of Oral Polio Vaccine (OPV)?
back: Administered at birth (within 15 days) to provide early intestinal immunity before the primary vaccination series starts at 6 weeks.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 213 (Book Page): [A dose of OPV (zero-dose) is required to be given to all children delivered in health institutions before their discharge from the hospital... within the first 15 days.]

category: Discuss the historical and current global impact of poliomyelitis vaccination efforts
front: Q: State the eradication status of Wild Poliovirus (WPV) Types 2 and 3 by 2014.
back: Type 2: Eradicated globally in 1999. Type 3: Lowest-ever levels, with the last case reported in November 2012 (Nigeria).
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 209 (Book Page): [Wild poliovirus type 2 was eradicated in 1999 and case numbers of type 3 are down to the lowest-ever levels with the last case reported in November 2012.]

category: Evaluate the effectiveness of different poliovirus vaccines (OPV and IPV) and outline the vaccination schedules
front: Q: Compare the basic composition and type of virus used in OPV versus IPV.
back:
- OPV (Sabin): Live attenuated virus (Types 1, 2, 3).
- IPV (Salk): Inactivated (killed) virus (Types 1, 2, 3).
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 212 (Book Page): [Two types of vaccines are used throughout the world; they are : 1. Inactivated (Salk) polio vaccine (IPV). 2. Oral (Sabin) polio vaccine (OPV).] ... Page 214 (Book Page): [IPV: Killed formolised virus / OPV: Live attenuated virus]

category: Evaluate the effectiveness of different poliovirus vaccines (OPV and IPV) and outline the vaccination schedules
front: Q: Why is OPV superior to IPV in achieving community-wide 'herd immunity'?
back:
- OPV induces intestinal (mucosal) IgA, preventing gut reinfection.
- Vaccine progeny is excreted in faeces, immunizing non-vaccinated contacts.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 213 (Book Page): [Intestinal infection stimulates the production of IgA secretory antibodies... effective in limiting virus transmission in the community... secondary spread occurs to household contacts.]

category: Evaluate the effectiveness of different poliovirus vaccines (OPV and IPV) and outline the vaccination schedules
front: Q: What is the primary clinical limitation of Inactivated Polio Vaccine (IPV) regarding transmission?
back:
- It induces humoral antibodies (IgG/IgM) but lacks local intestinal immunity.
- It protects the individual from paralysis but does not stop wild virus multiplication in the gut.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 212 (Book Page): [IPV... does not induce intestinal or local immunity... for the community, it offers nothing because the wild viruses can still multiply in the gut.]

category: Evaluate the effectiveness of different poliovirus vaccines (OPV and IPV) and outline the vaccination schedules
front: Q: Define the 'Zero Dose' of Oral Polio Vaccine (OPV) according to the Indian schedule.
back:
- Administered at birth or within the first 15 days of life.
- Purpose: Early protection before routine sessions begin.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 123 (Book Page): [OPV-0 At birth or as early as possible within the first 15 days... given to all children delivered in health institutions before their discharge.]

category: Evaluate the effectiveness of different poliovirus vaccines (OPV and IPV) and outline the vaccination schedules
front: Q: What is the recommended National Immunization Schedule (India) for the primary OPV series?
back:
- Three doses at 6, 10, and 14 weeks of age.
- Booster dose at 16–24 months.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 123 (Book Page): [OPV 1,2 &3 At 6 weeks, 10 weeks & 14 weeks... OPV Booster 16-24 months]

category: Evaluate the effectiveness of different poliovirus vaccines (OPV and IPV) and outline the vaccination schedules
front: Q: Why is IPV specifically indicated for immunocompromised patients instead of OPV?
back:
- OPV contains live virus, posing risks of paralytic polio in deficient immunity.
- IPV contains no living virus and is safe for these individuals.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 212 (Book Page): [Inactivated polio vaccine, because it does not contain living virus, is safe to administer (i) to persons with immune deficiency diseases.]

category: Evaluate the effectiveness of different poliovirus vaccines (OPV and IPV) and outline the vaccination schedules
front: Q: Explain the primary objective of using a sequential IPV-OPV vaccination schedule.
back:
- Reduces or prevents Vaccine-Associated Paralytic Poliomyelitis (VAPP).
- Maintains high intestinal mucosal immunity while minimizing live-virus risks.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 214 (Book Page): [Combined schedules of IPV and OPV appear to reduce or prevent VAPP while maintaining the high levels of intestinal mucosal immunity conferred by OPV.]

category: Evaluate the effectiveness of different poliovirus vaccines (OPV and IPV) and outline the vaccination schedules
front: Q: Why is IPV considered unsuitable for combating active polio epidemics?
back:
- Immunity is not rapid (requires multiple doses).
- Injections during epidemics may precipitate paralysis.
- It does not block community transmission.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 212 (Book Page): [IPV is unsuitable because : (i) immunity is not rapidly achieved... and (ii) injections are to be avoided during epidemic times as they are likely to precipitate paralysis.]

category: Evaluate the effectiveness of different poliovirus vaccines (OPV and IPV) and outline the vaccination schedules
front: Q: Differentiate the storage requirements and thermal stability of OPV versus IPV.
back:
- OPV: Highly heat-unstable; requires sub-zero storage (-20°C).
- IPV: Stable at ambient temperature; stored at 2–8°C (must not freeze).
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 214 (Book Page): [OPV... instability of the vaccine at high ambient temperatures... IPV... stable at ambient temperature, but should be refrigerated.]

category: Evaluate the effectiveness of different poliovirus vaccines (OPV and IPV) and outline the vaccination schedules
front: Q: What is the primary course schedule for Inactivated Polio Vaccine (IPV)?
back:
- 4 inoculations total.
- First 3 doses at 1–2 month intervals (starting at 6 weeks).
- 4th dose given 6–12 months after the third.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 212 (Book Page): [The primary or initial course of immunization consists of 4 inoculations. The first 3 doses are given at intervals of 1-2 months and 4th dose 6-12 months after the third dose.]

category: Discuss the historical and current global impact of poliomyelitis vaccination efforts
front: Q: How has the Global Polio Eradication Initiative impacted the number of endemic countries since 1988?
back:
* Reduction from over 125 countries (1988) to 3 (2014: Afghanistan, Pakistan, Nigeria).
* 80% of the world's population now lives in certified polio-free areas.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 208 (Book Page): [the implementation of the eradication strategies has reduced the number of polio endemic countries from more than 125 in 1988 to 3 in 2014.]

category: Discuss the historical and current global impact of poliomyelitis vaccination efforts
front: Q: Describe the pathophysiological basis and most common strain associated with Vaccine-Associated Paralytic Poliomyelitis (VAPP).
back:
* Cause: Attenuated Sabin strains revert to neurovirulence during replication.
* Primary Strain: Sabin Type 3 (associated with 60% of cases).
* Incidence: Approximately 4 cases per million birth cohort annually.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 212 (Book Page): [Vaccine-associated paralytic poliomyelitis (VAPP) is the most important of these rare adverse events... associated with Sabin 3 (60% of cases)]

category: Discuss the historical and current global impact of poliomyelitis vaccination efforts
front: Q: Contrast the local and systemic immune responses generated by IPV versus OPV.
back:
* IPV: Induces humoral antibodies (IgG/IgM) but lacks intestinal IgA immunity.
* OPV: Induces both humoral and local secretory IgA immunity in the gut.
* Impact: Only OPV prevents community spread by blocking gut reinfection.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 213 (Book Page): [IPV induces, humoral antibodies (IgM, IgG and IgA serum antibodies) but does not induce intestinal or local immunity... OPV induces both local and systemic immunity]

category: Discuss the historical and current global impact of poliomyelitis vaccination efforts
front: Q: A district reports zero AFP cases; what specific indicator evaluates if the surveillance sensitivity is sufficient?
back:
* Non-polio AFP rate: Minimum detection of 1 case per 100,000 children under 15 years annually.
* Endemic regions: Target increases to 2 per 100,000 for higher sensitivity.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 210 (Book Page): [A country's surveillance system needs to be sensitive enough to detect at least one case of AFP for every 100,000 children under 15 — even in the absence of polio.]

category: Discuss the historical and current global impact of poliomyelitis vaccination efforts
front: Q: State the standardized viral concentrations (TCID 50) for types 1, 2, and 3 in trivalent OPV.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 213 (Book Page): [The vaccine contains (i) over 3,00,000 TCID 50 of type 1 poliovirus (ii) over 1,00,000 TCID 50 of type 2 virus, and (iii) over 3,00,000 TCID 50 of type 3 virus]

category: Discuss the historical and current global impact of poliomyelitis vaccination efforts
front: Q: Define the three categories of Vaccine-Derived Polioviruses (VDPV) recognized globally.
back:
* cVDPVs: Evidence of person-to-person community transmission.
* iVDPVs: Prolonged infection in primary immunodeficiency patients.
* aVDPVs: Ambiguous isolates from sewage or unknown source individuals.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 212 (Book Page): [VDPVs are divided into three categories as (1) cVDPVs, when evidence of person-to-person transmission in the community exists; (2) immunodeficiency-associated VDPVs (iVDPVs)... and (3) ambiguous VDPVs (aVDPVs)]

category: Discuss the historical and current global impact of poliomyelitis vaccination efforts
front: Q: Why does the Global Endgame Strategy mandate replacing trivalent OPV with bivalent OPV (bOPV)?
back:
* Wild Poliovirus (WPV) Type 2 was eradicated in 1999.
* The Type 2 Sabin component is the primary cause of cVDPV outbreaks.
* Switch eliminates Type 2 risk while maintaining protection against WPV 1 and 3.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 209 (Book Page): [As wild poliovirus type 2 was eradicated in 1999, and the main cause of VDPV outbreaks is currently type 2 component of OPV, this component must be removed]

category: Discuss the historical and current global impact of poliomyelitis vaccination efforts
front: Q: For differentiating AFP causes, what three criteria define 'adequate' stool specimens?
back:
* Quantity: Two specimens collected 24-48 hours apart.
* Timing: Collected within 14 days of paralysis onset.
* Logistics: Arrive at lab via reverse cold chain (4-8°C).
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 211 (Book Page): [‘Adequate’ stool specimens are two stool specimens of sufficient quantity... collected at least 24 hours apart, within 14 days after the onset of paralysis, and arriving in the laboratory by reverse cold chain]

category: Discuss the historical and current global impact of poliomyelitis vaccination efforts
front: Q: Detail the physiological 'loop' from OPV administration to the development of local and systemic immunity.
back:
* Step 1: Epithelial infection and replication in Peyer's patches.
* Step 2: Viraemia leading to humoral IgG production.
* Step 3: Local mucosal stimulation producing secretory IgA in the gut.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 214 (Book Page): [On administration, the live vaccine strains infect intestinal epithelial cells. After replication, the virus is transported to the Peyer’s patches where a secondary multiplication with subsequent viraemia occurs... production of circulating antibodies... Intestinal infection stimulates the production of IgA secretory antibodies]

category: Discuss the historical and current global impact of poliomyelitis vaccination efforts
front: Q: When was India declared polio-free and which WHO region achieved certification simultaneously?
back:
* Date: 27th March 2014.
* Region: WHO South-East Asia Region (SEAR).
* Prerequisite: Three years without a case (last case January 2011).
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 209 (Book Page): [India has not reported any polio case since January 2011, and has been declared polio-free since 27th March 2014... certified as polio-free : ... SEAR (2014).]

category: Discuss the historical and current global impact of poliomyelitis vaccination efforts
front: Q: Which three countries remained polio-endemic as of 2014?
back:
* Afghanistan
* Pakistan
* Nigeria
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 209 (Book Page): These countries are Afghanistan, Pakistan and Nigeria.

category: Discuss the historical and current global impact of poliomyelitis vaccination efforts
front: Q: Why is OPV more effective than IPV in controlling community-level polio outbreaks?
back:
* OPV induces intestinal (mucosal) immunity
* It prevents reinfection of the gut by wild viruses
* It reduces shedding and community transmission
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 213 (Book Page): Intestinal infection stimulates the production of IgA secretory antibodies which prevent subsequent infection of the alimentary tract with wild strains of poliovirus, and thus is effective in limiting virus transmission in the community.

category: Discuss the historical and current global impact of poliomyelitis vaccination efforts
front: Q: How is Vaccine-Associated Paralytic Poliomyelitis (VAPP) differentiated from wild poliovirus infection?
back:
* They are clinically indistinguishable
* Differentiation requires laboratory analysis of poliovirus isolates
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 212 (Book Page): Cases of VAPP are clinically indistinguishable from poliomyelitis caused by WPV, but can be distinguished by laboratory analysis.

category: Discuss the historical and current global impact of poliomyelitis vaccination efforts
front: Q: What are the 'adequate' stool specimen requirements for an AFP clinical surveillance investigation?
back:
* Two specimens collected 24–48 hours apart
* Collected within 14 days of paralysis onset
* Arrival at laboratory under cold chain (4–8°C)
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 210 (Book Page): ‘Adequate’ stool specimens are two stool specimens... collected at least 24 hours apart, within 14 days after the onset of paralysis, and arriving in the laboratory by reverse cold chain.

category: Discuss the historical and current global impact of poliomyelitis vaccination efforts
front: Q: Why is the global strategy switching from trivalent OPV to bivalent OPV?
back:
* To eliminate the risk of Type 2 Vaccine-Derived Poliovirus (VDPV)
* Wild poliovirus type 2 was already eradicated in 1999
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 209 (Book Page): As wild poliovirus type 2 was eradicated in 1999... this component must be removed from the vaccine by mid-2016... replacing the trivalent OPV with bivalent OPV in all OPV using countries.

category: Discuss the historical and current global impact of poliomyelitis vaccination efforts
front: Q: What is the minimum sensitivity indicator for certification-standard non-polio AFP surveillance?
back: * Detection of at least 1 case of non-polio AFP annually per 100,000 population under 15 years
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 210 (Book Page): At least one case of non-polio AFP should be detected annually per 100,000 population aged less than 15 years.

category: Discuss the historical and current global impact of poliomyelitis vaccination efforts
front: Q: What defines the 'Pulse' strategy in the Pulse Polio Immunization (PPI) campaign?
back:
* Sudden, simultaneous mass administration of OPV
* Targets all children aged 0–5 years regardless of prior vaccination status
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 215 (Book Page): The term "pulse" has been used to describe this sudden, simultaneous, mass administration of OPV on a single day to all children 0-5 years of age, regardless to previous immunization.

category: Discuss the historical and current global impact of poliomyelitis vaccination efforts
front: Q: Which three specific neurological conditions are the primary differentials for Acute Flaccid Paralysis (AFP)?
back:
* Guillain-Barre Syndrome
* Transverse myelitis
* Traumatic neuritis
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 210 (Book Page): Polio may be difficult to differentiate from other forms of acute flaccid paralysis, such as Guillain-Barre Syndrome, transverse myelitis, or traumatic neuritis.

category: Discuss the historical and current global impact of poliomyelitis vaccination efforts
front: Q: Describe the physiological loop by which OPV prevents the spread of wild poliovirus.
back:
* Live attenuated virus infects intestinal cells
* Replicates in Peyer's patches
* Induces secretory IgA antibodies in mucosal secretions
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 213 (Book Page): After replication, the virus is transported to the Peyer’s patches... Intestinal infection stimulates the production of IgA secretory antibodies which prevent subsequent infection of the alimentary tract.

category: Discuss the historical and current global impact of poliomyelitis vaccination efforts
front: Q: Which wild poliovirus serotype was officially eradicated globally in 1999?
back: * Wild poliovirus type 2
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 209 (Book Page): wild poliovirus type 2 was eradicated in 1999.

category: Evaluate the effectiveness of different poliovirus vaccines (OPV and IPV) and outline the vaccination schedules
front: Q: Contrast the viral state and administration route of OPV versus IPV.
back:
- OPV (Sabin): Live attenuated virus; administered orally.
- IPV (Salk): Killed/Inactivated virus; administered via IM or SC injection.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 214 (Book Page): [Table 1: IPV (Salk type) / OPV (Sabin type): 1. Killed formolised virus / Live attenuated virus. 2. Given subcutaneously or IM / Given orally.]

category: Evaluate the effectiveness of different poliovirus vaccines (OPV and IPV) and outline the vaccination schedules
front: Q: Why is OPV superior to IPV in blocking wild poliovirus transmission?
back:
- OPV induces intestinal IgA (local mucosal immunity).
- Blocks wild virus replication in the gut.
- IPV only induces humoral IgG, preventing paralysis but not gut reinfection.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 213 (Book Page): [Intestinal infection stimulates the production of IgA secretory antibodies which prevent subsequent infection of the alimentary tract with wild strains of poliovirus, and thus is effective in limiting virus transmission in the community.]

category: Evaluate the effectiveness of different poliovirus vaccines (OPV and IPV) and outline the vaccination schedules
front: Q: Which polio vaccine is indicated for use during an active epidemic?
back:
- OPV (Sabin).
- Rationale: Single dose provides rapid immunity and prevents community spread via intestinal barrier induction.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 214 (Book Page): [Table 1: 5. Not useful in controlling epidemics / Can be effectively used in controlling epidemics. Even a single dose elicits substantial immunity.]

category: Evaluate the effectiveness of different poliovirus vaccines (OPV and IPV) and outline the vaccination schedules
front: Q: What is the mandatory vaccination choice for children with primary immunodeficiencies?
back:
- IPV (Inactivated Polio Vaccine).
- OPV is contraindicated due to the risk of Vaccine-Associated Paralytic Poliomyelitis (VAPP).
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 212 (Book Page): [Inactivated polio vaccine, because it does not contain living virus, is safe to administer (i) to persons with immune deficiency diseases.]

category: Evaluate the effectiveness of different poliovirus vaccines (OPV and IPV) and outline the vaccination schedules
front: Q: Describe the chemical process used to produce IPV.
back:
- Viral strains (Mahoney, MEF-1, Saukett) are grown in cell cultures.
- Harvested components are inactivated using formaldehyde.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 212 (Book Page): [Harvested viral components are inactivated with formaldehyde.]

category: Evaluate the effectiveness of different poliovirus vaccines (OPV and IPV) and outline the vaccination schedules
front: Q: Outline the National Immunization Schedule (NIS) for the primary OPV series in infants.
back:
- OPV-0: Birth (within 15 days).
- OPV 1, 2, 3: 6 weeks, 10 weeks, and 14 weeks of age.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 129 (Book Page): [Table 43: OPV-0: At birth or as early as possible within the first 15 days. OPV 1,2 & 3: At 6 weeks, 10 weeks & 14 weeks.]

category: Evaluate the effectiveness of different poliovirus vaccines (OPV and IPV) and outline the vaccination schedules
front: Q: Explain how OPV achieves 'Herd Immunity' in a community.
back:
- Vaccinees excrete the live attenuated virus progeny in faeces.
- This secondary spread immunizes unvaccinated household and community contacts.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 213 (Book Page): [The vaccine progeny is excreted in the faeces and secondary spread occurs to household contacts and susceptible contacts in the community. Non-immunized persons may therefore, be immunized.]

category: Evaluate the effectiveness of different poliovirus vaccines (OPV and IPV) and outline the vaccination schedules
front: Q: What defines Vaccine-Associated Paralytic Poliomyelitis (VAPP) compared to Wild Poliovirus (WPV)?
back:
- Clinically: Indistinguishable (both cause paralysis).
- Laboratory: Distinguished by genetic analysis (rRT-PCR) of the virus isolate.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 212 (Book Page): [Cases of VAPP are clinically indistinguishable from poliomyelitis caused by WPV, but can be distinguished by laboratory analysis.]

category: Evaluate the effectiveness of different poliovirus vaccines (OPV and IPV) and outline the vaccination schedules
front: Q: Contrast the storage temperature requirements for OPV and IPV.
back:
- OPV: Sub-zero/Freezing (highly heat-labile).
- IPV: 2°C to 8°C (Refrigerated); must NEVER be frozen.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 212 (Book Page): [IPV... Freezing should be avoided as it could diminish potency.] Page 214 (Book Page): [OPV... Requires to be stored and transported at sub-zero temperatures.]

category: Evaluate the effectiveness of different poliovirus vaccines (OPV and IPV) and outline the vaccination schedules
front: Q: When is the recommended booster dose for OPV in the NIS?
back: - 16 to 24 months of age.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 129 (Book Page): [Table 43: OPV Booster: 16-24 months.]

category: Evaluate the effectiveness of different poliovirus vaccines (OPV and IPV) and outline the vaccination schedules
front: Q: Compare the types of immunity induced by OPV versus IPV.
back:
• OPV: Induces both humoral (IgG) and local intestinal (secretory IgA) immunity.
• IPV: Induces only humoral immunity; lacks local intestinal protection.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 213 (Book Page): [OPV] induces both local and systemic immunity... [IPV] induces, humoral antibodies (IgM, IgG and IgA serum antibodies) but does not induce intestinal or local immunity.

category: Evaluate the effectiveness of different poliovirus vaccines (OPV and IPV) and outline the vaccination schedules
front: Q: Why is OPV specifically effective in controlling polio epidemics compared to IPV?
back:
• Rapidly induces substantial immunity.
• Prevents intestinal reinfection by wild virus.
• Herd immunity: Vaccinees excrete attenuated virus, immunizing contacts.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 214 (Book Page): [OPV] Can be effectively used in controlling epidemics. Even a single dose elicits substantial immunity... [IPV] Not useful in controlling epidemics.

category: Evaluate the effectiveness of different poliovirus vaccines (OPV and IPV) and outline the vaccination schedules
front: Q: What is the primary community-level drawback of Inactivated Polio Vaccine (IPV)?
back:
• Does not prevent wild virus multiplication in the gut.
• Vaccinated individuals can still act as sources of infection to others.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 213 (Book Page): For the community, it [IPV] offers nothing because the wild viruses can still multiply in the gut and be a source of infection to others.

category: Evaluate the effectiveness of different poliovirus vaccines (OPV and IPV) and outline the vaccination schedules
front: Q: Outline the National Immunization Schedule (NIS) for primary OPV administration in infants.
back:
• Zero dose: At birth (within 15 days).
• Primary series: 3 doses at 6, 10, and 14 weeks.
• Booster: 16–24 months.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 123 (Book Page): OPV-0: At birth or as early as possible within the first 15 days. OPV 1,2 &3: At 6 weeks, 10 weeks & 14 weeks... OPV Booster: 16-24 months.

category: Evaluate the effectiveness of different poliovirus vaccines (OPV and IPV) and outline the vaccination schedules
front: Q: Define Vaccine-Associated Paralytic Poliomyelitis (VAPP) and its primary cause.
back:
• Rare paralysis clinically indistinguishable from wild polio.
• Occurs in OPV recipients or contacts.
• Most associated with Sabin Type 3 strain (60%).
