citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 212 (Book Page): VAPP is the most important of these rare adverse events... most frequently associated with Sabin 3 (60% of cases), followed by Sabin 2 and Sabin 1.

category: Evaluate the effectiveness of different poliovirus vaccines (OPV and IPV) and outline the vaccination schedules
front: Q: A child with primary immunodeficiency requires polio vaccination. Which vaccine is indicated?
back:
• Inactivated Polio Vaccine (IPV) is mandatory.
• OPV is contraindicated due to the risk of prolonged excretion or VAPP.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 213 (Book Page): [IPV] is safe to administer (i) to persons with immune deficiency diseases... [Page 212 (Book Page)] OPV use will be discontinued worldwide... to limit the emergence of VDPVs.

category: Evaluate the effectiveness of different poliovirus vaccines (OPV and IPV) and outline the vaccination schedules
front: Q: What defines the 'Pulse' in the Pulse Polio Immunization (PPI) strategy?
back:
• Sudden, simultaneous mass administration of OPV.
• Targeted to all children 0–5 years on a single day.
• Supplements, rather than replaces, routine doses.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 216 (Book Page): The term "pulse" has been used to describe this sudden, simultaneous, mass administration of OPV on a single day to all children 0-5 years of age, regardless to previous immunization.

category: Evaluate the effectiveness of different poliovirus vaccines (OPV and IPV) and outline the vaccination schedules
front: Q: Contrast the storage requirements for OPV and IPV.
back:
• OPV: Must be frozen; extremely heat-labile.
• IPV: Refrigerated (2–8°C); stable at ambient temperature but loses potency if frozen.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 214 (Book Page): [OPV] Requires to be stored and transported at sub-zero temperatures... [Page 213 (Book Page)] IPV... should be refrigerated... Freezing should be avoided as it could diminish potency.

category: Evaluate the effectiveness of different poliovirus vaccines (OPV and IPV) and outline the vaccination schedules
front: Q: Explain the benefit of a sequential IPV-OPV vaccination schedule.
back:
• IPV doses prevent VAPP by providing early humoral protection.
• Subsequent OPV doses ensure high intestinal mucosal immunity for community protection.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 214 (Book Page): Combined schedules of IPV and OPV appear to reduce or prevent VAPP while maintaining the high levels of intestinal mucosal immunity conferred by OPV.

category: Evaluate the effectiveness of different poliovirus vaccines (OPV and IPV) and outline the vaccination schedules
front: Q: What is the correct mode and dose for OPV administration?
back:
• Dose: 2 drops administered orally.
• Procedure: Use dropper onto the child's tongue; repeat if the child spits.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 213 (Book Page): The dose is 2 drops or as stated on the label... Let the drops fall from the dropper onto the child’s tongue. Repeat the process if the child spits out the vaccine.

category: Evaluate the effectiveness of different poliovirus vaccines (OPV and IPV) and outline the vaccination schedules
front: Q: What is the primary epidemiological advantage of Oral Polio Vaccine (OPV) over Inactivated Polio Vaccine (IPV)?
back: OPV induces intestinal/mucosal immunity (secretory IgA). This prevents the replication and shedding of wild poliovirus, thus interrupting community transmission.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 213 (Book Page): Intestinal infection stimulates the production of IgA secretory antibodies which prevent subsequent infection of the alimentary tract with wild strains of poliovirus, and thus is effective in limiting virus transmission in the community.

category: Evaluate the effectiveness of different poliovirus vaccines (OPV and IPV) and outline the vaccination schedules
front: Q: Why is Inactivated Polio Vaccine (IPV) alone insufficient for achieving global community eradication?
back: IPV induces humoral antibodies (IgG) that prevent paralysis but does not induce local intestinal immunity. Wild virus can still multiply in the gut and spread to others.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 213 (Book Page): For the community, it [IPV] offers nothing because the wild viruses can still multiply in the gut and be a source of infection to others.

category: Evaluate the effectiveness of different poliovirus vaccines (OPV and IPV) and outline the vaccination schedules
front: Q: Define the 'Zero Dose' of OPV and its timing in the National Immunization Schedule.
back: A dose given at birth or within the first 15 days of life. It provides early protection in endemic areas before the primary series begins.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 123 (Book Page): OPV-0: At birth or as early as possible within the first 15 days. Page 213 (Book Page): It is recommended that a dose of OPV (zero-dose) is required to be given to all children delivered in health institutions.

category: Evaluate the effectiveness of different poliovirus vaccines (OPV and IPV) and outline the vaccination schedules
front: Q: In an immunodeficient child, which polio vaccine is strictly contraindicated and why?
back: OPV is contraindicated. There is a risk of prolonged viral replication/excretion (iVDPV) and development of Vaccine-Associated Paralytic Polio (VAPP).
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 213 (Book Page): Inactivated polio vaccine... is safe to administer (i) to persons with immune deficiency diseases. Page 212 (Book Page): VDPVs are divided into... immunodeficiency-associated VDPVs (iVDPVs), which are isolates from persons with primary immunodeficiencies.

category: Evaluate the effectiveness of different poliovirus vaccines (OPV and IPV) and outline the vaccination schedules
front: Q: What is the physiological rationale for a sequential IPV-OPV vaccination schedule?
back: 1–2 doses of IPV provide systemic immunity to prevent VAPP. Subsequent OPV doses provide the necessary intestinal mucosal immunity for community protection.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 214 (Book Page): Combined schedules of IPV and OPV appear to reduce or prevent VAPP while maintaining the high levels of intestinal mucosal immunity conferred by OPV.

category: Evaluate the effectiveness of different poliovirus vaccines (OPV and IPV) and outline the vaccination schedules
front: Q: List the primary series schedule for OPV doses 1, 2, and 3 according to the EPI.
back: Doses are given at 6 weeks, 10 weeks, and 14 weeks. The minimum interval between doses is 4 weeks.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 123 (Book Page): OPV 1, 2 & 3: At 6 weeks, 10 weeks & 14 weeks. Note: Interval between 2 doses of... OPV... should not be less than one month.

category: Evaluate the effectiveness of different poliovirus vaccines (OPV and IPV) and outline the vaccination schedules
front: Q: Why is IPV considered ineffective for combating an active polio epidemic?
back: 1. Immunity is slow (requires multiple doses). 2. Injections during epidemics can precipitate paralysis. 3. It does not stop viral shedding in stools.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 213 (Book Page): IPV is unsuitable because: (i) immunity is not rapidly achieved... and (ii) injections are to be avoided during epidemic times as they are likely to precipitate paralysis.

category: Evaluate the effectiveness of different poliovirus vaccines (OPV and IPV) and outline the vaccination schedules
front: Q: Contrast the storage requirements for OPV and IPV regarding temperature stability.
back: OPV is highly heat-sensitive and must be stored at sub-zero temperatures (-20°C). IPV is relatively stable at 2–8°C but must not be frozen.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 214 (Book Page): [OPV] Requires to be stored and transported at sub-zero temperatures... [IPV] Does not require stringent conditions... has a longer shelf-life.

category: Evaluate the effectiveness of different poliovirus vaccines (OPV and IPV) and outline the vaccination schedules
front: Q: What is the 'Switch' in the Polio Endgame Strategic Plan (2013-2018)?
back: Replacing Trivalent OPV (tOPV) with Bivalent OPV (bOPV) and introducing IPV. This removes the Type 2 component, which is the main cause of VDPV outbreaks.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 210 (Book Page): As wild poliovirus type 2 was eradicated in 1999... this component must be removed... replacing the trivalent OPV with bivalent OPV.

category: Evaluate the effectiveness of different poliovirus vaccines (OPV and IPV) and outline the vaccination schedules
front: Q: What defines 'Pulse Polio' immunization compared to routine scheduling?
back: Mass administration of OPV on a single day to all children 0–5 years, regardless of previous status. These are extra doses to supplement routine coverage.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 216 (Book Page): The term "pulse" has been used to describe this sudden, simultaneous, mass administration of OPV on a single day... supplement, and do not replace the doses received during routine immunization.

category: Evaluate the effectiveness of different poliovirus vaccines (OPV and IPV) and outline the vaccination schedules
front: Q: Which poliovirus vaccine induces both systemic humoral and local intestinal immunity?
back: Oral Polio Vaccine (OPV). It stimulates serum IgG and secretory IgA in the gut, preventing both paralysis and intestinal reinfection.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 213 (Book Page): 'OPV induces both local and systemic immunity... Intestinal infection stimulates the production of IgA secretory antibodies which prevent subsequent infection of the alimentary tract.'

category: Evaluate the effectiveness of different poliovirus vaccines (OPV and IPV) and outline the vaccination schedules
front: Q: Explain the primary epidemiological disadvantage of Inactivated Polio Vaccine (IPV) regarding transmission.
back: IPV induces humoral IgG but lacks intestinal IgA. Vaccinated individuals are protected from paralysis but can still shed wild virus from the gut.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 213 (Book Page): 'IPV induces humoral antibodies... but does not induce intestinal or local immunity... the wild viruses can still multiply in the gut and be a source of infection to others.'

category: Evaluate the effectiveness of different poliovirus vaccines (OPV and IPV) and outline the vaccination schedules
front: Q: What is the clinical purpose of the 'Zero Dose' of OPV administered at birth?
back: To establish early intestinal immunity and overcome interference from maternal antibodies before the infant is exposed to possible infection.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 213 (Book Page): 'It is recommended that a dose of OPV (zero-dose) is required to be given to all children delivered in health institutions before their discharge.'

category: Evaluate the effectiveness of different poliovirus vaccines (OPV and IPV) and outline the vaccination schedules
front: Q: A child with active diarrhea receives an OPV dose. How is this managed in the schedule?
back: Give the dose but do not count it towards the schedule. Instruct the mother to return in 4 weeks for a replacement dose.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 129 (Book Page): 'If the child has diarrhoea, give a dose of OPV, but do not count the dose and ask the mother to return in 4 weeks for the missing dose.'

category: Evaluate the effectiveness of different poliovirus vaccines (OPV and IPV) and outline the vaccination schedules
front: Q: Why is OPV considered the preparation of choice for controlling polio epidemics?
back: 1. Rapid immunity (even single dose). 2. Secondary spread to unimmunized contacts (herd immunity). 3. Prevents gut reinfection, breaking transmission chains.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 214 (Book Page): 'Useful in controlling epidemics... the vaccinee excretes the virus and so infects others who are also immunized thereby... virtually eliminates wild polio strains.'

category: Evaluate the effectiveness of different poliovirus vaccines (OPV and IPV) and outline the vaccination schedules
front: Q: Outline the National Immunization Schedule (NIS) for primary OPV administration in infants.
back: 1. At Birth (Zero dose). 2. 6 Weeks (Dose 1). 3. 10 Weeks (Dose 2). 4. 14 Weeks (Dose 3). 5. 16-24 Months (Booster).
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 129 (Book Page): 'OPV-0: At birth... OPV 1,2 & 3: At 6 weeks, 10 weeks & 14 weeks... OPV Booster: 16-24 months.'

category: Evaluate the effectiveness of different poliovirus vaccines (OPV and IPV) and outline the vaccination schedules
front: Q: Define Vaccine-Associated Paralytic Poliomyelitis (VAPP) and its typical association.
back: Rare paralysis caused by OPV strains (primarily Sabin 3). Estimated incidence is ~4 cases per 1,000,000 birth cohort per year.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 212 (Book Page): 'Vaccine-associated paralytic poliomyelitis (VAPP)... incidence... 4 cases/1,000,000 birth cohort per year... most frequently associated with Sabin 3.'

category: Evaluate the effectiveness of different poliovirus vaccines (OPV and IPV) and outline the vaccination schedules
front: Q: Which polio vaccine is mandatory for immunodeficient patients and why?
back: IPV (Salk). It contains inactivated virus and is safe. OPV contains live attenuated virus and carries risks for immunocompromised persons.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 213 (Book Page): 'Inactivated polio vaccine, because it does not contain living virus, is safe to administer to persons with immune deficiency diseases.'

category: Evaluate the effectiveness of different poliovirus vaccines (OPV and IPV) and outline the vaccination schedules
front: Q: Explain the 'Pulse' concept in Pulse Polio Immunization (PPI) campaigns.
back: Simultaneous mass administration of extra OPV doses to all children 0-5 years on a single day, regardless of prior vaccination status.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 216 (Book Page): 'The term "pulse" has been used to describe this sudden, simultaneous, mass administration of OPV on a single day to all children 0-5 years of age, regardless to previous immunization.'

category: Evaluate the effectiveness of different poliovirus vaccines (OPV and IPV) and outline the vaccination schedules
front: Q: State the storage and transport requirements for maintaining OPV potency.
back: Must be kept frozen during long-term storage and transported at sub-zero temperatures. It is highly unstable at ambient temperatures.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 214 (Book Page): 'Instability of the vaccine at high ambient temperatures. The vaccine has to be kept frozen during storage, and kept cold during transportation... Requires to be stored and transported at sub-zero temperatures.'

category: Discuss community health strategies for poliovirus surveillance, outbreak response, and vaccination campaigns
front: Q: Which three countries remained endemic for wild poliovirus as of 2014?
back:
The three remaining endemic countries are:
- Afghanistan
- Pakistan
- Nigeria
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 209 (Book Page): [These countries are Afghanistan, Pakistan and Nigeria.]

category: Discuss community health strategies for poliovirus surveillance, outbreak response, and vaccination campaigns
front: Q: Explain why Oral Polio Vaccine (OPV) is superior to IPV for community outbreak control.
back:
- Induces intestinal (local) IgA immunity
- Limits wild virus transmission/shedding
- Provides secondary spread to unimmunized contacts (herd effect)
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 214 (Book Page): [OPV induces both local and systemic immunity... Intestinal infection stimulates the production of IgA secretory antibodies which prevent subsequent infection of the alimentary tract... thus is effective in limiting virus transmission in the community.]

category: Discuss community health strategies for poliovirus surveillance, outbreak response, and vaccination campaigns
front: Q: What defines 'adequate' stool specimens for Acute Flaccid Paralysis (AFP) surveillance?
back:
- Two specimens collected 24–48 hours apart
- Collected within 14 days of paralysis onset
- Arrive at lab in reverse cold chain (4–8°C)
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 210 (Book Page): [To test for polio, faecal specimens are analyzed... two specimens — taken 24-48 hours apart are required... highest concentrations... found during the first two weeks after onset.]

category: Discuss community health strategies for poliovirus surveillance, outbreak response, and vaccination campaigns
front: Q: In a polio-free region, how should the notification of a single case of AFP be managed?
back:
- Treat as a public health emergency/epidemic
- Immediate epidemiological investigation within 48 hours
- Active search for additional cases in the locality
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 215 (Book Page): [The occurrence of a single case of polio is now considered as an epidemic, and should prompt an immediate epidemiological investigation... usually within 48 hours of notification.]

category: Discuss community health strategies for poliovirus surveillance, outbreak response, and vaccination campaigns
front: Q: Why is Inactivated Polio Vaccine (IPV) being introduced globally into routine schedules using OPV?
back:
- Mitigates risk of Vaccine-Derived Poliovirus (VDPV)
- Prevents Vaccine-Associated Paralytic Polio (VAPP)
- Prepares for the eventual total withdrawal of OPV
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 212 (Book Page): [Because of these risks of emergence of vaccine-derived polioviruses, OPV use will be discontinued worldwide... inactivated polio vaccine (IPV) will replace OPV.]

category: Discuss community health strategies for poliovirus surveillance, outbreak response, and vaccination campaigns
front: Q: What is the key performance indicator for the sensitivity of an AFP surveillance system?
back:
- Detection of at least 1 case of non-polio AFP annually
- Per 100,000 children aged under 15 years
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 210 (Book Page): [A country's surveillance system needs to be sensitive enough to detect at least one case of AFP for every 100,000 children under 15 — even in the absence of polio.]

category: Discuss community health strategies for poliovirus surveillance, outbreak response, and vaccination campaigns
front: Q: Define the 'Pulse' strategy in Pulse Polio Immunization (PPI) campaigns.
back:
- Simultaneous mass administration of OPV
- Targeted at all children 0–5 years on a single day
- Regardless of previous immunization status
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 216 (Book Page): [The term "pulse" has been used to describe this sudden, simultaneous, mass administration of OPV on a single day to all children 0-5 years of age, regardless to previous immunization.]

category: Discuss community health strategies for poliovirus surveillance, outbreak response, and vaccination campaigns
front: Q: Distinguish Vaccine-Associated Paralytic Polio (VAPP) from Vaccine-Derived Poliovirus (VDPV).
back:
- VAPP: Sporadic adverse event in recipient/contact; no community spread
- VDPV: Mutated strain with genetic properties of prolonged replication/transmission; can cause outbreaks (cVDPV)
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 212 (Book Page): [VAPP occurs in both OPV recipients and their unimmunized contacts... VDPVs resemble WPVs biologically... have genetic properties consistent with prolonged replication or transmission.]

category: Discuss community health strategies for poliovirus surveillance, outbreak response, and vaccination campaigns
front: Q: What is the role of environmental surveillance in the Polio Eradication Initiative?
back:
- Testing sewage for poliovirus
- Detects wild poliovirus or VDPV circulation
- Identifies silent transmission in the absence of clinical paralysis cases
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 212 (Book Page): [Environmental surveillance involves testing sewage... Environmental surveillance often confirms wild poliovirus infections in the absence of cases of paralysis.]

category: Discuss community health strategies for poliovirus surveillance, outbreak response, and vaccination campaigns
front: Q: What is the 'Zero Dose' in the polio immunization schedule?
back:
- OPV dose given at birth
- Administered within first 15 days
- Required for infants delivered in health institutions before discharge
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 213 (Book Page): [It is recommended that a dose of OPV (zero-dose) is required to be given to all children delivered in health institutions before their discharge from the hospital... within the first 15 days.]

category: Evaluate the effectiveness of different poliovirus vaccines (OPV and IPV) and outline the vaccination schedules
front: Q: Compare the types of immunity induced by OPV versus IPV.
back:
- OPV: Induces both systemic (IgG) and local intestinal (IgA) immunity.
- IPV: Induces systemic (IgG) immunity only; no intestinal immunity.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 213 (Book Page): IPV induces, humoral antibodies (IgM, IgG and IgA serum antibodies) but does not induce intestinal or local immunity... Thus OPV induces both local and systemic immunity.

category: Evaluate the effectiveness of different poliovirus vaccines (OPV and IPV) and outline the vaccination schedules
front: Q: Why is OPV preferred over IPV for controlling polio epidemics?
back:
- Induces intestinal IgA to prevent gut reinfection/viral shedding.
- Excreted vaccine virus provides 'herd immunity' to household contacts.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 214 (Book Page): OPV prevents not only paralysis, but also intestinal reinfection. Can be effectively used in controlling epidemics... the vaccinee excretes the virus and so infects others who are also immunized.

category: Evaluate the effectiveness of different poliovirus vaccines (OPV and IPV) and outline the vaccination schedules
front: Q: Outline the National Immunization Schedule (NIS) for OPV administration.
back:
- Birth (Zero dose): Within 15 days.
- Primary Doses: 6, 10, and 14 weeks.
- Booster: 16–24 months.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 129 (Book Page): OPV-0 At birth... OPV 1,2 & 3 At 6 weeks, 10 weeks & 14 weeks... OPV Booster 16-24 months.

category: Evaluate the effectiveness of different poliovirus vaccines (OPV and IPV) and outline the vaccination schedules
front: Q: Which polio vaccine is safe for immunocompromised patients and why?
back:
- IPV (Salk type).
- It contains inactivated (killed) virus, eliminating the risk of paralysis or vaccine-derived outbreaks.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 213 (Book Page): Inactivated polio vaccine, because it does not contain living virus, is safe to administer (i) to persons with immune deficiency diseases.

category: Evaluate the effectiveness of different poliovirus vaccines (OPV and IPV) and outline the vaccination schedules
front: Q: What is the primary clinical rationale for the sequential IPV-OPV schedule?
back:
- Prevents Vaccine-Associated Paralytic Poliomyelitis (VAPP) through initial IPV.
- Maintains high intestinal immunity through subsequent OPV doses.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 214 (Book Page): Combined schedules of IPV and OPV appear to reduce or prevent VAPP while maintaining the high levels of intestinal mucosal immunity conferred by OPV.

category: Evaluate the effectiveness of different poliovirus vaccines (OPV and IPV) and outline the vaccination schedules
front: Q: Contrast the storage requirements and temperature sensitivity of OPV and IPV.
back:
- OPV: Heat-unstable; must be stored/transported at sub-zero temperatures.
- IPV: More stable; store at 2–8°C; must NEVER be frozen.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 214 (Book Page): IPV... Does not require stringent conditions... OPV... Requires to be stored and transported at sub-zero temperatures, unless stabilized.

category: Evaluate the effectiveness of different poliovirus vaccines (OPV and IPV) and outline the vaccination schedules
front: Q: Define the 'Pulse' strategy in Pulse Polio Immunization (PPI).
back:
- Sudden, simultaneous mass administration of OPV.
- Targets all children 0–5 years on a single day, regardless of previous status.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 216 (Book Page): The term 'pulse' has been used to describe this sudden, simultaneous, mass administration of OPV on a single day to all children 0-5 years of age, regardless to previous immunization.

category: Evaluate the effectiveness of different poliovirus vaccines (OPV and IPV) and outline the vaccination schedules
front: Q: What is the 'Zero Dose' of OPV and why is it administered?
back:
- Dose given at birth or within the first 15 days.
- Aims to induce early intestinal immunity before the infant is exposed to infection.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 213 (Book Page): it is recommended that a dose of OPV (zero-dose) is required to be given to all children delivered in health institutions before their discharge... to avoid infection.

category: Evaluate the effectiveness of different poliovirus vaccines (OPV and IPV) and outline the vaccination schedules
front: Q: Scenario: A child in a polio-free region develops paralysis after OPV. Identify the likely adverse event.
back:
- Vaccine-Associated Paralytic Poliomyelitis (VAPP).
- Occurs rarely due to residual neurovirulence or reversion of the Sabin strain.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 212 (Book Page): Vaccine-associated paralytic poliomyelitis (VAPP) is the most important of these rare adverse events. Cases of VAPP are clinically indistinguishable from poliomyelitis caused by WPV.

category: Evaluate the effectiveness of different poliovirus vaccines (OPV and IPV) and outline the vaccination schedules
front: Q: Why is IPV considered ineffective for global polio eradication as a standalone tool?
back:
- It does not prevent gut reinfection.
- Wild poliovirus can still multiply in the gut and spread to the community via faeces.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 213 (Book Page): for the community, it [IPV] offers nothing because the wild viruses can still multiply in the gut and be a source of infection to others. This is a major drawback.

category: Evaluate the effectiveness of different poliovirus vaccines (OPV and IPV) and outline the vaccination schedules
front: Distinguish between OPV and IPV based on the type of immunity induced.
back: OPV: Induces both humoral (systemic) and intestinal (local/IgA) immunity. IPV: Induces only humoral (IgM, IgG, IgA serum) immunity without local intestinal immunity.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 213 (Book Page): [OPV] induces both local and systemic immunity... [IPV] induces, humoral antibodies (IgM, IgG and IgA serum antibodies) but does not induce intestinal or local immunity

category: Evaluate the effectiveness of different poliovirus vaccines (OPV and IPV) and outline the vaccination schedules
front: Explain the physiological mechanism by which OPV limits the transmission of wild poliovirus in communities.
back: Stimulates intestinal IgA secretory antibodies. This prevents subsequent infection of the alimentary tract and stops the shedding of wild virus in feces.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 213 (Book Page): Intestinal infection stimulates the production of IgA secretory antibodies which prevent subsequent infection of the alimentary tract with wild strains of poliovirus, and thus is effective in limiting virus transmission in the community.

category: Evaluate the effectiveness of different poliovirus vaccines (OPV and IPV) and outline the vaccination schedules
front: Compare the effectiveness of OPV and IPV in controlling a polio epidemic.
back: OPV: Highly effective due to rapid immunity and secondary spread to contacts (herd immunity). IPV: Unsuitable because immunity is slow (requires multiple doses) and does not prevent gut reinfection.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 214 (Book Page): [OPV] Useful in controlling epidemics... [IPV] is unsuitable because : (i) immunity is not rapidly achieved, as more than one dose is required to induce immunity, and (ii) injections are to be avoided during epidemic times

category: Evaluate the effectiveness of different poliovirus vaccines (OPV and IPV) and outline the vaccination schedules
front: A child diagnosed with a primary immunodeficiency needs polio vaccination. Which vaccine is contraindicated and why?
back: OPV is contraindicated. It contains live attenuated virus which can cause Vaccine-Associated Paralytic Poliomyelitis (VAPP) or persistent excretion in immunocompromised patients.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 213 (Book Page): Inactivated polio vaccine, because it does not contain living virus, is safe to administer (i) to persons with immune deficiency diseases

category: Evaluate the effectiveness of different poliovirus vaccines (OPV and IPV) and outline the vaccination schedules
front: What is the primary pharmacological storage requirement for OPV to ensure its effectiveness?
back: OPV is highly thermolabile; it must be kept frozen at sub-zero temperatures (usually -20°C) during storage and cold during transportation to prevent loss of potency.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 214 (Book Page): A primary problem is the instability of the vaccine at high ambient temperatures. The vaccine has to be kept frozen during storage, and kept cold during transportation

category: Evaluate the effectiveness of different poliovirus vaccines (OPV and IPV) and outline the vaccination schedules
front: Define the 'Zero Dose' of OPV and its timing in the National Immunization Schedule.
back: OPV-0 is the dose administered at birth (or within the first 15 days). It provides early protection before the primary series begins at 6 weeks.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 123 (Book Page): OPV-0: At birth or as early as possible within the first 15 days.

category: Evaluate the effectiveness of different poliovirus vaccines (OPV and IPV) and outline the vaccination schedules
front: Explain the concept of 'herd immunity' achieved through OPV administration.
back: The vaccine virus is excreted in the feces of vaccinees, spreading to and immunizing non-vaccinated household and community contacts.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 213 (Book Page): The vaccine progeny is excreted in the faeces and secondary spread occurs to household contacts and susceptible contacts in the community. Non-immunized persons may therefore, be immunized.

category: Evaluate the effectiveness of different poliovirus vaccines (OPV and IPV) and outline the vaccination schedules
front: Case: A community with low vaccine coverage reports a cluster of paralysis cases genetically linked to the Sabin strain. Identify this phenomenon.
back: Vaccine-Derived Poliovirus (cVDPV). It occurs when attenuated strains replicate in under-immunized populations, regaining neurovirulence and causing outbreaks.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 212 (Book Page): cVDPVs, when evidence of person-to-person transmission in the community exists... [they] pose the same public health threat as WPVs and require the same control measures.

category: Evaluate the effectiveness of different poliovirus vaccines (OPV and IPV) and outline the vaccination schedules
front: Describe the standard primary vaccination schedule for OPV and its boosters in infants.
back: Primary: Three doses at 6, 10, and 14 weeks. Booster: One dose at 16–24 months of age.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 123 (Book Page): OPV 1, 2 & 3 At 6 weeks, 10 weeks & 14 weeks... OPV Booster 16-24 months

category: Evaluate the effectiveness of different poliovirus vaccines (OPV and IPV) and outline the vaccination schedules
front: What is the recommended route and dosage for the administration of trivalent OPV?
back: Route: Oral. Dosage: 2 drops administered directly onto the child's tongue.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 123 (Book Page): 2 drops Oral Oral... Let the drops fall from the dropper onto the child’s tongue.

category: Evaluate the effectiveness of different poliovirus vaccines (OPV and IPV) and outline the vaccination schedules
front: Q: Outline the National Immunization Schedule (NIS) for the primary series of OPV in infants.
back: 1. OPV-0: At birth (within 15 days). 2. OPV-1: 6 weeks. 3. OPV-2: 10 weeks. 4. OPV-3: 14 weeks. 5. OPV Booster: 16–24 months.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 129 (Book Page): [OPV-0 At birth or as early as possible within the first 15 days... OPV 1,2 & 3 At 6 weeks, 10 weeks & 14 weeks... OPV Booster 16-24 months]

category: Evaluate the effectiveness of different poliovirus vaccines (OPV and IPV) and outline the vaccination schedules
front: Q: How does the immunological mechanism of OPV prevent the community spread of wild poliovirus?
back: OPV infects intestinal cells, stimulating secretory IgA production. This local intestinal immunity prevents wild virus multiplication and excretion in the gut, stopping transmission.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 213 (Book Page): [Intestinal infection stimulates the production of IgA secretory antibodies which prevent subsequent infection of the alimentary tract with wild strains of poliovirus, and thus is effective in limiting virus transmission in the community.]

category: Evaluate the effectiveness of different poliovirus vaccines (OPV and IPV) and outline the vaccination schedules
front: Q: Contrast the types of immunity induced by Inactivated Polio Vaccine (IPV) versus Oral Polio Vaccine (OPV).
back: 1. IPV: Humoral immunity (Serum IgG) only; no intestinal immunity. 2. OPV: Both humoral (IgG) and local intestinal immunity (IgA).
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 214 (Book Page): [Table 1: IPV (Salk type) induces circulating antibody, but no local (intestinal) immunity / OPV (Sabin type) Immunity is both humoral and intestinal.]

category: Evaluate the effectiveness of different poliovirus vaccines (OPV and IPV) and outline the vaccination schedules
front: Q: A child with primary immunodeficiency requires polio vaccination. Which vaccine is indicated and why?
back: IPV is indicated. OPV is contraindicated as it contains live virus which may cause prolonged excretion or Vaccine-Associated Paralytic Poliomyelitis (VAPP) in immunocompromised hosts.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 213 (Book Page): [Inactivated polio vaccine, because it does not contain living virus, is safe to administer (i) to persons with immune deficiency diseases]

category: Evaluate the effectiveness of different poliovirus vaccines (OPV and IPV) and outline the vaccination schedules
front: Q: What is the correct dosage and administration technique for the Oral Polio Vaccine (OPV)?
back: Dose: 2 drops orally. Technique: Tilt head back, squeeze cheeks to open mouth, and let drops fall from the dropper onto the tongue.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 213 (Book Page): [The dose is 2 drops... Tilt the child’s back, and gently squeeze the cheeks or pinch the nose to make the mouth open. Let the drops fall from the dropper onto the child’s tongue.]

category: Evaluate the effectiveness of different poliovirus vaccines (OPV and IPV) and outline the vaccination schedules
front: Q: Define the 'Zero Dose' of OPV and its specific clinical purpose.
back: The dose given at birth (within 15 days). Purpose: To provide early intestinal immunity before the child is exposed to infection in the community.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 213 (Book Page): [OPV (zero-dose) is required to be given to all children delivered in health institutions before their discharge from the hospital... to avoid infection.]

category: Evaluate the effectiveness of different poliovirus vaccines (OPV and IPV) and outline the vaccination schedules
front: Q: Why is OPV specifically utilized for controlling polio epidemics rather than IPV?
back: 1. Rapid induction of immunity. 2. Single dose effectiveness. 3. Stops community transmission via intestinal immunity. 4. Easier mass administration without needles.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 214 (Book Page): [Table 1: OPV... Can be effectively used in controlling epidemics. Even a single dose elicits substantial immunity... useful in controlling epidemics]

category: Evaluate the effectiveness of different poliovirus vaccines (OPV and IPV) and outline the vaccination schedules
front: Q: How is Vaccine-Associated Paralytic Poliomyelitis (VAPP) distinguished from Wild Poliovirus (WPV) infection?
back: Clinical signs are indistinguishable. Differentiation requires specialized laboratory analysis (rRT-PCR) to identify genetic markers of Sabin-strain reversion versus wild strains.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 211 (Book Page): [Cases of VAPP are clinically indistinguishable from poliomyelitis caused by WPV, but can be distinguished by laboratory analysis... The diagnosis is made by real-time reverse transcription-polymerase chain reaction (rRT-PCR)]

category: Evaluate the effectiveness of different poliovirus vaccines (OPV and IPV) and outline the vaccination schedules
front: Q: Describe the physiological interference of breastfeeding with OPV and the recommended clinical approach.
back: Colostrum (first 3 days) contains secretory IgA that may neutralize OPV. However, breastfeeding is not a contraindication; 20-40% still seroconvert, and older infants are unaffected.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 213 (Book Page): [Colostrum produced in the first three days... contains secretory IgA antibody, which might interfere with the immune response to OPV... There is no significant effect of breast-feeding on the response of older infants to OPV]

category: Evaluate the effectiveness of different poliovirus vaccines (OPV and IPV) and outline the vaccination schedules
front: Q: Contrast the storage requirements and stability of OPV and IPV.
back: 1. OPV: Highly heat-labile; requires sub-zero storage (-20°C). 2. IPV: More stable; store at 2-8°C but MUST NOT be frozen.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 214 (Book Page): [Table 1: OPV... Requires to be stored and transported at sub-zero temperatures... IPV... Does not require stringent conditions... longer shelf-life. Page 213 (Book Page): Freezing should be avoided [for IPV] as it could diminish potency.]

category: Discuss community health strategies for poliovirus surveillance, outbreak response, and vaccination campaigns
front: Q: What is the primary indicator for monitoring poliovirus circulation in a community?
back: Acute Flaccid Paralysis (AFP) surveillance in children under 15 years of age.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 210 (Book Page): Finding and reporting children with acute flaccid paralysis (AFP)... staff in all health facilities... must promptly report every case of acute flaccid paralysis (AFP) in any child under 15 years of age.

category: Discuss community health strategies for poliovirus surveillance, outbreak response, and vaccination campaigns
front: Q: Define the 'Pulse' strategy used in mass oral polio vaccination campaigns.
back: Sudden, simultaneous administration of OPV to all children aged 0–5 years on a single day, regardless of prior immunization status.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 216 (Book Page): The term 'pulse' has been used to describe this sudden, simultaneous, mass administration of OPV on a single day to all children 0-5 years of age, regardless to previous immunization.

category: Discuss community health strategies for poliovirus surveillance, outbreak response, and vaccination campaigns
front: Q: What are the three criteria for an 'adequate' stool specimen in AFP surveillance?
back:
1. Two samples 24–48 hours apart.
2. Collected within 14 days of paralysis onset.
3. Arrives via reverse cold chain.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 210 (Book Page): two specimens — taken 24-48 hours apart are required... within 14 days after the onset of paralysis, and arriving in the laboratory by reverse cold chain.

category: Discuss community health strategies for poliovirus surveillance, outbreak response, and vaccination campaigns
front: Q: Clinical Scenario: A single case of paralytic polio is detected in a previously polio-free district. Immediate response?
back: Treat as an epidemic: Initiate investigation and outbreak control/mop-up immunization within 48 hours of notification.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 215 (Book Page): The occurrence of a single case of polio is now considered as an epidemic... Even a single case is treated as an outbreak and preventive measures are initiated, usually within 48 hours.

category: Discuss community health strategies for poliovirus surveillance, outbreak response, and vaccination campaigns
front: Q: Why must the Type 2 component be removed from the trivalent OPV (tOPV)?
back: Type 2 is the primary cause of vaccine-derived poliovirus (VDPV) outbreaks; bOPV reduces this risk while wild Type 2 is eradicated.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 210 (Book Page): as the main cause of VDPV outbreaks is currently type 2 component of OPV, this component must be removed... replacing the trivalent OPV with bivalent OPV in all OPV using countries.

category: Discuss community health strategies for poliovirus surveillance, outbreak response, and vaccination campaigns
front: Q: What is the minimum non-polio AFP rate required to certify high-quality surveillance in endemic regions?
back: At least 2 cases of non-polio AFP per 100,000 children under 15 years annually.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 210 (Book Page): A country's surveillance system needs to be sensitive enough to detect at least one case of AFP for every 100,000 children under 15... In endemic regions... this rate should be two per 100,000.

category: Discuss community health strategies for poliovirus surveillance, outbreak response, and vaccination campaigns
front: Q: What is the role of environmental surveillance in polio eradication strategies?
back: Testing sewage to detect poliovirus presence in the absence of clinical paralytic cases, helping track silent circulation.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 211 (Book Page): Environmental surveillance often confirms wild poliovirus infections in the absence of cases of paralysis. Systematic environmental sampling... provides important supplementary surveillance data.

category: Discuss community health strategies for poliovirus surveillance, outbreak response, and vaccination campaigns
front: Q: Differentiate 'Mopping Up' from routine National Immunization Days (NIDs).
back: Mopping Up involves door-to-door immunization specifically in high-risk districts where wild virus is suspected to still circulate.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 216 (Book Page): The strategy of 'mopping up' involves door-to-door immunization in high-risk districts, where wild polio virus is known or suspected to be still circulating.

category: Discuss community health strategies for poliovirus surveillance, outbreak response, and vaccination campaigns
front: Q: What is the immunological advantage of OPV over IPV for community health?
back: OPV induces local intestinal IgA immunity, preventing gut reinfection and transmission of wild virus (herd immunity).
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 214 (Book Page): Intestinal infection stimulates the production of IgA secretory antibodies which prevent subsequent infection of the alimentary tract... effective in limiting virus transmission in the community.

category: Discuss community health strategies for poliovirus surveillance, outbreak response, and vaccination campaigns
front: Q: What is the 'Zero Dose' of OPV in the context of vaccination campaigns?
back: An OPV dose given at birth to institutional deliveries before hospital discharge to maximize early immunity.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 213 (Book Page): It is recommended that a dose of OPV (zero-dose) is required to be given to all children delivered in health institutions before their discharge from the hospital.

category: Discuss community health strategies for poliovirus surveillance, outbreak response, and vaccination campaigns
front: Q: What is the primary objective of the Polio Eradication and Endgame Strategic Plan 2013-2018?
back: To deliver a polio-free world by 2018 by simultaneously eradicating all wild polioviruses (WPV) and vaccine-derived polioviruses (VDPV).
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 209 (Book Page): [The new Polio Eradication and Endgame Strategic Plan 2013-2018... is the first plan to eradicate all types of polio disease simultaneously — both due to wild poliovirus and due to vaccine-derived poliovirus.]

category: Discuss community health strategies for poliovirus surveillance, outbreak response, and vaccination campaigns
front: Q: List the four essential steps of Acute Flaccid Paralysis (AFP) surveillance in community health.
back:
1. Case finding and reporting (children <15 years).
2. Stool sample transport.
3. Poliovirus isolation in laboratory.
4. Virus mapping and genetic sequencing.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 210 (Book Page): [There are four steps of acute flaccid paralysis (AFP) surveillance: 1. Finding and reporting children... 2. Transporting stool samples... 3. Isolating poliovirus... 4. Mapping the virus.]

category: Discuss community health strategies for poliovirus surveillance, outbreak response, and vaccination campaigns
front: Q: Which two indicators define 'certification standard' sensitivity in an AFP surveillance system?
back:
1. Non-polio AFP rate: ≥1 case per 100,000 population <15 years.
2. Completeness: ≥80% of expected routine reports received on time.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 210 (Book Page): [Sensitivity of surveillance: At least one case of non-polio AFP should be detected annually per 100,000 population aged less than 15 years. Completeness of reporting: At least 80% of expected routine... reports should be received on time.]

category: Discuss community health strategies for poliovirus surveillance, outbreak response, and vaccination campaigns
front: Q: Define 'adequate' stool specimens required for laboratory investigation of suspected polio.
back: Two specimens collected 24–48 hours apart, within 14 days of paralysis onset, arriving at the laboratory within 72 hours under reverse cold chain (4-8°C).
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 210 (Book Page): ['Adequate' stool specimens are two stool specimens of sufficient quantity for laboratory analysis, collected at least 24 hours apart, within 14 days after the onset of paralysis, and arriving in the laboratory by reverse cold chain.]

category: Discuss community health strategies for poliovirus surveillance, outbreak response, and vaccination campaigns
front: Q: What is the public health utility of environmental surveillance in polio eradication?
back: It detects wild poliovirus circulation in sewage samples even in the absence of clinical paralysis cases, allowing detection of silent or imported transmission.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 210 (Book Page): [Environmental surveillance often confirms wild poliovirus infections in the absence of cases of paralysis. Systematic environmental sampling... provides important supplementary surveillance data.]

category: Discuss community health strategies for poliovirus surveillance, outbreak response, and vaccination campaigns
front: Q: Define the 'Pulse' strategy in Pulse Polio Immunization (PPI) campaigns.
back: Sudden, simultaneous, mass administration of Oral Polio Vaccine (OPV) on a single day to all children aged 0–5 years, regardless of prior immunization history.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 215 (Book Page): [The term "pulse" has been used to describe this sudden, simultaneous, mass administration of OPV on a single day to all children 0-5 years of age, regardless to previous immunization.]

category: Discuss community health strategies for poliovirus surveillance, outbreak response, and vaccination campaigns
front: Q: What does the 'Mopping Up' vaccination strategy involve in high-risk districts?
back: Intensive, door-to-door immunization in specific areas where wild poliovirus is known or suspected to be circulating, usually during the final stages of eradication.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 215 (Book Page): [The strategy of ‘mopping up’ involves door-to-door immunization in high-risk districts, where wild polio virus is known or suspected to be still circulating.]

category: Discuss community health strategies for poliovirus surveillance, outbreak response, and vaccination campaigns
front: Q: What are the three categories of Vaccine-Derived Polioviruses (VDPVs)?
back:
1. cVDPVs (circulating; person-to-person transmission).
2. iVDPVs (immunodeficiency-associated; prolonged infection).
3. aVDPVs (ambiguous; clinical/sewage isolates from unknown sources).
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 212 (Book Page): [VDPVs are divided into three categories as (1) cVDPVs... (2) immunodeficiency-associated VDPVs (iVDPVs)... and (3) ambiguous VDPVs (aVDPVs).]

category: Discuss community health strategies for poliovirus surveillance, outbreak response, and vaccination campaigns
front: Q: Why is Oral Polio Vaccine (OPV) superior to Inactivated Polio Vaccine (IPV) for outbreak control?
back: OPV induces local intestinal (secretory IgA) immunity which prevents wild virus multiplication and excretion, effectively breaking the chain of community transmission.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 213 (Book Page): [Intestinal infection stimulates the production of IgA secretory antibodies which prevent subsequent infection of the alimentary tract... and thus is effective in limiting virus transmission in the community.]

category: Discuss community health strategies for poliovirus surveillance, outbreak response, and vaccination campaigns
front: Q: What community health action is triggered by the occurrence of a single case of paralytic polio?
back: Immediately treated as an epidemic. Requires epidemiological investigation, active case search, and rapid response vaccination (outbreak control) within 48 hours.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 214 (Book Page): [The occurrence of a single case of polio is now considered as an epidemic, and should prompt an immediate epidemiological investigation, including an active search for other cases.]

category: Discuss community health strategies for poliovirus surveillance, outbreak response, and vaccination campaigns
front: Q: What is the gold-standard sensitivity indicator for non-polio Acute Flaccid Paralysis (AFP) surveillance?
back:
- Detection of at least 1 non-polio AFP case per 100,000 children under 15 years annually.
- In endemic regions, this requirement increases to 2 cases per 100,000.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 210 (Book Page): [A country's surveillance system needs to be sensitive enough to detect at least one case of AFP for every 100,000 children under 15 — even in the absence of polio.]

category: Discuss community health strategies for poliovirus surveillance, outbreak response, and vaccination campaigns
front: Q: What are the specific requirements for 'adequate stool specimens' in poliovirus surveillance?
back:
- Two stool specimens collected 24–48 hours apart.
- Must be taken within 14 days of paralysis onset.
- Stored at 4–8°C (reverse cold chain) and reached lab within 72 hours.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 210 (Book Page): [two specimens — taken 24-48 hours apart are required... Specimens should arrive at the laboratory within 72 hours of collection.]

category: Discuss community health strategies for poliovirus surveillance, outbreak response, and vaccination campaigns
front: Q: Contrast AFP surveillance with Environmental Surveillance in the Polio Eradication Initiative.
back:
- AFP Surveillance: Clinical detection of paralytic cases in children <15.
- Environmental Surveillance: Periodic testing of sewage for poliovirus to detect circulation in the absence of clinical paralysis.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 211 (Book Page): [Environmental surveillance often confirms wild poliovirus infections in the absence of cases of paralysis. Systematic environmental sampling... provides important supplementary surveillance data.]

category: Discuss community health strategies for poliovirus surveillance, outbreak response, and vaccination campaigns
front: Q: A 10-year-old child in an endemic district presents with sudden-onset leg weakness. What is the mandatory immediate action?
back:
- Notify authorities as an 'outbreak' within 48 hours.
- Immediate epidemiological investigation.
- Collection of two stool samples and clinical follow-up at 60 days.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 215 (Book Page): [The occurrence of a single case of polio is now considered as an epidemic, and should prompt an immediate epidemiological investigation... within 48 hours of notification.]

category: Discuss community health strategies for poliovirus surveillance, outbreak response, and vaccination campaigns
front: Q: What is the public health rationale behind the 'Pulse' in Pulse Polio Immunization (PPI)?
back:
- Sudden, simultaneous mass administration of OPV to all children 0–5 years.
- Aim: To flood the community with vaccine virus and interrupt the transmission of wild poliovirus.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 216 (Book Page): [The term "pulse" has been used to describe this sudden, simultaneous, mass administration of OPV on a single day... regardless to previous immunization.]

category: Discuss community health strategies for poliovirus surveillance, outbreak response, and vaccination campaigns
front: Q: List three core certification standards for AFP surveillance reporting completeness.
back:
- 80% of expected routine reports received on time.
- 80% of AFP cases must have 'adequate' stool specimens.
- 80% of cases must have a 60-day follow-up for residual paralysis.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 211 (Book Page): [At least 80% of expected routine... surveillance reports should be received on time... 80% of AFP cases having ‘adequate’ stool specimens collected.]

category: Discuss community health strategies for poliovirus surveillance, outbreak response, and vaccination campaigns
front: Q: How is 'mopping-up' immunization applied during the final stages of polio eradication?
back:
- Door-to-door immunization in high-risk districts.
- Targeted at areas where wild poliovirus is known or suspected to be circulating after NIDs/SNIDs.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 216 (Book Page): [The strategy of “mopping up” involves door—to-door immunization in high-risk districts, where wild polio virus is known or suspected to be still circulating.]

category: Discuss community health strategies for poliovirus surveillance, outbreak response, and vaccination campaigns
front: Q: Differentiate between circulating Vaccine-Derived Poliovirus (cVDPV) and immunodeficiency-associated VDPV (iVDPV).
back:
- cVDPV: Shows evidence of person-to-person community transmission.
- iVDPV: Isolated from individuals with primary immunodeficiencies showing prolonged virus replication (longer than 4–6 weeks).
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 212 (Book Page): [cVDPVs, when evidence of person-to-person transmission in the community exists; (2) immunodeficiency-associated VDPVs (iVDPVs), which are isolates from persons with primary immunodeficiencies.]

category: Discuss community health strategies for poliovirus surveillance, outbreak response, and vaccination campaigns
front: Q: Why is a 'zero dose' of OPV recommended for children born in health institutions?
back:
- Administered at birth (within 15 days).
- Protects the newborn immediately and reduces the chance of infection before the first scheduled dose at 6 weeks.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 213 (Book Page): [a dose of OPV (zero-dose) is required to be given to all children delivered in health institutions before their discharge... within the first 15 days.]

category: Discuss community health strategies for poliovirus surveillance, outbreak response, and vaccination campaigns
front: Q: What is the primary role of the Global Polio Laboratory Network (GPLN) in mapping the virus?
back:
- Genomic sequencing to determine the exact genetic make-up.
- Allows investigators to identify the geographical origin and track cross-border importation of wild strains.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 211 (Book Page): [By determining the exact genetic make-up of the virus, wild viruses can be compared to others and classified into genetic families... identifying the source of importation.]

category: Discuss community health strategies for poliovirus surveillance, outbreak response, and vaccination campaigns
front: What is the primary global sensitivity indicator for standard AFP surveillance?
back: Detection of at least 1 case of non-polio acute flaccid paralysis (AFP) annually per 100,000 children under 15 years of age.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 210 (Book Page): [A country's surveillance system needs to be sensitive enough to detect at least one case of AFP for every 100,000 children under 15]

category: Discuss community health strategies for poliovirus surveillance, outbreak response, and vaccination campaigns
front: State the mandatory criteria for 'adequate' stool specimen collection in polio surveillance.
back:
- Two specimens collected 24–48 hours apart
- Collected within 14 days of paralysis onset
- Arriving at lab under reverse cold chain
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 210 (Book Page): [‘Adequate’ stool specimens are two stool specimens... collected at least 24 hours apart, within 14 days after the onset of paralysis, and arriving in the laboratory by reverse cold chain]

category: Discuss community health strategies for poliovirus surveillance, outbreak response, and vaccination campaigns
front: How is a polio 'epidemic' defined in the current eradication era?
back: The occurrence of a single laboratory-confirmed case of paralytic polio is considered an epidemic requiring immediate response.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 215 (Book Page): [The occurrence of a single case of polio is now considered as an epidemic, and should prompt an immediate epidemiological investigation]

category: Discuss community health strategies for poliovirus surveillance, outbreak response, and vaccination campaigns
front: Describe the 'Mopping Up' strategy in polio outbreak response.
back: Door-to-door immunization campaigns conducted in high-risk districts where wild poliovirus is known or suspected to be circulating.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 215 (Book Page): [The strategy of “mopping up” involves door-to-door immunization in high-risk districts, where wild polio virus is known or suspected to be still circulating.]

category: Discuss community health strategies for poliovirus surveillance, outbreak response, and vaccination campaigns
front: What is the core mechanism of Pulse Polio Immunization (PPI)?
back: Simultaneous mass administration of OPV to all children 0–5 years on a single day, regardless of previous immunization status.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 215 (Book Page): [The term "pulse" has been used to describe this sudden, simultaneous, mass administration of OPV on a single day to all children 0-5 years of age, regardless to previous immunization.]

category: Discuss community health strategies for poliovirus surveillance, outbreak response, and vaccination campaigns
front: What is the role of Environmental Surveillance in polio eradication?
back: Testing sewage samples to detect poliovirus circulation in a community, even in the absence of clinical paralytic cases.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 210 (Book Page): [Environmental surveillance often confirms wild poliovirus infections in the absence of cases of paralysis.]

category: Discuss community health strategies for poliovirus surveillance, outbreak response, and vaccination campaigns
front: Differentiate between cVDPV and iVDPV categories.
back:
- cVDPV: Evidence of person-to-person community transmission.
- iVDPV: Prolonged infection/excretion in individuals with primary immunodeficiencies.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 212 (Book Page): [(1) cVDPVs, when evidence of person-to-person transmission in the community exists; (2) iVDPVs, which are isolates from persons with primary immunodeficiencies]

category: Discuss community health strategies for poliovirus surveillance, outbreak response, and vaccination campaigns
front: Explain the rationale for the global switch from tOPV to bOPV.
back: To eliminate the risk of Type 2 vaccine-derived outbreaks, as wild Type 2 virus was eradicated in 1999.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 210 (Book Page): [As wild poliovirus type 2 was eradicated in 1999, and the main cause of VDPV outbreaks is currently type 2 component of OPV, this component must be removed... replacing the trivalent OPV with bivalent OPV]

category: Discuss community health strategies for poliovirus surveillance, outbreak response, and vaccination campaigns
front: What are the required timelines for polio outbreak response and investigation?
back: Epidemiological investigation and preventive measures must be initiated within 48 hours of notification of a suspected case.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 215 (Book Page): [Even a single case is treated as an outbreak and preventive measures are initiated, usually within 48 hours of notification of the case.]

category: Discuss community health strategies for poliovirus surveillance, outbreak response, and vaccination campaigns
front: List the four objectives of the Polio Eradication and Endgame Strategic Plan 2013–2018.
back:
1. Detect and interrupt transmission
2. Strengthen immunization and withdraw OPV
3. Containment and certification
4. Legacy planning
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 210 (Book Page): [The plan has 4 objectives: 1. Detect and interrupt all poliovirus transmission... 2. Strengthen immunization system and withdraw oral polio vaccine... 3. Containment and certification... 4. Legacy planning]

category: Discuss community health strategies for poliovirus surveillance, outbreak response, and vaccination campaigns
front: What is the minimum non-polio AFP rate required per 100,000 children under 15 for sensitive surveillance?
back:
- At least 1 per 100,000 in non-endemic regions.
- At least 2 per 100,000 in endemic regions to ensure higher sensitivity.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 210 (Book Page): [A country's surveillance system needs to be sensitive enough to detect at least one case of AFP for every 100,000 children under 15 — even in the absence of polio. In endemic regions, to ensure even higher sensitivity, this rate should be two per 100,000.]

category: Discuss community health strategies for poliovirus surveillance, outbreak response, and vaccination campaigns
front: Why is OPV preferred over IPV for interrupting community transmission of wild poliovirus during outbreaks?
back:
- OPV induces local intestinal immunity (secretory IgA), preventing gut reinfection and shedding.
- IPV only provides humoral immunity, allowing the virus to multiply in the gut and spread.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 213 (Book Page): [Intestinal infection stimulates the production of IgA secretory antibodies which prevent subsequent infection of the alimentary tract... IPV... does not induce intestinal or local immunity.]

category: Discuss community health strategies for poliovirus surveillance, outbreak response, and vaccination campaigns
front: Distinguish between Vaccine-Associated Paralytic Polio (VAPP) and Vaccine-Derived Poliovirus (VDPV).
back:
- VAPP: Rare adverse event in individual recipients or close contacts.
- VDPV: Results from prolonged replication/transmission, behaving biologically like wild poliovirus and threatening community immunity.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 212 (Book Page): [Vaccine-associated paralytic poliomyelitis (VAPP) is the most important of these rare adverse events... VDPVs resemble WPVs biologically... have genetic properties consistent with prolonged replication or transmission.]

category: Discuss community health strategies for poliovirus surveillance, outbreak response, and vaccination campaigns
front: What defines 'adequate' stool specimens for polio investigation in a child with sudden-onset paralysis?
back:
- Two specimens taken 24–48 hours apart.
- Collected within 14 days of paralysis onset.
- Arrive at a WHO-accredited lab within 72 hours under reverse cold chain.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 210 (Book Page): [‘Adequate’ stool specimens are two stool specimens... collected at least 24 hours apart, within 14 days after the onset of paralysis, and arriving in the laboratory by reverse cold chain... within 72 hours of collection.]

category: Discuss community health strategies for poliovirus surveillance, outbreak response, and vaccination campaigns
front: What is the rationale for the global switch from trivalent OPV (tOPV) to bivalent OPV (bOPV)?
back:
- To eliminate Type 2 vaccine-derived poliovirus (cVDPV2) outbreaks.
- Wild poliovirus Type 2 was eradicated in 1999, making the Type 2 OPV component unnecessary and risky.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 209 (Book Page): [wild poliovirus type 2 was eradicated in 1999... as the main cause of VDPV outbreaks is currently type 2 component of OPV, this component must be removed... replacing the trivalent OPV with bivalent OPV.]

category: Discuss community health strategies for poliovirus surveillance, outbreak response, and vaccination campaigns
front: State the surveillance performance targets for 'completeness of reporting' and 'case investigation' in polio programs.
back:
- Reporting: At least 80% of expected routine reports received on time.
- Stool Adequacy: At least 80% of AFP cases must have 'adequate' specimens collected.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 210 (Book Page): [At least 80% of expected routine (weekly or monthly) AFP surveillance reports should be received on time... at least 80% of AFP cases having ‘adequate’ stool specimens collected.]

category: Discuss community health strategies for poliovirus surveillance, outbreak response, and vaccination campaigns
front: Define 'Mopping Up' activities in the context of the final stages of polio eradication.
back:
- Intensive door-to-door immunization campaigns.
- Targeted at high-risk districts where wild poliovirus is known or suspected to be still circulating.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 215 (Book Page): [The strategy of “mopping up” involves door—to—door immunization in high-risk districts, where wild polio virus is known or suspected to be still circulating.]

category: Discuss community health strategies for poliovirus surveillance, outbreak response, and vaccination campaigns
front: What immediate community actions are required within 48 hours of notifying a suspected polio case?
back:
- Rapid Response Team (RRT) activation.
- Active search for additional AFP cases.
- Collection of stool samples from the index case and high-risk contacts.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 215 (Book Page): [Even a single case is treated as an outbreak and preventive measures are initiated, usually within 48 hours of notification... active search for other cases... collection of stool samples.]

category: Discuss community health strategies for poliovirus surveillance, outbreak response, and vaccination campaigns
front: Explain the role of 'Environmental Surveillance' in the Polio Eradication Initiative.
back:
- Testing sewage/environmental samples for poliovirus presence.
- Detects circulating wild poliovirus or VDPVs in the absence of clinical paralysis cases.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 210 (Book Page): [Environmental surveillance involves testing sewage or other environmental samples for the presence of poliovirus... often confirms wild poliovirus infections in the absence of cases of paralysis.]

category: Discuss community health strategies for poliovirus surveillance, outbreak response, and vaccination campaigns
front: Identify the 'Zero Dose' of OPV and its specific administration timing.
back:
- Dose given at birth or within the first 15 days of life.
- Purpose: Provides early protection in endemic areas before the primary series begins at 6 weeks.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 129 (Book Page): [OPV-0: At birth or as early as possible within the first 15 days. 2 drops Oral.] Page 213 (Book Page): [recommended that a dose of OPV (zero-dose) is required to be given to all children delivered in health institutions before their discharge.]

category: Describe ‘end game strategy’ by WHO for polio eradication
front: Q: What is the official duration of the WHO Polio Eradication and Endgame Strategic Plan?
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 209 (Book Page): [Recognizing the epidemiological opportunity and the significant risk of potential failure, the new Polio Eradication and Endgame Strategic Plan 2013-2018 has been developed.]

category: Describe ‘end game strategy’ by WHO for polio eradication
front: Q: Why does the WHO Endgame Strategy mandate the withdrawal of Oral Polio Vaccine (OPV)?
back: To eliminate the risk of Vaccine-Derived Poliovirus (VDPV) disease, particularly following the global eradication of Wild Poliovirus Type 2.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 209 (Book Page): [It is the first plan to eradicate all types of polio disease simultaneously — both due to wild poliovirus and due to vaccine-derived poliovirus.]

category: Describe ‘end game strategy’ by WHO for polio eradication
front: Q: Contrast the focus of Objective 1 and Objective 2 in the Polio Endgame Strategic Plan.
back: Objective 1: Interrupt transmission of Wild Poliovirus (WPV). Objective 2: Strengthen immunization and withdraw OPV to eliminate VDPV risks.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 209 (Book Page): [1. Detect and interrupt all poliovirus transmission... 2. Strengthen immunization system and withdraw oral polio vaccine.]

category: Describe ‘end game strategy’ by WHO for polio eradication
front: Q: What is the mandated response time for a Vaccine-Derived Poliovirus (VDPV) outbreak in the Endgame Plan?
back: Stop any new polio outbreak due to VDPV within 6 months of the index case.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 209 (Book Page): [It also includes stopping any new polio outbreak due to vaccine-derived poliovirus (VDPV) within 6 months of the index case.]

category: Describe ‘end game strategy’ by WHO for polio eradication
front: Q: Describe the specific 'vaccine switch' mandated in Objective 2 of the Polio Endgame Plan.
back: Replacement of trivalent OPV (tOPV) with bivalent OPV (bOPV) across all OPV-using countries, plus global IPV introduction.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 209 (Book Page): [Preparation for this removal entails... replacing the trivalent OPV with bivalent OPV in all OPV using countries.]

category: Describe ‘end game strategy’ by WHO for polio eradication
front: Q: List the four primary objectives of the Polio Eradication and Endgame Strategic Plan.
back: 1. Detect/interrupt transmission. 2. Strengthen systems/withdraw OPV. 3. Containment/Certification. 4. Legacy planning.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 209 (Book Page)-210: [The plan has 4 objectives : 1. Detect and interrupt all poliovirus transmission... 2. Strengthen immunization system and withdraw oral polio vaccine... 3. Containment and certification... 4. Legacy planning.]

category: Describe ‘end game strategy’ by WHO for polio eradication
front: Q: Define 'Legacy Planning' as per the WHO Polio Eradication and Endgame Strategy.
back: Mainstreaming polio infrastructure into public health programs and transferring expertise/assets to other global health priorities.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 210 (Book Page): [successful legacy planning will include the mainstreaming of essential polio functions into on-going public health programmes... and the transition of assets and infrastructure to benefit other development goals.]

category: Describe ‘end game strategy’ by WHO for polio eradication
front: Q: Why was Type 2 component specifically prioritized for removal from OPV by mid-2016?
back: Wild Poliovirus Type 2 was eradicated in 1999; the Type 2 component in OPV is now the leading cause of VDPV outbreaks.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 209 (Book Page): [As wild poliovirus type 2 was eradicated in 1999, and the main cause of VDPV outbreaks is currently type 2 component of OPV, this component must be removed.]

category: Describe ‘end game strategy’ by WHO for polio eradication
front: Q: What is the role of Environmental Surveillance in the Polio Eradication Endgame?
back: Testing sewage for poliovirus to identify silent circulation in the community without clinically diagnosed paralysis cases.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 212 (Book Page): [Environmental surveillance often confirms wild poliovirus infections in the absence of cases of paralysis.]

category: Describe ‘end game strategy’ by WHO for polio eradication
front: Q: What is the certification goal year for global containment of all wild poliovirus under the WHO plan?
back: End of 2018.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 209 (Book Page): [certification of the eradication and containment of all wild poliovirus in all WHO regions by end of 2018.]

category: Discuss community health strategies for poliovirus surveillance, outbreak response, and vaccination campaigns
front: Q: What is the minimum sensitivity indicator for Acute Flaccid Paralysis (AFP) surveillance in endemic regions?
back: At least two non-polio AFP cases per 100,000 population under 15 years old should be detected annually.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 210 (Book Page): [Sensitivity of surveillance] At least one case of non-polio AFP should be detected annually per 100,000 population... In endemic regions... this rate should be two per 100,000.

category: Discuss community health strategies for poliovirus surveillance, outbreak response, and vaccination campaigns
coreConcept: OPV Mucosal Immunity and Herd Protection
front: Q: How does the Oral Polio Vaccine (OPV) contribute to 'herd immunity' during vaccination campaigns?
back:
• Stimulates intestinal IgA (secretory) immunity.
• Vaccine progeny is excreted in faeces, providing secondary immunization to non-immunized contacts.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 213 (Book Page): Intestinal infection stimulates the production of IgA secretory antibodies... The vaccine progeny is excreted in the faeces and secondary spread occurs to household contacts and susceptible contacts in the community.

category: Discuss community health strategies for poliovirus surveillance, outbreak response, and vaccination campaigns
front: Q: Why is Inactivated Polio Vaccine (IPV) considered insufficient as a primary tool for outbreak control?
back:
