• Does not prevent gut reinfection by wild virus.
• Wild viruses can still multiply in the gut and infect others.
• Fails to rapidly induce community-wide immunity.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 212 (Book Page): [IPV] does not induce intestinal or local immunity... wild viruses can still multiply in the gut and be a source of infection to others. Further, in the case of an epidemic, IPV is unsuitable.

category: Discuss community health strategies for poliovirus surveillance, outbreak response, and vaccination campaigns
front: Q: What is the clinical protocol for stool specimen collection in a suspected polio case?
back:
• Two 'adequate' specimens taken 24–48 hours apart.
• Must be collected within 14 days of paralysis onset.
• Transported at 4–8°C (reverse cold chain).
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 210 (Book Page): two specimens — taken 24-48 hours apart are required... within 14 days after the onset of paralysis, and arriving in the laboratory by reverse cold chain.

category: Discuss community health strategies for poliovirus surveillance, outbreak response, and vaccination campaigns
front: Q: What is the rationale for the global switch from trivalent OPV (tOPV) to bivalent OPV (bOPV)?
back:
• Wild poliovirus type 2 was eradicated in 1999.
• The type 2 component in tOPV is the primary cause of vaccine-derived poliovirus (VDPV) outbreaks.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 209 (Book Page): As wild poliovirus type 2 was eradicated in 1999, and the main cause of VDPV outbreaks is currently type 2 component of OPV, this component must be removed.

category: Discuss community health strategies for poliovirus surveillance, outbreak response, and vaccination campaigns
front: Q: Define 'Adequate' stool specimens as required for WHO certification-standard surveillance.
back: Two specimens of sufficient quantity collected 24 hours apart, within 14 days of paralysis onset, arriving via reverse cold chain.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 210 (Book Page): ‘Adequate’ stool specimens are two stool specimens... collected at least 24 hours apart, within 14 days after the onset of paralysis, and arriving in the laboratory by reverse cold chain.

category: Discuss community health strategies for poliovirus surveillance, outbreak response, and vaccination campaigns
front: Q: Describe the 'Pulse' strategy used in National Immunization Days (NIDs).
back: Sudden, simultaneous mass administration of OPV to all children aged 0–5 years on a single day, regardless of previous vaccination history.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 215 (Book Page): The term "pulse" has been used to describe this sudden, simultaneous, mass administration of OPV on a single day to all children 0-5 years of age, regardless to previous immunization.

category: Discuss community health strategies for poliovirus surveillance, outbreak response, and vaccination campaigns
front: Q: How is Vaccine-Derived Poliovirus (VDPV) biologically distinguished from standard vaccine-related isolates?
back:
• Genetic properties showing prolonged replication (over 4–6 weeks).
• Diagnosis via rRT-PCR nucleic acid amplification for specific early mutations.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 210 (Book Page): VDPVs... have genetic properties consistent with prolonged replication or transmission... diagnosis is made by real-time reverse transcription-polymerase chain reaction (rRT-PCR) nucleic acid amplification targetted to nucleotide substitution.

category: Discuss community health strategies for poliovirus surveillance, outbreak response, and vaccination campaigns
front: Q: What is the primary epidemiological utility of environmental (sewage) surveillance in polio control?
back:
• Identifies wild poliovirus circulation in the absence of paralytic cases.
• Tracks international spread/importation patterns.
• Provides supplementary data to AFP surveillance.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 210 (Book Page): Environmental surveillance often confirms wild poliovirus infections in the absence of cases of paralysis... provides insights into the international spread of poliovirus.

category: Discuss community health strategies for poliovirus surveillance, outbreak response, and vaccination campaigns
front: Q: When is the 'zero dose' of OPV administered according to the National Immunization Schedule?
back: At birth or within the first 15 days of life, typically before discharge for institutional deliveries.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 129 (Book Page): OPV-0: At birth or as early as possible within the first 15 days.

category: Discuss community health strategies for poliovirus surveillance, outbreak response, and vaccination campaigns
front: Q: What is the primary purpose of Acute Flaccid Paralysis (AFP) surveillance in polio eradication?
back:
1. Identify new polio cases.
2. Detect importation of wild poliovirus.
3. Verify eradication status by pinpointing remaining virus circulation.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 210 (Book Page): [Surveillance identifies new cases and detects importation of wild poliovirus. Without surveillance, it would be impossible to pinpoint where and how wild poliovirus is still circulating.]

category: Discuss community health strategies for poliovirus surveillance, outbreak response, and vaccination campaigns
front: Q: Describe the standard stool collection protocol for a child presenting with suspected poliomyelitis.
back:
1. Two specimens required 24–48 hours apart.
2. Collected within 14 days of paralysis onset.
3. Maintained in a reverse cold chain (4–8°C).
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 210 (Book Page): [two specimens — taken 24-48 hours apart are required. Speed is essential... during the first two weeks after onset of paralysis. Stool specimens have to be sealed... at 4-8°C in a cold box.]

category: Discuss community health strategies for poliovirus surveillance, outbreak response, and vaccination campaigns
front: Q: How does environmental surveillance supplement AFP surveillance in community polio monitoring?
back:
1. Tests sewage/environmental samples for poliovirus.
2. Detects silent wild poliovirus circulation in the absence of paralytic cases.
3. Provides insights into international virus spread.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 211 (Book Page): [Environmental surveillance often confirms wild poliovirus infections in the absence of cases of paralysis. Environmental surveillance... provides insights into the international spread of poliovirus.]

category: Discuss community health strategies for poliovirus surveillance, outbreak response, and vaccination campaigns
front: Q: Which specific clinical conditions must be differentiated from poliomyelitis in a child with AFP?
back:
1. Guillain-Barre Syndrome.
2. Transverse myelitis.
3. Traumatic neuritis.
4. Differentiation requires virological analysis of stool samples.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 210 (Book Page): [polio may be difficult to differentiate from other forms of acute flaccid paralysis, such as Guillain-Barre Syndrome, transverse myelitis, or traumatic neuritis.]

category: Discuss community health strategies for poliovirus surveillance, outbreak response, and vaccination campaigns
front: Q: What are the strict transport and timing requirements for poliovirus stool specimens?
back:
1. Transport in reverse cold chain (4–8°C) with frozen ice packs.
2. Specimens must arrive at the laboratory within 72 hours of collection.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 210 (Book Page): [packed between frozen ice packs at 4-8°C in a cold box... Specimens should arrive at the laboratory within 72 hours of collection.]

category: Discuss community health strategies for poliovirus surveillance, outbreak response, and vaccination campaigns
front: Q: State the minimum non-polio AFP detection rate required for certification standard surveillance.
back:
1. At least 1 case per 100,000 children under 15 years annually.
2. In endemic regions, the rate must be at least 2 per 100,000.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 211 (Book Page): [A country's surveillance system needs to be sensitive enough to detect at least one case of AFP for every 100,000 children under 15... In endemic regions... this rate should be two per 100,000.]

category: Discuss community health strategies for poliovirus surveillance, outbreak response, and vaccination campaigns
front: Q: Explain the strategy of Pulse Polio Immunization (PPI) campaigns used in India.
back:
1. Sudden mass administration of OPV to all children 0–5 years.
2. Regardless of previous immunization status.
3. Two rounds, 4–6 weeks apart, during low transmission season.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 215 (Book Page): [term "pulse" has been used to describe this sudden, simultaneous, mass administration of OPV on a single day to all children 0-5 years of age, regardless to previous immunization.]

category: Discuss community health strategies for poliovirus surveillance, outbreak response, and vaccination campaigns
front: Q: Distinguish between the three categories of Vaccine-Derived Polioviruses (VDPV).
back:
1. cVDPV: Evidence of person-to-person community transmission.
2. iVDPV: Isolates from individuals with primary immunodeficiencies.
3. aVDPV: Ambiguous isolates from unknown sources or sewage.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 212 (Book Page): [(1) cVDPVs, when evidence of person-to-person transmission in the community exists; (2) immunodeficiency-associated VDPVs (iVDPVs)... (3) ambiguous VDPVs (aVDPVs)... sewage isolates whose source is unknown.]

category: Discuss community health strategies for poliovirus surveillance, outbreak response, and vaccination campaigns
front: Q: How does the Oral Polio Vaccine (OPV) uniquely contribute to community herd immunity?
back:
1. Vaccine virus replicates in the gut and is excreted in faeces.
2. Excreted virus spreads to household and community contacts.
3. Passively immunizes non-vaccinated individuals in the environment.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 214 (Book Page): [The vaccine progeny is excreted in the faeces and secondary spread occurs to household contacts and susceptible contacts in the community. Non-immunized persons may therefore, be immunized.]

category: Discuss community health strategies for poliovirus surveillance, outbreak response, and vaccination campaigns
front: Q: Define the "Mopping Up" strategy in the final stages of poliovirus elimination.
back:
1. Door-to-door immunization in high-risk districts.
2. Targeted where wild poliovirus is known or suspected to be circulating.
3. Used to eliminate the final reservoirs of the virus.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 215 (Book Page): [The strategy of “mopping up” involves door—to—door immunization in high-risk districts, where wild polio virus is known or suspected to be still circulating.]

category: Describe ‘end game strategy’ by WHO for polio eradication
front: Q: What is the primary goal of the WHO Polio Eradication and Endgame Strategic Plan 2013-2018?
back:
- Eradicate all types of polio disease simultaneously.
- Target: Both wild poliovirus (WPV) and vaccine-derived poliovirus (VDPV).
- Aim: Deliver a polio-free world by 2018.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 209 (Book Page): [The new Polio Eradication and Endgame Strategic Plan 2013-2018 has been developed. It is the first plan to eradicate all types of polio disease simultaneously — both due to wild poliovirus and due to vaccine-derived poliovirus.]

category: Describe ‘end game strategy’ by WHO for polio eradication
front: Q: List the four main objectives of the Polio Eradication and Endgame Strategic Plan.
back:
1. Detect and interrupt all poliovirus transmission.
2. Strengthen immunization systems and withdraw OPV.
3. Containment and certification.
4. Legacy planning.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 209 (Book Page): [The plan has 4 objectives : 1. Detect and interrupt all poliovirus transmission... 2. Strengthen immunization system and withdraw oral polio vaccine... 3. Containment and certification... 4. Legacy planning.]

category: Describe ‘end game strategy’ by WHO for polio eradication
front: Q: What is the specific target for responding to new VDPV outbreaks under Objective 1?
back: Stop any new polio outbreak due to vaccine-derived poliovirus (VDPV) within 6 months of the index case.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 209 (Book Page): [It also includes stopping any new polio outbreak due to vaccine-derived poliovirus (VDPV) within 6 months of the index case.]

category: Describe ‘end game strategy’ by WHO for polio eradication
front: Q: Why was the type 2 component targeted for removal from OPV first in the Endgame Strategy?
back:
- Wild poliovirus type 2 was eradicated in 1999.
- Type 2 component in OPV is currently the main cause of VDPV outbreaks.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 210 (Book Page): [As wild poliovirus type 2 was eradicated in 1999, and the main cause of VDPV outbreaks is currently type 2 component of OPV, this component must be removed from the vaccine by mid-2016.]

category: Describe ‘end game strategy’ by WHO for polio eradication
front: Q: Describe the 'Switch' protocol in the Polio Endgame Strategy.
back:
- Introduction of Inactivated Polio Vaccine (IPV) globally.
- Replacement of trivalent OPV (tOPV) with bivalent OPV (bOPV).
- Goal: Eliminate all VDPV risks by removing OPV in the long-term.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 210 (Book Page): [Preparation for this removal entails strengthening routine immunization system... introducing IPV globally and then replacing the trivalent OPV with bivalent OPV in all OPV using countries.]

category: Describe ‘end game strategy’ by WHO for polio eradication
front: Q: What does the 'Containment' objective of the Polio Endgame entail?
back:
- Certification of eradication in all WHO regions by 2018.
- Minimize risk of re-introduction.
- Poliovirus stocks retained only in a small number of secure facilities for research/vaccine production.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 210 (Book Page): [certification of the eradication and containment of all wild poliovirus in all WHO regions by end of 2018, recognizing that a small number of facilities will need to retain poliovirus stocks... for the purposes of vaccine production, diagnosis and research.]

category: Describe ‘end game strategy’ by WHO for polio eradication
front: Q: Define the 'Legacy Planning' component of the Polio Eradication strategy.
back:
- Mainstreaming polio functions into existing health programs.
- Transferring assets, infrastructure, and knowledge to other global health priorities (e.g., measles control).
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 210 (Book Page): [mainstreaming of essential polio functions into on-going public health programmes... ensuring the transfer of learning... and the transition of assets and infrastructure to benefit other development goals.]

category: Describe ‘end game strategy’ by WHO for polio eradication
front: Q: What are the 'Adequate' stool specimen criteria for AFP surveillance certification?
back:
- Two specimens collected 24–48 hours apart.
- Collected within 14 days of paralysis onset.
- Arrive in laboratory via reverse cold chain with proper documentation.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 211 (Book Page): [‘Adequate’ stool specimens are two stool specimens... collected at least 24 hours apart, within 14 days after the onset of paralysis, and arriving in the laboratory by reverse cold chain.]

category: Describe ‘end game strategy’ by WHO for polio eradication
front: Q: State the target non-polio AFP detection rate for surveillance sensitivity in endemic regions.
back: Detection of at least 2 cases of non-polio AFP per 100,000 population aged less than 15 years annually.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 211 (Book Page): [At least one case of non-polio AFP should be detected annually per 100,000 population aged less than 15 years. In endemic regions, to ensure even higher sensitivity, this rate should be two per 100,000.]

category: Describe ‘end game strategy’ by WHO for polio eradication
front: Q: What is the role of 'Environmental Surveillance' in the Polio Endgame?
back:
- Tests sewage/water samples for poliovirus.
- Confirms viral circulation in the absence of clinical paralysis cases.
- Provides data on international spread/importation.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 211 (Book Page): [Environmental surveillance often confirms wild poliovirus infections in the absence of cases of paralysis. Systematic environmental sampling... provides important supplementary surveillance data.]

category: Describe ‘end game strategy’ by WHO for polio eradication
front: What are the four primary objectives of the WHO Polio Eradication and Endgame Strategic Plan 2013-2018?
back:
- Detect and interrupt all poliovirus transmission.
- Strengthen immunization systems and withdraw OPV.
- Containment and certification of all regions.
- Legacy planning for assets/infrastructure.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 209 (Book Page): [The plan has 4 objectives : 1. Detect and interrupt all poliovirus transmission... 2. Strengthen immunization system and withdraw oral polio vaccine... 3. Containment and certification... 4. Legacy planning.]

category: Describe ‘end game strategy’ by WHO for polio eradication
front: Why does the endgame strategy necessitate the switch from trivalent OPV (tOPV) to bivalent OPV (bOPV)?
back: Wild poliovirus Type 2 was eradicated in 1999. The Type 2 component in OPV is the primary cause of vaccine-derived poliovirus (VDPV) outbreaks.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 209 (Book Page): [As wild poliovirus type 2 was eradicated in 1999, and the main cause of VDPV outbreaks is currently type 2 component of OPV, this component must be removed from the vaccine... replacing the trivalent OPV with bivalent OPV.]

category: Describe ‘end game strategy’ by WHO for polio eradication
front: Contrast Acute Flaccid Paralysis (AFP) surveillance with Environmental Surveillance in the polio endgame context.
back:
- AFP: Detects clinical cases in children <15 years through reporting and stool analysis.
- Environmental: Tests sewage/water for poliovirus, identifying silent circulation without clinical paralysis.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 210 (Book Page): [Environmental surveillance often confirms wild poliovirus infections in the absence of cases of paralysis. Systematic environmental sampling... provides important supplementary surveillance data.]

category: Describe ‘end game strategy’ by WHO for polio eradication
front: A 12-year-old child presents with sudden onset flaccid limb weakness; what is the mandatory surveillance response?
back:
- Prompt reporting as AFP.
- Collection of two stool specimens 24-48 hours apart within 14 days of onset.
- Follow-up at 60 days for residual paralysis.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 210 (Book Page): [They must promptly report every case of acute flaccid paralysis (AFP) in any child under 15 years of age... two specimens — taken 24-48 hours apart are required.]

category: Describe ‘end game strategy’ by WHO for polio eradication
front: What is the pharmacological role of Inactivated Polio Vaccine (IPV) in the OPV withdrawal strategy?
back: IPV must be introduced globally before withdrawing OPV components to maintain immunity against Type 2 and mitigate VDPV emergence risks.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 212 (Book Page): [Because of these risks of emergence of vaccine-derived polioviruses, OPV use will be discontinued worldwide once all WPV transmission has been interrupted (i.e. inactivated polio vaccine (IPV) will replace OPV).]

category: Describe ‘end game strategy’ by WHO for polio eradication
front: State the minimum sensitivity indicator for AFP surveillance in a polio-endemic region.
back: Detect at least two cases of non-polio AFP annually per 100,000 population aged less than 15 years.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 210 (Book Page): [In endemic regions, to ensure even higher sensitivity, this rate should be two per 100,000.]

category: Describe ‘end game strategy’ by WHO for polio eradication
front: Define the three categories of Vaccine-Derived Polioviruses (VDPV) targeted in the endgame plan.
back:
- cVDPV: Circulating (community transmission).
- iVDPV: Immunodeficiency-associated (prolonged infection in patients).
- aVDPV: Ambiguous (source unknown/no known immunodeficiency).
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 210 (Book Page): [VDPVs are divided into three categories as (1) cVDPVs... (2) immunodeficiency-associated VDPVs (iVDPVs)... and (3) ambiguous VDPVs (aVDPVs).]

category: Describe ‘end game strategy’ by WHO for polio eradication
front: What criteria define 'adequate' stool specimens required for certifying polio eradication?
back:
- Two specimens of sufficient quantity.
- Collected ≥24 hours apart.
- Taken within 14 days of paralysis onset.
- Arrive in laboratory via reverse cold chain.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 210 (Book Page): [‘Adequate’ stool specimens are two stool specimens of sufficient quantity for laboratory analysis, collected at least 24 hours apart, within 14 days after the onset of paralysis, and arriving in the laboratory by reverse cold chain.]

category: Describe ‘end game strategy’ by WHO for polio eradication
front: How does 'Legacy Planning' contribute to the WHO polio endgame strategy?
back: It ensures the transfer of polio-funded infrastructure, learning, and personnel to benefit other public health goals and childhood immunization systems.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 210 (Book Page): [Successful legacy planning will include the mainstreaming of essential polio functions into on-going public health programmes... and the transition of assets and infrastructure to benefit other development goals.]

category: Describe ‘end game strategy’ by WHO for polio eradication
front: What are the storage and shipping temperature requirements for stool specimens in AFP surveillance?
back: Stored immediately at 4-8°C with frozen ice packs in a cold box; must arrive at the laboratory within 72 hours.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 210 (Book Page): [Stool specimens have to be sealed in containers and stored immediately inside a refrigerator or packed between frozen ice packs at 4-8°C in a cold box... arrive at the laboratory within 72 hours.]

category: Describe ‘end game strategy’ by WHO for polio eradication
front: What are the four primary objectives of the WHO Polio Eradication and Endgame Strategic Plan 2013-2018?
back:
1. Detect and interrupt all poliovirus transmission.
2. Strengthen immunization systems and withdraw OPV.
3. Containment and certification.
4. Legacy planning.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 209 (Book Page): The plan has 4 objectives: 1. Detect and interrupt all poliovirus transmission... 2. Strengthen immunization system and withdraw oral polio vaccine... 3. Containment and certification... 4. Legacy planning.

category: Describe ‘end game strategy’ by WHO for polio eradication
front: Explain the pathophysiological rationale for removing the Type 2 component from Oral Polio Vaccine (OPV).
back: Wild Type 2 is already eradicated. The Type 2 Sabin strain is the primary cause of vaccine-derived poliovirus (VDPV) outbreaks due to prolonged replication and mutation.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 209 (Book Page): As wild poliovirus type 2 was eradicated in 1999, and the main cause of VDPV outbreaks is currently type 2 component of OPV, this component must be removed.

category: Describe ‘end game strategy’ by WHO for polio eradication
front: Contrast the composition of bivalent OPV (bOPV) versus trivalent OPV (tOPV) in the end-game strategy.
back: tOPV contains Sabin types 1, 2, and 3. bOPV contains only types 1 and 3, effectively removing the VDPV-prone Type 2 component.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 209 (Book Page): Preparation for this removal entails... replacing the trivalent OPV with bivalent OPV in all OPV using countries.

category: Describe ‘end game strategy’ by WHO for polio eradication
front: A child presents with AFP 6 months after bOPV switch; isolates show cVDPV. Define the response target.
back: The WHO end-game strategy mandates the rapid interruption of any new VDPV outbreak within 6 months of the index case's detection.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 209 (Book Page): ensuring rapid outbreak response. It also includes stopping any new polio outbreak due to vaccine-derived poliovirus (VDPV) within 6 months of the index case.

category: Describe ‘end game strategy’ by WHO for polio eradication
front: What mandatory pharmacological step must countries take before switching from trivalent OPV to bivalent OPV?
back: Introduction of at least one dose of Inactivated Polio Vaccine (IPV) into the routine schedule to maintain population immunity against Type 2 poliovirus.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 212 (Book Page): OPV use will be discontinued worldwide once all WPV transmission has been interrupted (i.e. inactivated polio vaccine (IPV) will replace OPV).

category: Describe ‘end game strategy’ by WHO for polio eradication
front: State the minimum annual non-polio Acute Flaccid Paralysis (AFP) rate required for certification-standard surveillance.
back: At least 1 case of non-polio AFP per 100,000 population aged less than 15 years (2 per 100,000 in endemic regions).
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 210 (Book Page): A country's surveillance system needs to be sensitive enough to detect at least one case of AFP for every 100,000 children under 15.

category: Describe ‘end game strategy’ by WHO for polio eradication
front: How does the end-game strategy address poliovirus stocks in laboratories after global eradication certification?
back: Containment: All wild poliovirus stocks must be destroyed or strictly biocontained in a small number of WHO-certified facilities to prevent re-introduction.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 209 (Book Page): This objective encompasses the certification of the eradication and containment of all wild poliovirus... recognizing that a small number of facilities will need to retain poliovirus stocks.

category: Describe ‘end game strategy’ by WHO for polio eradication
front: Differentiate between VAPP and cVDPV regarding their risk of community transmission during the end-game.
back: VAPP is a rare individual adverse event with no community spread. cVDPVs are genetically shifted viruses capable of sustained person-to-person transmission.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 212 (Book Page): cVDPVs, when evidence of person-to-person transmission in the community exists... cVDPVs pose the same public health threat as WPVs.

category: Describe ‘end game strategy’ by WHO for polio eradication
front: Describe the physiological shift in immunity when IPV replaces OPV globally in the final stages.
back: IPV provides systemic humoral immunity (circulating antibodies) but lacks local intestinal immunity (IgA), eliminating viral shedding and mutation risks.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 213 (Book Page): IPV induces humoral antibodies... but does not induce intestinal or local immunity... circulating antibodies protect the individual against paralytic polio, but do not prevent reinfection of the gut.

category: Describe ‘end game strategy’ by WHO for polio eradication
front: Define 'Legacy Planning' as a core pillar of the WHO Polio Eradication Strategic Plan.
back: Mainstreaming polio infrastructure (surveillance, logistics) into existing health systems to benefit other initiatives like routine immunization and disaster response.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 209 (Book Page): successful legacy planning will include the mainstreaming of essential polio functions into on-going public health programmes... transition of assets and infrastructure.

category: Describe ‘end game strategy’ by WHO for polio eradication
front: Q: What is the official title and duration of the WHO strategy for final polio eradication?
back: Polio Eradication and Endgame Strategic Plan 2013-2018.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 209 (Book Page): [Recognizing the epidemiological opportunity and the significant risk of potential failure, the new Polio Eradication and Endgame Strategic Plan 2013-2018 has been developed.]

category: Describe ‘end game strategy’ by WHO for polio eradication
front: Q: What are the four primary objectives of the Polio Eradication and Endgame Strategic Plan?
back:
1. Detect and interrupt transmission
2. Strengthen systems and withdraw OPV
3. Containment and certification
4. Legacy planning
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 209 (Book Page): [The plan has 4 objectives : 1. Detect and interrupt all poliovirus transmission... 2. Strengthen immunization system and withdraw oral polio vaccine... 3. Containment and certification... 4. Legacy planning.]

category: Describe ‘end game strategy’ by WHO for polio eradication
front: Q: Which poliovirus type was specifically targeted for removal from routine immunization by mid-2016?
back: Wild Poliovirus Type 2 (the type 2 component of the Oral Polio Vaccine).
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 210 (Book Page): [As wild poliovirus type 2 was eradicated in 1999, and the main cause of VDPV outbreaks is currently type 2 component of OPV, this component must be removed from the vaccine by mid-2016.]

category: Describe ‘end game strategy’ by WHO for polio eradication
front: Q: In the Endgame strategy, what transition is required regarding the OPV formulation used globally?
back: Replacing trivalent OPV (tOPV) with bivalent OPV (bOPV) in all OPV-using countries.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 210 (Book Page): [Preparation for this removal entails... replacing the trivalent OPV with bivalent OPV in all OPV using countries.]

category: Describe ‘end game strategy’ by WHO for polio eradication
front: Q: Why is Inactivated Polio Vaccine (IPV) introduced into the schedule during the OPV withdrawal phase?
back: To mitigate the risk of outbreaks from vaccine-derived polioviruses (VDPV) and ensure baseline immunity.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 210 (Book Page): [To eliminate all VDPV risks, in the long-term, all OPV must be removed... OPV use will be discontinued worldwide once all WPV transmission has been interrupted (i.e. inactivated polio vaccine (IPV) will replace OPV)]

category: Describe ‘end game strategy’ by WHO for polio eradication
front: Q: What is the specific target timeframe for stopping new vaccine-derived poliovirus (VDPV) outbreaks?
back: Within 6 months of the index case.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 210 (Book Page): [It also includes stopping any new polio outbreak due to vaccine-derived poliovirus (VDPV) within 6 months of the index case.]

category: Describe ‘end game strategy’ by WHO for polio eradication
front: Q: What does 'Legacy Planning' entail in the context of the Polio Endgame strategy?
back: Transferring polio eradication infrastructure, knowledge, and assets to other national and global health priorities.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 210 (Book Page): [Legacy planning: ...include the mainstreaming of essential polio functions into on-going public health programmes... and the transition of assets and infrastructure to benefit other development goals.]

category: Describe ‘end game strategy’ by WHO for polio eradication
front: Q: A child is diagnosed with VDPV. Explain why this is a clinical priority in the Endgame strategy.
back: VDPVs resemble wild polioviruses biologically, can cause paralysis, and signal prolonged replication or transmission in low-immunity areas.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 212 (Book Page): [VDPVs resemble WPVs biologically... they have genetic properties consistent with prolonged replication or transmission... cVDPVs pose the same public health threat as WPVs.]

category: Describe ‘end game strategy’ by WHO for polio eradication
front: Q: What is the goal of the 'Containment' objective within the polio eradication framework?
back: Ensuring wild poliovirus stocks are safely handled and biocontained in a limited number of authorized facilities.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 210 (Book Page): [Containment and certification: ...recognizing that a small number of facilities will need to retain poliovirus stocks in the post-eradication era... Criteria for the safe handling and biocontainment of such poliovirus... are essential.]

category: Describe ‘end game strategy’ by WHO for polio eradication
front: Q: By what date was the WHO South-East Asia Region (SEAR), including India, certified polio-free?
back: 27th March 2014.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 209 (Book Page): [India has not reported any polio case since January 2011, and has been declared polio-free since 27th March 2014. ...SEAR (2014).]

category: Describe ‘end game strategy’ by WHO for polio eradication
front: Q: List the four primary objectives of the Polio Eradication and Endgame Strategic Plan 2013-2018.
back:
1. Detect and interrupt all poliovirus transmission.
2. Strengthen immunization systems and withdraw oral polio vaccine (OPV).
3. Containment and certification.
4. Legacy planning (mainstreaming assets).
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 209 (Book Page): The plan has 4 objectives : 1. Detect and interrupt all poliovirus transmission... 2. Strengthen immunization system and withdraw oral polio vaccine... 3. Containment and certification... 4. Legacy planning.

category: Describe ‘end game strategy’ by WHO for polio eradication
front: Q: Why does the WHO endgame strategy mandate the eventual withdrawal of all Oral Polio Vaccine (OPV)?
back: To eliminate the risk of Vaccine-Derived Polioviruses (VDPV) and Vaccine-Associated Paralytic Poliomyelitis (VAPP). Long-term eradication requires replacing live-attenuated OPV with Inactivated Polio Vaccine (IPV).
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 210 (Book Page): To eliminate all VDPV risks, in the long-term, all OPV must be removed from routine immunization programmes.

category: Describe ‘end game strategy’ by WHO for polio eradication
front: Q: Describe the significance of the 'tOPV to bOPV switch' in the polio endgame strategy.
back: Trivalent OPV is replaced by bivalent OPV (types 1 and 3). This removes the Type 2 component, which is the primary cause of circulating Vaccine-Derived Poliovirus (cVDPV) outbreaks.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 210 (Book Page): As wild poliovirus type 2 was eradicated in 1999, and the main cause of VDPV outbreaks is currently type 2 component of OPV, this component must be removed... replacing the trivalent OPV with bivalent OPV.

category: Describe ‘end game strategy’ by WHO for polio eradication
front: Q: What is the specific target for interrupting Vaccine-Derived Poliovirus (VDPV) outbreaks under the Endgame Plan?
back: The strategy aims to stop any new polio outbreak caused by vaccine-derived strains within 6 months of the index case's detection.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 209 (Book Page): It also includes stopping any new polio outbreak due to vaccine-derived poliovirus (VDPV) within 6 months of the index case.

category: Describe ‘end game strategy’ by WHO for polio eradication
front: Q: What is the pharmacological role of introducing IPV into routine schedules during the OPV withdrawal phase?
back: IPV provides systemic immunity against all three types (1, 2, and 3). It maintains population immunity against Type 2 while the Type 2 component is removed from OPV.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 210 (Book Page): Preparation for this removal entails strengthening routine immunization system... introducing immunization programme globally and then replacing the trivalent OPV with bivalent OPV.

category: Describe ‘end game strategy’ by WHO for polio eradication
front: Q: State the gold-standard surveillance method used to verify polio eradication in the endgame strategy.
back: Acute Flaccid Paralysis (AFP) Surveillance. It requires finding, reporting, and virological testing (stool samples) of every case of AFP in children under 15 years.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 210 (Book Page): Acute flaccid paralysis surveillance: ...Finding and reporting children with acute flaccid paralysis (AFP)... The number of AFP cases reported each year is used as an indicator of a country's ability to detect polio.

category: Describe ‘end game strategy’ by WHO for polio eradication
front: Q: Define 'Legacy Planning' as part of the WHO Polio Endgame Strategy.
back: The transition of polio infrastructure, learning, and assets into other national public health programs to ensure the eradication investment benefits other global health priorities.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 210 (Book Page): Legacy planning: ...mainstreaming of essential polio functions into on-going public health programmes... transition of assets and infrastructure to benefit other development goals.

category: Describe ‘end game strategy’ by WHO for polio eradication
front: Q: Differentiate between cVDPV and iVDPV within the context of endgame surveillance.
back:
cVDPV: Shows evidence of person-to-person transmission in the community. 
iVDPV: Isolated from individuals with primary immunodeficiencies who have prolonged virus excretion.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 212 (Book Page): (1) cVDPVs, when evidence of person-to-person transmission in the community exists; (2) immunodeficiency-associated VDPVs (iVDPVs), which are isolates from persons with primary immunodeficiencies.

category: Describe ‘end game strategy’ by WHO for polio eradication
front: Q: How does Objective 3 of the Endgame Plan address laboratory safety?
back: Through strict biocontainment: certifying the safe handling of retained poliovirus stocks in essential facilities (for research/vaccines) to prevent accidental re-introduction.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 210 (Book Page): Containment and certification: ...certification of the eradication and containment of all wild poliovirus... criteria for the safe handling and biocontainment of such poliovirus... are essential.

category: Describe ‘end game strategy’ by WHO for polio eradication
front: Q: What is the target year for the global certification of polio eradication under the Strategic Plan?
back: The strategy aims for certification of all WHO regions as polio-free by the end of 2018 (within the 2013-2018 framework).
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 210 (Book Page): This objective encompasses the certification of the eradication and containment of all wild poliovirus in all WHO regions by end of 2018.

category: Describe ‘end game strategy’ by WHO for polio eradication
front: Q: What are the four primary objectives of the WHO Polio Eradication and Endgame Strategic Plan 2013-2018?
back:
1. Detect and interrupt all poliovirus transmission.
2. Strengthen immunization systems and withdraw OPV.
3. Containment and certification.
4. Legacy planning.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 210 (Book Page): [The plan has 4 objectives : 1. Detect and interrupt all poliovirus transmission... 2. Strengthen immunization system and withdraw oral polio vaccine... 3. Containment and certification... 4. Legacy planning.]

category: Describe ‘end game strategy’ by WHO for polio eradication
front: Q: Why is the withdrawal of the Type 2 component from Oral Polio Vaccine (OPV) prioritized in the strategy?
back: Wild poliovirus Type 2 was eradicated in 1999, but its component in OPV is now the primary cause of vaccine-derived poliovirus (VDPV) outbreaks.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 210 (Book Page): [As wild poliovirus type 2 was eradicated in 1999, and the main cause of VDPV outbreaks is currently type 2 component of OPV, this component must be removed from the vaccine by mid-2016.]

category: Describe ‘end game strategy’ by WHO for polio eradication
front: Q: Describe the 'switch' required globally to eliminate VDPV risks according to the WHO strategy.
back: Replacing trivalent OPV (tOPV) with bivalent OPV (bOPV) in all routine immunization programs after introducing at least one dose of IPV.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 210 (Book Page): [Preparation for this removal entails strengthening routine immunization system... introducing immunization programme globally and then replacing the trivalent OPV with bivalent OPV in all OPV using countries.]

category: Describe ‘end game strategy’ by WHO for polio eradication
front: Q: A district reports zero AFP cases over 12 months. Does this satisfy WHO endgame surveillance sensitivity standards?
back: No. The system must detect at least 1 non-polio AFP case per 100,000 children under 15 (2 per 100,000 in endemic regions) to prove sensitivity.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 210 (Book Page): [A country's surveillance system needs to be sensitive enough to detect at least one case of AFP for every 100,000 children under 15 — even in the absence of polio. In endemic regions... this rate should be two per 100,000.]

category: Describe ‘end game strategy’ by WHO for polio eradication
front: Q: What is the specific purpose of introducing Inactivated Polio Vaccine (IPV) during the OPV withdrawal phase?
back: To provide essential immunity against Type 2 poliovirus and mitigate the risk of paralysis if Type 2 VDPV emerges or is imported.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 212 (Book Page): [Because of these risks of emergence of vaccine-derived polioviruses, OPV use will be discontinued worldwide once all WPV transmission has been interrupted (i.e. inactivated polio vaccine (IPV) will replace OPV)]

category: Describe ‘end game strategy’ by WHO for polio eradication
front: Q: Define the 'Adequate Stool Specimens' criteria required for AFP surveillance under WHO guidelines.
back: Two specimens collected 24–48 hours apart, within 14 days of paralysis onset, arriving at the laboratory via reverse cold chain.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 210 (Book Page): [‘Adequate’ stool specimens are two stool specimens of sufficient quantity for laboratory analysis, collected at least 24 hours apart, within 14 days after the onset of paralysis, and arriving in the laboratory by reverse cold chain.]

category: Describe ‘end game strategy’ by WHO for polio eradication
front: Q: How does Environmental Surveillance supplement AFP monitoring in the Endgame Strategy?
back: It detects poliovirus (WPV or VDPV) in sewage or environmental samples, identifying silent circulation in the absence of clinical paralysis cases.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 210 (Book Page): [Environmental surveillance often confirms wild poliovirus infections in the absence of cases of paralysis. Systematic environmental sampling... provides important supplementary surveillance data.]

category: Describe ‘end game strategy’ by WHO for polio eradication
front: Q: Differentiate between iVDPV and cVDPV in the context of WHO surveillance.
back: iVDPV: Isolated from persons with primary immunodeficiencies (prolonged infection). cVDPV: Evidence of person-to-person transmission in the community exists.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 212 (Book Page): [cVDPVs, when evidence of person-to-person transmission in the community exists; (2) immunodeficiency-associated VDPVs (iVDPVs), which are isolates from persons with primary immunodeficiencies...]

category: Describe ‘end game strategy’ by WHO for polio eradication
front: Q: What is the primary goal of the 'Legacy Planning' component in the Polio Endgame Strategy?
back: Mainstreaming polio assets and infrastructure (surveillance, logistics) into existing health programs to benefit other global health priorities post-eradication.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 210 (Book Page): [Legacy planning: ...mainstreaming of essential polio functions into on-going public health programmes... and the transition of assets and infrastructure to benefit other development goals...]

category: Describe ‘end game strategy’ by WHO for polio eradication
front: Q: Within the endgame strategy, what constitutes an 'outbreak' requiring immediate response?
back: The detection of even a single case of wild poliovirus (WPV) is considered an outbreak and requires response within 48 hours.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 215 (Book Page): [The occurrence of a single case of polio is now considered as an epidemic, and should prompt an immediate epidemiological investigation... preventive measures are initiated, usually within 48 hours of notification.]

category: Discuss the global distribution of measles, mumps, rubella, and their occurrence in different population groups
front: Q: At what threshold of community susceptibility do measles epidemics typically occur?
back: - Occur when the proportion of susceptible children reaches approximately 40%.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 152 (Book Page): Measles is endemic virtually in all parts of the world. It tends to occur in epidemics when the proportion of susceptible children reaches about 40 per cent.

category: Discuss the global distribution of measles, mumps, rubella, and their occurrence in different population groups
front: Q: Why is measles mortality significantly higher in malnourished children?
back:
- Poor cell-mediated immune response.
- Prolonged excretion of the measles virus.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 153 (Book Page): This may possibly be related to poor cell-mediated immunity response, secondary to malnutrition... Additionally, severely malnourished children have been shown to excrete measles virus for longer periods.

category: Discuss the global distribution of measles, mumps, rubella, and their occurrence in different population groups
front: Q: Contrast the subclinical infection rates between Measles and Rubella.
back:
- Measles: Subclinical cases are rare.
- Rubella: A large number of infections are subclinical (major epidemiological difference).
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 156 (Book Page): A large number of rubella infections are, in fact, subclinical. This represents one of the major differences between measles and rubella.

category: Discuss the global distribution of measles, mumps, rubella, and their occurrence in different population groups
front: Q: What is the primary risk to a non-immune pregnant woman in a community with endemic Rubella?
back:
- Vertical transmission across the placenta.
- Resulting in Congenital Rubella Syndrome (CRS) or fetal death.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 156 (Book Page): Infection in early pregnancy may result in serious congenital defects, including death of the foetus... The virus can cross the placenta (vertical transmission) and infect the foetus in utero.

category: Discuss the global distribution of measles, mumps, rubella, and their occurrence in different population groups
front: Q: Why is the Measles vaccine age-shifted to 12 months in developed versus 9 months in developing countries?
back: - To avoid the blocking effect of persistent transplacentally acquired maternal antibodies, which last longer in lower-incidence areas.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 155 (Book Page): In countries where the incidence of measles has declined, the age of immunization is being raised to 12 months in order to avoid the blocking effect of persistent transplacentally acquired antibody.

category: Discuss the global distribution of measles, mumps, rubella, and their occurrence in different population groups
front: Q: State the clinical surveillance case definition for Mumps.
back:
- Acute onset of unilateral/bilateral tender swelling of parotid or other salivary glands.
- Lasting 2 or more days without other cause.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 159 (Book Page): Clinical mumps : acute onset of unilateral or bilateral tender, self-limited swelling of the parotid or other salivary gland, lasting 2 or more days and without other apparent cause.

category: Discuss the global distribution of measles, mumps, rubella, and their occurrence in different population groups
front: Q: How has widespread immunization altered the age-group distribution of Rubella?
back:
- Shift from children (3-10 years) to adolescents/adults.
- Over 70% of cases in developed countries now occur in persons >15 years old.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 156 (Book Page): Mainly a disease of childhood particularly in the age group 3 to 10 years. Persons older than 15 years now account for over 70 per cent cases in developed countries.

category: Discuss the global distribution of measles, mumps, rubella, and their occurrence in different population groups
front: Q: Compare Measles infection rates between virgin communities and endemic areas.
back:
- Virgin communities: >90% infection rate.
- Endemic areas: Periodic epidemics when susceptibles reach 40%.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 152 (Book Page): When the disease is introduced into a virgin community more than 90 per cent of that community will be infected.

category: Discuss the global distribution of measles, mumps, rubella, and their occurrence in different population groups
front: Q: Explain the seasonal distribution of Measles in tropical vs. temperate zones.
back:
- Tropical: Peak during the dry season.
- Temperate: Peak during winter (due to indoor crowding).
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 153 (Book Page): In tropical zones, most cases of measles occur during the dry season. In temperate climates, measles is a winter disease, probably because people crowd together indoors.

category: Discuss the global distribution of measles, mumps, rubella, and their occurrence in different population groups
front: Q: What percentage of Indian women of child-bearing age remain susceptible to Rubella?
back: - Approximately 40%.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 156 (Book Page): Studies in India indicate that approximately 40 per cent of women of child-bearing age are susceptible to rubella.

category: Discuss the global distribution of measles, mumps, rubella, and their occurrence in different population groups
front: Q: Contrast the current global distribution of measles between industrialized and developing nations.
back:
- Rare in industrialized countries due to high vaccine coverage.
- Endemic in virtually all parts of the world.
- Remains a common illness and major mortality cause in developing countries.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 152 (Book Page): [Measles is endemic virtually in all parts of the world... While measles is now rare in industrialized countries, it remains a common illness in many developing countries.]

category: Discuss the global distribution of measles, mumps, rubella, and their occurrence in different population groups
front: Q: How does the age of measles incidence vary between developing and developed countries?
back:
- Developing countries: Infancy and early childhood (6 months to 3 years).
- Developed countries: Older children, usually over 5 years of age.
- Environmental and socioeconomic factors determine this shift.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 153 (Book Page): [between 6 months and 3 years of age in developing countries... and older children usually over 5 years in developed countries (10).]

category: Discuss the global distribution of measles, mumps, rubella, and their occurrence in different population groups
front: Q: At what threshold of population susceptibility do measles epidemics typically occur?
back:
- Occurs when the proportion of susceptible children reaches approximately 40%.
- Introduction into virgin communities infects over 90% of the population.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 152 (Book Page): [It tends to occur in epidemics when the proportion of susceptible children reaches about 40 per cent (1). When the disease is introduced into a virgin community more than 90 per cent of that community will be infected (2).]

category: Discuss the global distribution of measles, mumps, rubella, and their occurrence in different population groups
front: Q: What is the typical epidemic cycle of rubella in non-immunized populations worldwide?
back:
- Worldwide distribution.
- Epidemics occur every 6 to 8 years in non-immunized groups.
- Primarily targets children aged 3 to 10 years.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 156 (Book Page): [The disease is worldwide in distribution and tends to occur in epidemics, in non-immunized populations, every 6 to 8 years (1).]

category: Discuss the global distribution of measles, mumps, rubella, and their occurrence in different population groups
front: Q: Describe the shift in rubella age-groups observed in developed countries following vaccination campaigns.
back:
- Shift from childhood (3-10 years) to adolescents and adults.
- Persons older than 15 years now account for over 70% of cases.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 156 (Book Page): [Mainly a disease of childhood particularly in the age group 3 to 10 years. Persons older than 15 years now account for over 70 per cent cases in developed countries]

category: Discuss the global distribution of measles, mumps, rubella, and their occurrence in different population groups
front: Q: What percentage of Indian women of child-bearing age remain susceptible to rubella?
back:
- Approximately 40% of women of child-bearing age.
- High risk for Congenital Rubella Syndrome (CRS) outbreaks in non-immunized populations.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 156 (Book Page): [Studies in India indicate that approximately 40 per cent of women of child-bearing age are susceptible to rubella (5).]

category: Discuss the global distribution of measles, mumps, rubella, and their occurrence in different population groups
front: Q: What is the global annual incidence and epidemic frequency of mumps in non-immunized communities?
back:
- Incidence: 100–1000 cases per 100,000 population.
- Epidemic peaks occur every 2 to 5 years.
- Distribution is worldwide.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 158 (Book Page): [the annual incidence of mumps in the absence of immunization is in the range of 100-1000 cases/100,000 population with epidemic peak every 2—5 years.]

category: Discuss the global distribution of measles, mumps, rubella, and their occurrence in different population groups
front: Q: Which specific age group is most frequently affected by mumps parotitis?
back:
- Children in the age group 5 to 9 years.
- Incidence age is typically higher than measles, chickenpox, or whooping cough.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 158 (Book Page): [Mumps is the most frequent cause of parotitis in children in the age group 5—9 years. The average age of incidence of mumps is higher than with measles, chickenpox or whooping cough.]

category: Discuss the global distribution of measles, mumps, rubella, and their occurrence in different population groups
front: Q: How does population nutrition status affect measles mortality in developing regions?
back:
- Malnourished children have mortality rates 400 times higher than well-nourished children.
- Associated with poor cell-mediated immunity and prolonged viral excretion.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 153 (Book Page): [Measles tends to be very severe in the malnourished child, carrying a mortality upto 400 times higher than in well-nourished children... secondary to malnutrition (13).]

category: Discuss the global distribution of measles, mumps, rubella, and their occurrence in different population groups
front: Q: Identify the primary target population for rubella vaccination to prevent congenital infection.
back:
- First Priority: Women of child-bearing age (15–34 or 39 years).
- Second Priority: Interrupt transmission by vaccinating all children aged 1–14 years.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 157 (Book Page): [priorities being first to protect women of child-bearing age (15-34 or 39 years of age) and then to interrupt transmission of rubella by vaccinating all children currently aged 1-14 years]

category: Describe ‘end game strategy’ by WHO for polio eradication
front: Q: Primary goal of the WHO Polio Eradication and Endgame Strategic Plan 2013-2018?
back: Simultaneous eradication of all types of polio disease, including both wild poliovirus (WPV) and vaccine-derived poliovirus (VDPV).
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 209 (Book Page): [The Polio Eradication and Endgame Strategic Plan 2013-2018... is the first plan to eradicate all types of polio disease simultaneously — both due to wild poliovirus and due to vaccine-derived poliovirus.]

category: Describe ‘end game strategy’ by WHO for polio eradication
front: Q: Specific timelines for interrupting transmission under Objective 1 of the Polio Endgame Plan?
back:
1. Stop all wild polio transmission by end of 2014.
2. Stop any new VDPV outbreak within 6 months of the index case.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 209 (Book Page): [Objective 1: ...stop all wild polio transmission by the end of 2014... and ensuring rapid outbreak response. It also includes stopping any new polio outbreak due to vaccine-derived poliovirus (VDPV) within 6 months of the index case.]

category: Describe ‘end game strategy’ by WHO for polio eradication
front: Q: What vaccine transition is mandated under Objective 2 of the Polio Endgame Strategy?
back: Replacement of trivalent OPV (tOPV) with bivalent OPV (bOPV) in all OPV-using countries, plus global introduction of Inactivated Polio Vaccine (IPV).
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 209 (Book Page): [Objective 2: ...introducing IPV globally and then replacing the trivalent OPV with bivalent OPV in all OPV using countries.]

category: Describe ‘end game strategy’ by WHO for polio eradication
front: Q: How is the diagnosis of Vaccine-Derived Poliovirus (VDPV) laboratory-confirmed in surveillance?
back: Using real-time reverse transcription-polymerase chain reaction (rRT-PCR) to target specific nucleotide substitutions occurring early in VDPV emergence.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 212 (Book Page): [The diagnosis is made by real-time reverse transcription-polymerase chain reaction (rRT-PCR) nucleic acid amplification targetted to nucleotide substitution that occur early in VDPV emergence.]

category: Describe ‘end game strategy’ by WHO for polio eradication
front: Q: Why does the Polio Endgame Plan prioritize withdrawing the Type 2 component from OPV first?
back:
1. Wild Poliovirus Type 2 was eradicated in 1999.
2. The Sabin Type 2 component in tOPV is the primary cause of VDPV outbreaks.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 209 (Book Page): [As wild poliovirus type 2 was eradicated in 1999, and the main cause of VDPV outbreaks is currently type 2 component of OPV, this component must be removed.]

category: Describe ‘end game strategy’ by WHO for polio eradication
front: Q: What are the two key goals of Objective 3 in the Polio Eradication Endgame?
back:
1. Certification of global polio eradication.
2. Containment of all remaining wild poliovirus stocks in laboratory facilities by the end of 2018.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 209 (Book Page): [Objective 3: Containment and certification: This objective encompasses the certification of the eradication and containment of all wild poliovirus in all WHO regions by end of 2018.]

category: Describe ‘end game strategy’ by WHO for polio eradication
front: Q: Define 'Legacy Planning' as an objective of the WHO Polio Eradication strategy.
back: Transitioning polio program infrastructure, assets, and learning to on-going national public health programs and other global health priorities.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 210 (Book Page): [Objective 4: Legacy planning... successful legacy planning will include the mainstreaming of essential polio functions into on-going public health programmes... and the transition of assets and infrastructure to benefit other development goals.]

category: Describe ‘end game strategy’ by WHO for polio eradication
front: Q: Why is 'Containment' critical post-2018 according to the WHO Polio Strategy?
back: To minimize the risk of poliovirus re-introduction from the small number of facilities retaining stocks for vaccine production, diagnosis, and research.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 209 (Book Page): [Criteria for the safe handling and biocontainment of such poliovirus... are essential to minimize the risk of poliovirus re-introduction in the post-eradication era.]

category: Describe ‘end game strategy’ by WHO for polio eradication
front: Q: What immunization strategy reduces the risk of VAPP and VDPV while maintaining mucosal immunity?
back: Sequential administration of 1–2 doses of Inactivated Polio Vaccine (IPV) followed by at least 2 doses of Oral Polio Vaccine (OPV).
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 214 (Book Page): [Combined schedules of IPV and OPV appear to reduce or prevent VAPP while maintaining the high levels of intestinal mucosal immunity conferred by OPV.]

category: Describe ‘end game strategy’ by WHO for polio eradication
front: Q: What is the minimum standard for Acute Flaccid Paralysis (AFP) surveillance sensitivity?
back: Detection of at least one case of non-polio AFP annually per 100,000 population aged less than 15 years.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 210 (Book Page): [A country's surveillance system needs to be sensitive enough to detect at least one case of AFP for every 100,000 children under 15 — even in the absence of polio.]

category: Discuss the global distribution of measles, mumps, rubella, and their occurrence in different population groups
front: Q: Describe the global distribution pattern of Measles in industrialized versus developing countries.
back: Endemic worldwide. It is rare in industrialized countries due to high vaccine coverage, but remains a common illness with high morbidity/mortality in many developing countries.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 152 (Book Page): [Measles is endemic virtually in all parts of the world. While measles is now rare in industrialized countries, it remains a common illness in many developing countries.]

category: Discuss the global distribution of measles, mumps, rubella, and their occurrence in different population groups
front: Q: How does the age distribution of Measles differ between developing and developed countries?
back: Developing countries: Children between 6 months and 3 years. Developed countries: Older children, usually over 5 years of age.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 153 (Book Page): [AGE : Affects virtually everyone in infancy or childhood — between 6 months and 3 years of age in developing countries... and older children usually over 5 years in developed countries]

category: Discuss the global distribution of measles, mumps, rubella, and their occurrence in different population groups
front: Q: At what threshold of population susceptibility do Measles epidemics typically occur?
back: Epidemics tend to occur when the proportion of susceptible children in a community reaches approximately 40%.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 152 (Book Page): [It tends to occur in epidemics when the proportion of susceptible children reaches about 40 per cent (1).]

category: Discuss the global distribution of measles, mumps, rubella, and their occurrence in different population groups
front: Q: What is the prevalence of Rubella susceptibility among Indian women of child-bearing age?
back: Approximately 40% of women of child-bearing age in India are estimated to be susceptible to rubella infection.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 156 (Book Page): [Studies in India indicate that approximately 40 per cent of women of child-bearing age are susceptible to rubella (5).]

category: Discuss the global distribution of measles, mumps, rubella, and their occurrence in different population groups
front: Q: Describe the seasonal distribution of Measles in tropical versus temperate zones.
back: Tropical zones: Primarily the dry season. Temperate zones: Primarily winter and early spring, often due to indoor crowding.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 153 (Book Page): [In tropical zones, most cases of measles occur during the dry season. In temperate climates, measles is a winter disease, probably because people crowd together indoors.]

category: Discuss the global distribution of measles, mumps, rubella, and their occurrence in different population groups
front: Q: Which specific age group is most frequently affected by Mumps globally?
back: Mumps most frequently affects children in the 5–9 years age group, though no age is exempt if immunity is lacking.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 158 (Book Page): [Mumps is the most frequent cause of parotitis in children in the age group 5—9 years.]

category: Discuss the global distribution of measles, mumps, rubella, and their occurrence in different population groups
front: Q: Why is the malnourished population group at extreme risk during Measles outbreaks?
back: Mortality is up to 400 times higher. Malnutrition causes poor cell-mediated immunity and leads to prolonged viral excretion.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 153 (Book Page): [Measles tends to be very severe in the malnourished child, carrying a mortality upto 400 times higher than in well-nourished children... related to poor cell-mediated immunity response, secondary to malnutrition]

category: Discuss the global distribution of measles, mumps, rubella, and their occurrence in different population groups
front: Q: What change in Measles/Rubella epidemiology has been observed post-widespread immunization?
back: There is a shift in the average age of incidence, with increased transmission now seen among adolescents and adults.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 152 (Book Page): [the changing epidemiology of measles which has led to increased transmission among adolescents and adults; (6)]

category: Discuss the global distribution of measles, mumps, rubella, and their occurrence in different population groups
front: Q: What is the typical epidemic interval for Rubella in non-immunized populations?
back: Rubella tends to occur in epidemics every 6 to 9 years (some texts cite 6-8 years) in non-immunized groups.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 156 (Book Page): [The disease is worldwide in distribution and tends to occur in epidemics, in non-immunized populations, every 6 to 8 years (1).]

category: Discuss the global distribution of measles, mumps, rubella, and their occurrence in different population groups
front: Q: Does Measles distribution rely on an animal reservoir for persistence?
back: No. Measles occurs only in humans; there is no animal reservoir, making it a candidate for global eradication.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 152 (Book Page): [Measles occurs only in humans. There is no animal reservoir of infection.]

category: Discuss the global distribution of measles, mumps, rubella, and their occurrence in different population groups
front: Q: What is the global endemicity status and epidemic threshold for measles?
back:
- Endemic worldwide.
- Epidemics occur when the susceptible child population reaches approximately 40%.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 152 (Book Page): [Measles is endemic virtually in all parts of the world. It tends to occur in epidemics when the proportion of susceptible children reaches about 40 per cent]

category: Discuss the global distribution of measles, mumps, rubella, and their occurrence in different population groups
front: Q: Contrast the age-wise occurrence of measles in developing versus developed countries.
back:
- Developing: Infancy/childhood (6 months to 3 years).
- Developed: Older children (usually over 5 years).
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 153 (Book Page): [Affects virtually everyone in infancy or childhood — between 6 months and 3 years of age in developing countries... and older children usually over 5 years in developed countries]

category: Discuss the global distribution of measles, mumps, rubella, and their occurrence in different population groups
front: Q: What is the typical epidemic frequency for Rubella in non-immunized populations?
back:
- Worldwide distribution.
- Epidemics tend to occur every 6 to 8 years.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 156 (Book Page): [The disease is worldwide in distribution and tends to occur in epidemics, in non-immunized populations, every 6 to 8 years]

category: Discuss the global distribution of measles, mumps, rubella, and their occurrence in different population groups
front: Q: Based on Indian studies, what is the susceptibility of women of child-bearing age to Rubella?
back:
- Approximately 40% are susceptible.
- This group remains at high risk for vertical transmission (Congenital Rubella).
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 156 (Book Page): [Studies in India indicate that approximately 40 per cent of women of child-bearing age are susceptible to rubella]

category: Discuss the global distribution of measles, mumps, rubella, and their occurrence in different population groups
front: Q: Describe the global annual incidence and epidemic peak of Mumps without immunization.
back:
- Incidence: 100–1000 cases/100,000 population.
- Epidemic peaks: Every 2 to 5 years.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 158 (Book Page): [In most parts of the world, the annual incidence of mumps in the absence of immunization is in the range of 100-1000 cases/100,000 population with epidemic peak every 2—5 years.]

category: Discuss the global distribution of measles, mumps, rubella, and their occurrence in different population groups
front: Q: Which pediatric age group is most frequently affected by Mumps?
back:
- Children aged 5 to 9 years.
- Note: Average age is higher than measles or chickenpox.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 158 (Book Page): [Mumps is the most frequent cause of parotitis in children in the age group 5—9 years. The average age of incidence of mumps is higher than with measles, chickenpox or whooping cough.]

category: Discuss the global distribution of measles, mumps, rubella, and their occurrence in different population groups
front: Q: How has mass immunization impacted the 'immunity gap' and age of incidence for these diseases?
back:
- Traditional epidemiological patterns are disrupted.
- Average age of incidence is rising, shifting targets to the 10–19 year age group.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 129 (Book Page): [raising the average age of incidence, the adolescent age group of 10-19 years represent an important additional target group for immunization.]

category: Discuss the global distribution of measles, mumps, rubella, and their occurrence in different population groups
front: Q: In a 'virgin community', what is the expected infection rate upon introduction of measles?
back:
- Extremely high infectivity.
- More than 90% of the community will be infected.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 152 (Book Page): [When the disease is introduced into a virgin community more than 90 per cent of that community will be infected]

category: Discuss the global distribution of measles, mumps, rubella, and their occurrence in different population groups
front: Q: What is the relationship between malnutrition and measles mortality in developing countries?
back:
- Mortality up to 400 times higher in malnourished children.
- Associated with poor cell-mediated immunity and prolonged virus excretion.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 153 (Book Page): [Measles tends to be very severe in the malnourished child, carrying a mortality upto 400 times higher than in well-nourished children... related to poor cell-mediated immunity response]

category: Discuss the global distribution of measles, mumps, rubella, and their occurrence in different population groups
front: Q: Contrast the seasonal distribution of measles in tropical vs. temperate zones.
back:
- Tropical: Primarily during the dry season.
- Temperate: Primarily a winter disease (due to indoor crowding).
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 153 (Book Page): [In tropical zones, most cases of measles occur during the dry season. In temperate climates, measles is a winter disease, probably because people crowd together indoors.]

category: Discuss the global distribution of measles, mumps, rubella, and their occurrence in different population groups
front: Q: What is the global distribution of measles and the threshold for epidemic occurrence in a population?
back:
• Endemic virtually in all parts of the world.
• Epidemics occur when susceptible children reach approximately 40% of the population.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 152 (Book Page): Measles is endemic virtually in all parts of the world. It tends to occur in epidemics when the proportion of susceptible children reaches about 40 per cent.

category: Discuss the global distribution of measles, mumps, rubella, and their occurrence in different population groups
front: Q: How does malnutrition specifically impact the clinical severity and mortality of measles in childhood populations?
back:
• Increases mortality risk up to 400 times compared to well-nourished children.
• Malnourished children excrete the virus for longer periods, increasing community spread.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 153 (Book Page): Measles tends to be very severe in the malnourished child, carrying a mortality upto 400 times higher than in well-nourished children having measles.

category: Discuss the global distribution of measles, mumps, rubella, and their occurrence in different population groups
front: Q: Contrast the typical age group of measles occurrence in developing countries versus developed countries.
back:
• Developing countries: Infants/children between 6 months and 3 years.
• Developed countries: Older children, usually over 5 years of age.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 153 (Book Page): between 6 months and 3 years of age in developing countries where environmental conditions are generally poor, and older children usually over 5 years in developed countries.

category: Discuss the global distribution of measles, mumps, rubella, and their occurrence in different population groups
front: Q: According to epidemiological studies, what is the rubella susceptibility status of women of child-bearing age in India?
back:
• High susceptibility: Approximately 40% of women in this group remain susceptible.
• This group is prioritized to prevent future Congenital Rubella Syndrome cases.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 156 (Book Page): Studies in India indicate that approximately 40 per cent of women of child-bearing age are susceptible to rubella.

category: Discuss the global distribution of measles, mumps, rubella, and their occurrence in different population groups
front: Q: What are the primary age-group priorities in the vaccination strategy to interrupt rubella transmission globally?
back:
