1. Women of child-bearing age (15–39 years).
2. All children aged 1–14 years.
3. Routine universal immunization of all children at age 1.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 157 (Book Page): priorities being first to protect women of child-bearing age (15-34 or 39 years of age) and then to interrupt transmission of rubella by vaccinating all children currently aged 1-14 years.

category: Discuss the global distribution of measles, mumps, rubella, and their occurrence in different population groups
front: Q: For public health surveillance, what clinical criteria define mumps in an affected population?
back:
• Acute onset of unilateral/bilateral parotid or salivary gland swelling.
• Tenderness and self-limited swelling lasting 2 or more days without other cause.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 159 (Book Page): Clinical mumps : acute onset of unilateral or bilateral tender, self-limited swelling of the parotid or other salivary gland, lasting 2 or more days.

category: Discuss the global distribution of measles, mumps, rubella, and their occurrence in different population groups
front: Q: What is the expected infection rate when measles is introduced into a previously unexposed 'virgin community'?
back:
• Over 90% of the community will become infected.
• This demonstrates the high infectious nature of the measles RNA paramyxovirus.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 152 (Book Page): When the disease is introduced into a virgin community more than 90 per cent of that community will be infected.

category: Discuss the global distribution of measles, mumps, rubella, and their occurrence in different population groups
front: Q: Identify the major epidemiological difference regarding subclinical infections between measles and rubella cases.
back:
• Measles: Subclinical cases are not known to occur.
• Rubella: A large number of infections are subclinical, complicating reservoir control.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 156 (Book Page): A large number of rubella infections are, in fact, subclinical. This represents one of the major differences between measles and rubella.

category: Discuss the global distribution of measles, mumps, rubella, and their occurrence in different population groups
front: Q: What proportion of mumps cases are subclinical, and how does this affect the infection cycle?
back:
• 30–40% of cases are subclinical.
• These cases are responsible for maintaining the continuous cycle of infection in the community.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 158 (Book Page): Subclinical cases which account for 30-40 per cent of all cases appear to be responsible for maintaining the cycle of infection.

category: Discuss the global distribution of measles, mumps, rubella, and their occurrence in different population groups
front: Q: How does the average age of incidence for mumps compare to measles and chickenpox?
back: • Mumps incidence typically occurs at a higher average age than measles, chickenpox, or whooping cough.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 158 (Book Page): The average age of incidence of mumps is higher than with measles, chickenpox or whooping cough.

category: Discuss the global distribution of measles, mumps, rubella, and their occurrence in different population groups
front: Q: What is the global distribution pattern and epidemic threshold for Measles?
back:
• Endemic worldwide
• Epidemics occur when susceptible children reach ~40%
• Rare in industrialized nations; common in developing countries
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 152 (Book Page): [Measles is endemic virtually in all parts of the world. It tends to occur in epidemics when the proportion of susceptible children reaches about 40 per cent (1).]

category: Discuss the global distribution of measles, mumps, rubella, and their occurrence in different population groups
front: Q: Contrast the peak age of Measles incidence in developing versus developed countries.
back:
• Developing: 6 months to 3 years (poor environmental conditions)
• Developed: Older children (>5 years)
• Post-vaccination: Shift toward older age groups
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 153 (Book Page): [between 6 months and 3 years of age in developing countries... and older children usually over 5 years in developed countries (10).]

category: Discuss the global distribution of measles, mumps, rubella, and their occurrence in different population groups
coreConcept: Measles Secondary Attack Rate in Virgin Communities
front: Q: What is the expected infection rate of Measles in a 'virgin' community?
back:
• Greater than 90%
• High infectivity ensures rapid spread in non-immune populations
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 152 (Book Page): [When the disease is introduced into a virgin community more than 90 per cent of that community will be infected (2).]

category: Discuss the global distribution of measles, mumps, rubella, and their occurrence in different population groups
front: Q: Describe the global distribution and epidemic cycle of Rubella.
back:
• Worldwide distribution
• Epidemics occur every 6 to 8 years in non-immunized populations
• Seasonal peaks in late winter and spring (temperate zones)
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 156 (Book Page): [The disease is worldwide in distribution and tends to occur in epidemics, in non-immunized populations, every 6 to 8 years (1).]

category: Discuss the global distribution of measles, mumps, rubella, and their occurrence in different population groups
front: Q: What percentage of Indian women of child-bearing age are susceptible to Rubella?
back:
• Approximately 40%
• Significance: High risk for Congenital Rubella Syndrome (CRS) during pregnancy
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 156 (Book Page): [Studies in India indicate that approximately 40 per cent of women of child-bearing age are susceptible to rubella (5).]

category: Discuss the global distribution of measles, mumps, rubella, and their occurrence in different population groups
front: Q: How has immunization changed the population distribution of Rubella cases in developed countries?
back:
• Shift to older age groups
• Over 70% of cases now occur in persons older than 15 years
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 156 (Book Page): [Persons older than 15 years now account for over 70 per cent cases in developed countries — this is similar to the changing epidemiological pattern with measles]

category: Discuss the global distribution of measles, mumps, rubella, and their occurrence in different population groups
front: Q: What is the typical annual incidence and epidemic peak frequency of Mumps?
back:
• Incidence: 100-1000 cases per 100,000 population
• Epidemic peaks: Every 2–5 years (in absence of immunization)
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 158 (Book Page): [the annual incidence of mumps in the absence of immunization is in the range of 100-1000 cases/100,000 population with epidemic peak every 2—5 years.]

category: Discuss the global distribution of measles, mumps, rubella, and their occurrence in different population groups
front: Q: Which pediatric age group is most frequently affected by Mumps?
back:
• Most frequent in 5–9 year olds
• Note: Average age of incidence is higher than measles or chickenpox
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 158 (Book Page): [Mumps is the most frequent cause of parotitis in children in the age group 5—9 years. The average age of incidence of mumps is higher than with measles]

category: Discuss the global distribution of measles, mumps, rubella, and their occurrence in different population groups
front: Q: What is the primary environmental factor influencing Mumps epidemics?
back:
• Overcrowding
• Peak incidence occurs in winter and spring
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 158 (Book Page): [Epidemics are often associated with overcrowding... the peak incidence is in winter and spring.]

category: Discuss the global distribution of measles, mumps, rubella, and their occurrence in different population groups
front: Q: Why is Measles occurrence particularly lethal in malnourished population groups?
back:
• Mortality is up to 400 times higher
• Related to poor cell-mediated immunity
• Malnourished children excrete virus for longer periods
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 153 (Book Page): [Measles tends to be very severe in the malnourished child, carrying a mortality upto 400 times higher than in well-nourished children... related to poor cell-mediated immunity response]

category: Discuss the global distribution of measles, mumps, rubella, and their occurrence in different population groups
front: Q: How does the age distribution of measles differ between developing and developed countries?
back:
* Developing countries: Children between 6 months and 3 years.
* Developed countries: Older children, usually over 5 years.
* Trend: Shifting toward older age groups due to vaccination.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 154 (Book Page): [Age : Affects virtually everyone in infancy or childhood — between 6 months and 3 years of age in developing countries... and older children usually over 5 years in developed countries.]

category: Discuss the global distribution of measles, mumps, rubella, and their occurrence in different population groups
front: Q: What factor determines the occurrence of measles epidemics in a community?
back:
* Susceptibility threshold: Epidemics occur when susceptible children reach ~40%.
* Introduction: In virgin communities, >90% become infected.
* Cyclical peaks: Occurred every 3 years in India pre-immunization.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 153 (Book Page): [It tends to occur in epidemics when the proportion of susceptible children reaches about 40 per cent... In India, measles is a major cause of morbidity... cyclical increase in the incidence of measles were recorded every third year.]

category: Discuss the global distribution of measles, mumps, rubella, and their occurrence in different population groups
front: Q: How does malnutrition influence measles occurrence and severity in children?
back:
* Mortality: Up to 400 times higher than well-nourished children.
* Viral Shedding: Malnourished children excrete the virus for longer periods.
* Complication: Severe measles can precipitate acute malnutrition in healthy children.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 154 (Book Page): [Measles tends to be very severe in the malnourished child, carrying a mortality upto 400 times higher... malnourished children have been shown to excrete measles virus for longer periods.]

category: Discuss the global distribution of measles, mumps, rubella, and their occurrence in different population groups
front: Q: Describe the global incidence pattern of mumps in non-immunized populations.
back:
* Annual Incidence: 100–1000 cases per 100,000 population.
* Epidemic Peaks: Occur every 2–5 years.
* Geography: Worldwide distribution with high morbidity but negligible mortality.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 159 (Book Page): [In most parts of the world, the annual incidence of mumps in the absence of immunization is in the range of 100-1000 cases/100,000 population with epidemic peak every 2—5 years.]

category: Discuss the global distribution of measles, mumps, rubella, and their occurrence in different population groups
front: Q: What epidemiological role do subclinical mumps cases play in population transmission?
back:
* Frequency: Account for 30–40% of all mumps cases.
* Impact: Responsible for maintaining the cycle of infection in the community.
* Difficulty: Makes control hard as cases are infectious before diagnosis.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 159 (Book Page): [Subclinical cases which account for 30-40 per cent of all cases appear to be responsible for maintaining the cycle of infection.]

category: Discuss the global distribution of measles, mumps, rubella, and their occurrence in different population groups
front: Q: What is the risk of rubella susceptibility among adult women in India?
back:
* Susceptibility: Approximately 40% of women of child-bearing age are susceptible.
* Significance: High risk of Congenital Rubella Syndrome (CRS) if infected during early pregnancy.
* Global Pattern: 10-40% may reach adulthood without infection in absence of vaccine.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 157 (Book Page): [Studies in India indicate that approximately 40 per cent of women of child-bearing age are susceptible to rubella... It is estimated that 10 to 40 per cent of the population could reach adulthood without experiencing rubella infection.]

category: Discuss the global distribution of measles, mumps, rubella, and their occurrence in different population groups
front: Q: Why is rubella less communicable than measles globally?
back:
* Primary Reason: Absence of coughing in rubella compared to measles.
* Transmission: Direct person-to-person via droplets and vertical transmission to fetus.
* Seasonality: Peak incidence in winter and spring (temperate zones).
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 157 (Book Page): [Rubella is much less communicable than measles, probably because of the absence of coughing in rubella.]

category: Discuss the global distribution of measles, mumps, rubella, and their occurrence in different population groups
front: Q: Contrast the occurrence of rubella in areas of high vs. intermediate endemicity.
back:
* High Endemicity (Poor hygiene): Children infected early (90% by age 10); epidemics rare.
* Intermediate Endemicity (Improving hygiene): Children escape infection; leads to higher susceptibility in adolescents/adults and larger outbreaks.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 217 (Book Page): [In developing countries with very poor sanitary conditions... most children (90%) have been infected... before the age of 10 years... paradoxically... improved economic and sanitary conditions may lead to a higher susceptibility in older age groups.]

category: Discuss the global distribution of measles, mumps, rubella, and their occurrence in different population groups
front: Q: What are the current global incidence targets for measles elimination?
back:
* Target Incidence: Maintain <5 cases per million annually.
* Coverage: ≥90% routine coverage nationally; ≥80% in every district.
* Strategy: 2 doses of Measles Containing Vaccine (MCV) via routine services and SIAs.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 153 (Book Page): [(1) raise routine coverage with the first dose of MCV (MCV1) to ≥ 90 per cent nationally... (2) reduce and maintain annual measles incidence to < 5 cases per million.]

category: Discuss the global distribution of measles, mumps, rubella, and their occurrence in different population groups
front: Q: Explain the global trend of 'changing epidemiology' regarding measles and rubella.
back:
* Trend: Average age of incidence is rising to adolescents/adults.
* Cause: Partial immunization success reducing childhood transmission while leaving gaps in older susceptible cohorts.
* Outcome: Increased risk of outbreaks in older populations.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 153 (Book Page): [the changing epidemiology of measles which has led to increased transmission among adolescents and adults... raising the average age of incidence.]

category: Discuss the global distribution of measles, mumps, rubella, and their occurrence in different population groups
front: Q: What is the global distribution and primary reservoir of the measles virus?
back: Measles is endemic worldwide. Humans are the only reservoir; no animal reservoir exists.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 152 (Book Page): [Measles is endemic virtually in all parts of the world... Measles occurs only in humans. There is no animal reservoir of infection.]

category: Discuss the global distribution of measles, mumps, rubella, and their occurrence in different population groups
front: Q: What threshold of population susceptibility triggers a measles epidemic?
back: Epidemics tend to occur when the proportion of susceptible children reaches approximately 40%.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 152 (Book Page): [It tends to occur in epidemics when the proportion of susceptible children reaches about 40 per cent (1).]

category: Discuss the global distribution of measles, mumps, rubella, and their occurrence in different population groups
front: Q: Contrast the age distribution of measles in developing versus developed countries.
back: Developing: 6 months to 3 years. Developed: Older children, usually over 5 years of age.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 153 (Book Page): [AGE : Affects virtually everyone in infancy or childhood — between 6 months and 3 years of age in developing countries... and older children usually over 5 years in developed countries]

category: Discuss the global distribution of measles, mumps, rubella, and their occurrence in different population groups
front: Q: Why is measles mortality vastly higher in malnourished populations?
back: Poor cell-mediated immunity leads to severe disease; mortality can be 400 times higher than in well-nourished children.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 153 (Book Page): [Measles tends to be very severe in the malnourished child, carrying a mortality upto 400 times higher... related to poor cell-mediated immunity response, secondary to malnutrition]

category: Discuss the global distribution of measles, mumps, rubella, and their occurrence in different population groups
front: Q: Describe the global incidence and epidemic peak frequency of Mumps.
back: Incidence: 100-1000 cases per 100,000 population. Epidemic peaks occur every 2 to 5 years.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 158 (Book Page): [the annual incidence of mumps in the absence of immunization is in the range of 100-1000 cases/100,000 population with epidemic peak every 2—5 years.]

category: Discuss the global distribution of measles, mumps, rubella, and their occurrence in different population groups
front: Q: What is the typical epidemic interval for Rubella in non-immunized populations?
back: Rubella occurs in global epidemics approximately every 6 to 8 years.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 156 (Book Page): [The disease is worldwide in distribution and tends to occur in epidemics, in non-immunized populations, every 6 to 8 years]

category: Discuss the global distribution of measles, mumps, rubella, and their occurrence in different population groups
front: Q: How do climatic zones influence the seasonality of measles transmission?
back: Tropical: Dry season. Temperate: Winter (due to indoor crowding). India: Winter and early spring (January–April).
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 153 (Book Page): [In tropical zones, most cases of measles occur during the dry season. In temperate climates, measles is a winter disease... Epidemics of measles are common in India during winter and early spring]

category: Discuss the global distribution of measles, mumps, rubella, and their occurrence in different population groups
front: Q: What percentage of women reach adulthood susceptible to Rubella in some populations?
back: Between 10% and 40% of women may reach child-bearing age without rubella immunity (natural or vaccine).
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 156 (Book Page): [It is estimated that 10 to 40 per cent of the population could reach adulthood without experiencing rubella infection in the absence of immunization]

category: Discuss the global distribution of measles, mumps, rubella, and their occurrence in different population groups
front: Q: How does socioeconomic status impact the age of measles infection?
back: Lower socioeconomic conditions correlate with earlier exposure and a lower average age of infection.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 153 (Book Page): [In general, the less favourable the prevailing socio-economic conditions, the lower the average age at which children are attacked.]

category: Discuss the global distribution of measles, mumps, rubella, and their occurrence in different population groups
front: Q: What was the primary WHO 2015 milestone for global measles mortality?
back: Reduce measles-related deaths by ≥ 95% compared to year 2000 estimated levels.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 153 (Book Page): [(3) reduce measles mortality by ≥ 95 per cent in comparison with the estimated level in the year 2000 (5).]

category: Discuss the global distribution of measles, mumps, rubella, and their occurrence in different population groups
front: Q: What is the global distribution pattern and epidemic trigger for measles?
back: * Endemic worldwide. * Epidemics occur when the proportion of susceptible children reaches approximately 40%. * High morbidity and mortality persist in developing countries due to failure in vaccine delivery.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 152 (Book Page): Measles is endemic virtually in all parts of the world. It tends to occur in epidemics when the proportion of susceptible children reaches about 40 per cent.

category: Discuss the global distribution of measles, mumps, rubella, and their occurrence in different population groups
front: Q: Contrast the age of measles occurrence between developing and developed countries.
back: * Developing: Primarily affects infants and children between 6 months and 3 years. * Developed: Primarily affects older children over 5 years. * Vaccination has shifted incidence toward older age groups.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 153 (Book Page): between 6 months and 3 years of age in developing countries where environmental conditions are generally poor, and older children usually over 5 years in developed countries.

category: Discuss the global distribution of measles, mumps, rubella, and their occurrence in different population groups
front: Q: What is the global distribution and typical epidemic frequency of Rubella?
back: * Worldwide distribution. * Epidemics occur every 6 to 8 years in non-immunized populations. * In developed countries, over 70% of cases now occur in persons older than 15 years.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 156 (Book Page): The disease is worldwide in distribution and tends to occur in epidemics, in non-immunized populations, every 6 to 8 years.

category: Discuss the global distribution of measles, mumps, rubella, and their occurrence in different population groups
front: Q: Predict the infection rate when measles is introduced into a virgin community.
back: * Extremely high transmission rate. * More than 90% of the community will be infected due to lack of prior immunity. * No animal reservoir exists to mitigate human-to-human spread.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 152 (Book Page): When the disease is introduced into a virgin community more than 90 per cent of that community will be infected.

category: Discuss the global distribution of measles, mumps, rubella, and their occurrence in different population groups
front: Q: What population groups are prioritized in the vaccination strategy to prevent Congenital Rubella Syndrome?
back: * Priority 1: Women of child-bearing age (15-34 or 39 years). * Priority 2: Interrupting transmission by vaccinating all children aged 1-14 years. * Goal: Universal immunization at age 1.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 157 (Book Page): the priorities being first to protect women of child-bearing age (15-34 or 39 years of age) and then to interrupt transmission of rubella by vaccinating all children.

category: Discuss the global distribution of measles, mumps, rubella, and their occurrence in different population groups
front: Q: What is the annual incidence and epidemic pattern of mumps in non-immunized populations?
back: * Incidence: 100-1000 cases per 100,000 population. * Epidemic peaks: Every 2 to 5 years. * Morbidity is high, though mortality is negligible globally.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 158 (Book Page): the annual incidence of mumps in the absence of immunization is in the range of 100-1000 cases/100,000 population with epidemic peak every 2—5 years.

category: Discuss the global distribution of measles, mumps, rubella, and their occurrence in different population groups
front: Q: How do socio-economic conditions and population density influence measles onset age?
back: * Inverse relationship. * Lower socio-economic status and higher population density lead to a lower average age of infection. * Overcrowding facilitates earlier exposure to respiratory droplets.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 153 (Book Page): In general, the less favourable the prevailing socio-economic conditions, the lower the average age at which children are attacked.

category: Discuss the global distribution of measles, mumps, rubella, and their occurrence in different population groups
front: Q: Which of the three (Measles, Mumps, Rubella) has the highest epidemiological significance regarding subclinical cases?
back: * Rubella: Large numbers of subclinical infections (a major difference from measles). * Mumps: 30-40% of cases are subclinical. * Subclinical cases maintain the infection cycle.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 156 (Book Page): A large number of rubella infections are, in fact, subclinical. This represents one of the major differences between measles and rubella.

category: Discuss the global distribution of measles, mumps, rubella, and their occurrence in different population groups
front: Q: Why is measles mortality significantly higher in malnourished population groups?
back: * Mortality up to 400 times higher. * Attributed to poor cell-mediated immunity. * Malnourished children excrete the virus for longer periods, increasing transmission intensity.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 153 (Book Page): Measles tends to be very severe in the malnourished child, carrying a mortality upto 400 times higher than in well-nourished children.

category: Discuss the global distribution of measles, mumps, rubella, and their occurrence in different population groups
front: Q: Does Measles have an animal reservoir, and why is this important?
back: * No animal reservoir. * Measles occurs only in humans. * This factor makes the disease a candidate for global eradication.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 152 (Book Page): Measles occurs only in humans. There is no animal reservoir of infection.

category: Describe the mode of transmission and the highly contagious nature of measles, mumps, and rubella
front: Q: What is the primary mode of transmission for the measles virus?
back:
- Droplet infection
- Droplet nuclei (aerosols)
- Direct person-to-person contact
- Portal of entry: Respiratory tract
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 154 (Book Page): [Transmission occurs directly from person to person mainly by droplet infection and droplet nuclei... The portal of entry is the respiratory tract.]

category: Describe the mode of transmission and the highly contagious nature of measles, mumps, and rubella
front: Q: Define the period of communicability for a measles patient.
back:
- 4 days before the rash appears
- 4 days after the rash appears
- Highly infectious during prodromal stage
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 153 (Book Page): [The period of communicability is approximately 4 days before and 4 days after the appearance of the rash.]

category: Describe the mode of transmission and the highly contagious nature of measles, mumps, and rubella
front: Q: What statistic illustrates the highly contagious nature of measles in a virgin community?
back:
- Secondary attack rate exceeds 90%
- Nearly everyone in the community becomes infected
- Occurs when susceptibles reach ~40%
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 152 (Book Page): [When the disease is introduced into a virgin community more than 90 per cent of that community will be infected.]

category: Describe the mode of transmission and the highly contagious nature of measles, mumps, and rubella
front: Q: How is Rubella virus transmitted postnatally?
back:
- Droplets from nose and throat
- Droplet nuclei (aerosols)
- Direct person-to-person contact
- Respiratory route entry
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 157 (Book Page): [The virus is transmitted directly from person to person by droplets from nose and throat, and droplet nuclei (aerosols)... The portal of entry is via the respiratory route.]

category: Describe the mode of transmission and the highly contagious nature of measles, mumps, and rubella
front: Q: Besides respiratory droplets, how else can Rubella be transmitted?
back:
- Vertical transmission
- Virus crosses the placenta
- Infects the foetus in utero
- Causes Congenital Rubella Syndrome
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 157 (Book Page): [The virus can cross the placenta (vertical transmission) and infect the foetus in utero, leading to congenital rubella in the newborn.]

category: Describe the mode of transmission and the highly contagious nature of measles, mumps, and rubella
front: Q: Why is Rubella considered less communicable than Measles?
back:
- Absence of coughing in Rubella
- Infectivity period: 1 week before to 1 week after rash
- Greatest infectivity during rash eruption
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 157 (Book Page): [Rubella is much less communicable than measles, probably because of the absence of coughing in rubella.]

category: Describe the mode of transmission and the highly contagious nature of measles, mumps, and rubella
front: Q: What are the primary transmission mechanisms for Mumps?
back:
- Droplet infection
- Direct contact with an infected person
- Virus found in saliva and respiratory secretions
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 159 (Book Page): [The disease is spread mainly by droplet infection and after direct contact with an infected person.]

category: Describe the mode of transmission and the highly contagious nature of measles, mumps, and rubella
front: Q: Identify the period of maximum infectivity for Mumps.
back:
- Just before and at the onset of parotitis
- Total period: 4-6 days before symptoms to 1 week after
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 159 (Book Page): [The period of maximum infectivity is just before and at the onset of parotitis.]

category: Describe the mode of transmission and the highly contagious nature of measles, mumps, and rubella
front: Q: Which MMR virus relies heavily on subclinical cases to maintain the infection cycle?
back:
- Mumps virus
- 30-40% of cases are subclinical
- Subclinical cases maintain the community transmission cycle
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 159 (Book Page): [Subclinical cases which account for 30-40 per cent of all cases appear to be responsible for maintaining the cycle of infection.]

category: Describe the mode of transmission and the highly contagious nature of measles, mumps, and rubella
front: Q: Which environmental factor is most critical for MMR epidemics?
back:
- Overcrowding
- High population density
- Seasonal peaks (Winter/Spring) leading to indoor crowding
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 153 (Book Page)/159: [Epidemics of measles are common... because people crowd together indoors. / Epidemics [of mumps] are often associated with overcrowding.]

category: Discuss the global distribution of measles, mumps, rubella, and their occurrence in different population groups
front: Q: Where is Measles currently considered endemic and how does its global incidence vary?
back:
* Endemic worldwide; rare in industrialized countries due to high vaccine coverage.
* Common in developing countries due to failure in delivering the first vaccine dose.
* Occurs in epidemics when susceptible children reach ~40%.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 152 (Book Page): [Measles is endemic virtually in all parts of the world. It tends to occur in epidemics when the proportion of susceptible children reaches about 40 per cent... measles is now rare in industrialized countries, it remains a common illness in many developing countries.]

category: Discuss the global distribution of measles, mumps, rubella, and their occurrence in different population groups
front: Q: Contrast the age group distribution of Measles in developing versus developed countries.
back:
* Developing: Infancy/childhood (6 months to 3 years) due to poor conditions.
* Developed: Older children, typically over 5 years.
* Post-vaccination era: Shift towards older age groups (adolescents/adults).
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 153 (Book Page): [AGE : Affects virtually everyone in infancy or childhood — between 6 months and 3 years of age in developing countries... and older children usually over 5 years in developed countries... disease is now seen in somewhat older age—groups.]

category: Discuss the global distribution of measles, mumps, rubella, and their occurrence in different population groups
front: Q: What is the typical epidemic periodicity and distribution pattern of Rubella?
back:
* Worldwide distribution.
* Epidemics occur every 6 to 8 years in non-immunized populations.
* Seasonal pattern: Peak in late winter and spring in temperate zones.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 156 (Book Page): [The disease is worldwide in distribution and tends to occur in epidemics, in non-immunized populations, every 6 to 8 years... temperate zones during the late winter and spring.]

category: Discuss the global distribution of measles, mumps, rubella, and their occurrence in different population groups
front: Q: How has widespread immunization changed the age distribution of Rubella in developed countries?
back:
* Shift from childhood (3-10 years) to adults.
* Persons older than 15 years now account for >70% of cases.
* Increased risk for child-bearing age women if not vaccinated.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 156 (Book Page): [Mainly a disease of childhood particularly in the age group 3 to 10 years. Persons older than 15 years now account for over 70 per cent cases in developed countries — this is similar to the changing epidemiological pattern with measles.]

category: Discuss the global distribution of measles, mumps, rubella, and their occurrence in different population groups
front: Q: In the Indian population, what percentage of child-bearing women remain susceptible to Rubella?
back:
* Approximately 40% of women are susceptible.
* Globally: 10-40% reach adulthood without infection in the absence of immunization.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 156 (Book Page): [Studies in India indicate that approximately 40 per cent of women of child-bearing age are susceptible to rubella... 10 to 40 per cent of the population could reach adulthood without experiencing rubella infection.]

category: Discuss the global distribution of measles, mumps, rubella, and their occurrence in different population groups
front: Q: What is the annual incidence of Mumps in non-immunized populations globally?
back:
* Range: 100-1000 cases per 100,000 population.
* Epidemic peaks: Occur every 2-5 years.
* Highest frequency: Children aged 5-9 years.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 158 (Book Page): [the annual incidence of mumps in the absence of immunization is in the range of 100-1000 cases/100,000 population with epidemic peak every 2—5 years... most frequent cause of parotitis in children in the age group 5—9 years.]

category: Discuss the global distribution of measles, mumps, rubella, and their occurrence in different population groups
front: Q: Describe the subclinical distribution and source of infection for Mumps.
back:
* 30-40% of cases are subclinical.
* Subclinical cases are responsible for maintaining the cycle of infection.
* Occurs globally; morbidity high, mortality negligible.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 158 (Book Page): [Subclinical cases which account for 30-40 per cent of all cases (2) appear to be responsible for maintaining the cycle of infection... morbidity rate tends to be high, mortality rate is negligible.]

category: Discuss the global distribution of measles, mumps, rubella, and their occurrence in different population groups
front: Q: How does the environment and socioeconomic status influence the occurrence of Measles?
back:
* Low socioeconomic status: Lower average age of attack.
* Tropical zones: Dry season peak.
* Temperate zones: Winter disease (crowding indoors).
* High density/movement increases epidemicity.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 153 (Book Page): [In general, the less favourable the prevailing socio-economic conditions, the lower the average age at which children are attacked... In tropical zones, most cases of measles occur during the dry season.]

category: Discuss the global distribution of measles, mumps, rubella, and their occurrence in different population groups
front: Q: Compare the risk of Measles mortality in well-nourished versus malnourished population groups.
back:
* Malnourished: Mortality 400x higher.
* Mechanism: Poor cell-mediated immunity.
* Impact: Malnourished excrete virus for longer periods, intensifying spread.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 153 (Book Page): [Measles tends to be very severe in the malnourished child, carrying a mortality upto 400 times higher than in well-nourished children... related to poor cell-mediated immunity response... excrete measles virus for longer periods.]

category: Discuss the global distribution of measles, mumps, rubella, and their occurrence in different population groups
front: Q: Does Measles, Mumps, or Rubella show a significant gender-based distribution?
back:
* Measles: Incidence is equal between males and females.
* Mumps: Primarily childhood disease; no significant gender disparity mentioned.
* Rubella: Primary infection is equal; however, congenital risk affects only females.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 153 (Book Page): [(b) SEX Incidence equal.] & Page 158 (Book Page): [(a) AGE AND SEX: Mumps is the most frequent cause... in the age group 5-9 years.]

category: Describe the mode of transmission and the highly contagious nature of measles, mumps, and rubella
front: Q: What are the primary modes of transmission for the measles virus?
back:
* Droplet infection
* Droplet nuclei
* Conjunctival inoculation
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 153 (Book Page): Transmission occurs directly from person to person mainly by droplet infection and droplet nuclei... Infection through conjunctiva is also considered likely.

category: Describe the mode of transmission and the highly contagious nature of measles, mumps, and rubella
front: Q: Define the period of communicability for a patient with measles.
back: Approximately 4 days before to 4 days after the appearance of the rash.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 153 (Book Page): The period of communicability is approximately 4 days before and 4 days after the appearance of the rash.

category: Describe the mode of transmission and the highly contagious nature of measles, mumps, and rubella
front: Q: What is the secondary attack rate of measles in a previously unexposed (virgin) community?
back: Greater than 90 percent.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 152 (Book Page): When the disease is introduced into a virgin community more than 90 per cent of that community will be infected.

category: Describe the mode of transmission and the highly contagious nature of measles, mumps, and rubella
front: Q: How is the Rubella virus transmitted between individuals?
back:
* Respiratory droplets
* Droplet nuclei (aerosols)
* Vertical transmission (transplacental)
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 156 (Book Page): The virus is transmitted directly from person to person by droplets from nose and throat, and droplet nuclei (aerosols)... The virus can cross the placenta (vertical transmission).

category: Describe the mode of transmission and the highly contagious nature of measles, mumps, and rubella
front: Q: Why is rubella clinically considered less communicable than measles?
back: Due to the typical absence of coughing in rubella patients.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 156 (Book Page): Rubella is much less communicable than measles, probably because of the absence of coughing in rubella.

category: Describe the mode of transmission and the highly contagious nature of measles, mumps, and rubella
front: Q: State the duration of communicability for Rubella.
back: From one week before the onset of symptoms to about one week after the rash appears.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 156 (Book Page): It probably extends from a week before symptoms to about a week after rash appears.

category: Describe the mode of transmission and the highly contagious nature of measles, mumps, and rubella
front: Q: What are the primary modes of transmission for the Mumps virus?
back:
* Droplet infection
* Direct contact with an infected person
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 158 (Book Page): The disease is spread mainly by droplet infection and after direct contact with an infected person.

category: Describe the mode of transmission and the highly contagious nature of measles, mumps, and rubella
front: Q: When is a patient with Mumps considered at their peak level of infectivity?
back: Just before and at the onset of parotitis (glandular swelling).
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 158 (Book Page): The period of maximum infectivity is just before and at the onset of parotitis.

category: Describe the mode of transmission and the highly contagious nature of measles, mumps, and rubella
front: Q: A child has Mumps. When can they safely return to school to prevent transmission?
back: Once the swelling of the parotid glands has completely subsided.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 158 (Book Page): Once the swelling of the glands has subsided, the case may be regarded as no longer infectious.

category: Describe the mode of transmission and the highly contagious nature of measles, mumps, and rubella
front: Q: What is the typical incubation period for Rubella compared to Mumps?
back:
* Rubella: 2-3 weeks (avg 18 days)
* Mumps: 2-4 weeks (avg 14-18 days)
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 156 (Book Page): Rubella incubation period 2 to 3 weeks; average 18 days. Page 158 (Book Page): Mumps varies from 2 to 4 weeks, usually 14-18 days.

category: Describe the mode of transmission and the highly contagious nature of measles, mumps, and rubella
front: What is the primary mode of transmission for the Measles (Rubeola) virus?
back:
Direct person-to-person spread via:
- Droplet infection
- Droplet nuclei (aerosols)
Portal of entry: Respiratory tract and conjunctiva.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 153 (Book Page): [Transmission occurs directly from person to person mainly by droplet infection and droplet nuclei... The portal of entry is the respiratory tract.]

category: Describe the mode of transmission and the highly contagious nature of measles, mumps, and rubella
front: State the specific period of communicability for a patient with Measles relative to the rash.
back: Approximately 4 days before to 4 days after the appearance of the rash. It is highly infectious during the prodromal (catarrhal) stage.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 153 (Book Page): [The period of communicability is approximately 4 days before and 4 days after the appearance of the rash.]

category: Describe the mode of transmission and the highly contagious nature of measles, mumps, and rubella
front: Why is Rubella epidemiologically considered less communicable than Measles?
back: Due to the absence of coughing in Rubella, which results in fewer aerosolized droplet nuclei compared to the intense catarrhal symptoms of Measles.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 156 (Book Page): [Rubella is much less communicable than measles, probably because of the absence of coughing in rubella.]

category: Describe the mode of transmission and the highly contagious nature of measles, mumps, and rubella
front: Q: A child develops a Measles rash today. For how long should they be isolated to prevent transmission?
back: Isolate for 7 days from the onset of the rash. This duration ensures the entire infectious period (4 days post-rash) is covered.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 153 (Book Page): [Isolation of the patient for a week from the onset of rash more than covers the period of communicability.]

category: Describe the mode of transmission and the highly contagious nature of measles, mumps, and rubella
front: Describe the period of communicability for the Rubella virus.
back:
- Starts: 1 week before rash onset.
- Ends: 1 week after the rash has faded.
- Peak infectivity: During the eruption of the rash.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 156 (Book Page): [It probably extends from a week before symptoms to about a week after rash appears. Infectivity is greatest when the rash is erupting.]

category: Describe the mode of transmission and the highly contagious nature of measles, mumps, and rubella
front: What is the primary mode of transmission for Mumps (Myxovirus parotiditis)?
back:
- Droplet infection
- Direct contact with an infected person
- Virus is present in saliva 4-6 days before symptoms.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 158 (Book Page): [The disease is spread mainly by droplet infection and after direct contact with an infected person.]

category: Describe the mode of transmission and the highly contagious nature of measles, mumps, and rubella
front: What is the Secondary Attack Rate (SAR) of Measles in a non-immune (virgin) community?
back: The SAR exceeds 90%. It is highly contagious; epidemics occur when the proportion of susceptible children reaches roughly 40%.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 152 (Book Page): [When the disease is introduced into a virgin community more than 90 per cent of that community will be infected.]

category: Describe the mode of transmission and the highly contagious nature of measles, mumps, and rubella
front: Q: Apart from droplets, what unique transmission route allows Rubella to affect a developing fetus?
back: Vertical transmission (transplacental). The virus crosses the placenta to infect the fetus in utero, potentially causing Congenital Rubella Syndrome (CRS).
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 156 (Book Page): [The virus can cross the placenta (vertical transmission) and infect the foetus in utero, leading to congenital rubella.]

category: Describe the mode of transmission and the highly contagious nature of measles, mumps, and rubella
front: When is a Mumps patient considered to be at their maximum level of infectivity?
back: Just before and at the onset of parotitis (salivary gland swelling). Infectivity typically ends once the swelling subsides.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 158 (Book Page): [The period of maximum infectivity is just before and at the onset of parotitis.]

category: Describe the mode of transmission and the highly contagious nature of measles, mumps, and rubella
front: Which group of viruses do Measles, Mumps, and Rubella belong to, facilitating their respiratory spread?
back:
- Measles: Paramyxovirus (RNA)
- Mumps: Rubulavirus/Paramyxoviridae (RNA)
- Rubella: Togavirus (RNA)
All utilize respiratory droplet transmission.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 152 (Book Page), 156, 158: [Measles is caused by an RNA paramyxovirus... Rubella is caused by an RNA virus of the togavirus family... Mumps is caused by an RNA virus... family paramyxoviridae.]

category: Describe the mode of transmission and the highly contagious nature of measles, mumps, and rubella
front: Q: What is the causative agent and primary reservoir for measles?
back:
- Agent: RNA paramyxovirus.
- Reservoir: Humans only (no animal reservoir exists).
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 152 (Book Page): [Measles is caused by a specific virus of the group myxoviruses... Measles occurs only in humans. There is no animal reservoir of infection.]

category: Describe the mode of transmission and the highly contagious nature of measles, mumps, and rubella
front: Q: Describe the mode of transmission and portal of entry for measles.
back:
- Mode: Person-to-person via droplet infection and droplet nuclei.
- Portal: Respiratory tract (conjunctival entry is also likely).
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 154 (Book Page): [Transmission occurs directly from person to person mainly by droplet infection and droplet nuclei... The portal of entry is the respiratory tract. Infection through conjunctiva is also considered likely.]

category: Describe the mode of transmission and the highly contagious nature of measles, mumps, and rubella
front: Q: Define the period of communicability for a measles patient.
back:
- Timing: Approximately 4 days before to 4 days after the rash appears.
- Peak: Highly infectious during the prodromal period.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 153 (Book Page): [The period of communicability is approximately 4 days before and 4 days after the appearance of the rash. Measles is highly infectious during the prodromal period.]

category: Describe the mode of transmission and the highly contagious nature of measles, mumps, and rubella
front: Q: What is the expected infectivity rate of measles in a non-immune (virgin) community?
back:
- Secondary Attack Rate: >90%.
- Epidemic Threshold: Occurs when susceptible children reach ~40%.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 152 (Book Page): [When the disease is introduced into a virgin community more than 90 per cent of that community will be infected... tends to occur in epidemics when the proportion of susceptible children reaches about 40 per cent.]

category: Describe the mode of transmission and the highly contagious nature of measles, mumps, and rubella
front: Q: Why is rubella clinically considered less communicable than measles?
back: - Rationale: Primarily due to the absence of coughing in rubella compared to measles catarrhal symptoms.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 157 (Book Page): [Rubella is much less communicable than measles, probably because of the absence of coughing in rubella.]

category: Describe the mode of transmission and the highly contagious nature of measles, mumps, and rubella
front: Q: List the causative virus and transmission routes for Rubella.
back:
- Agent: RNA Togavirus.
- Routes: Respiratory droplets/nuclei and Vertical (transplacental) transmission to the fetus.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 157 (Book Page): [Rubella is caused by an RNA virus of the togavirus family... transmitted directly from person to person by droplets... The virus can cross the placenta (vertical transmission).]

category: Describe the mode of transmission and the highly contagious nature of measles, mumps, and rubella
front: Q: Define the period of communicability for Rubella.
back:
- Duration: One week before symptoms to one week after the rash appears.
- Maximum infectivity: Occurs during rash eruption.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 157 (Book Page): [It probably extends from a week before symptoms to about a week after rash appears. Infectivity is greatest when the rash is erupting.]

category: Describe the mode of transmission and the highly contagious nature of measles, mumps, and rubella
front: Q: What is the mode of transmission for mumps and its period of maximum infectivity?
back:
- Mode: Droplet infection and direct contact with infected persons.
- Peak Infectivity: Just before and at the onset of parotitis.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 159 (Book Page): [The disease is spread mainly by droplet infection and after direct contact... The period of maximum infectivity is just before and at the onset of parotitis.]

category: Describe the mode of transmission and the highly contagious nature of measles, mumps, and rubella
front: Q: When is a mumps patient no longer considered infectious to others?
back: - Rule: Once the swelling of the parotid/salivary glands has subsided.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 159 (Book Page): [Once the swelling of the glands has subsided, the case may be regarded as no longer infectious.]

category: Describe the mode of transmission and the highly contagious nature of measles, mumps, and rubella
front: Q: Compare the Secondary Attack Rate (SAR) of Mumps with the subclinical infection rate.
back:
- SAR: Approximately 86%.
- Subclinical rate: 30-40% (responsible for maintaining infection cycles).
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 159 (Book Page): [Secondary Attack Rate: Estimated to be about 86 per cent... Subclinical cases which account for 30-40 per cent of all cases.]

category: Describe the mode of transmission and the highly contagious nature of measles, mumps, and rubella
front: Q: What is the causative agent and primary transmission mode of Measles?
back:
• Agent: RNA paramyxovirus.
• Transmission: Person-to-person via droplet infection and droplet nuclei (aerosols).
• Portal: Respiratory tract or conjunctiva.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 153 (Book Page): [Measles is caused by an RNA paramyxovirus... Transmission occurs directly from person to person mainly by droplet infection and droplet nuclei... The portal of entry is the respiratory tract.]

category: Describe the mode of transmission and the highly contagious nature of measles, mumps, and rubella
front: Q: Why is Measles categorized as a highly contagious disease in virgin communities?
back:
• Highly infectious during prodromal stage.
• Secondary attack rate (SAR) exceeds 90% in non-immune/virgin populations.
• Droplet nuclei facilitate rapid airborne spread.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 152 (Book Page): [When the disease is introduced into a virgin community more than 90 per cent of that community will be infected... (2) high infectious nature of measles.]

category: Describe the mode of transmission and the highly contagious nature of measles, mumps, and rubella
front: Q: What is the exact period of communicability for a patient with Measles rash?
back:
• Approximately 4 days before the appearance of the rash.
• 4 days after the appearance of the rash.
• Communicability declines rapidly post-eruption.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 153 (Book Page): [The period of communicability is approximately 4 days before and 4 days after the appearance of the rash. Communicability declines rapidly after the appearance of the rash.]

category: Describe the mode of transmission and the highly contagious nature of measles, mumps, and rubella
front: Q: Describe the modes of transmission for the Rubella virus, including vertical spread.
back:
• Horizontal: Droplets and droplet nuclei (aerosols) via respiratory route.
• Vertical: Transplacental transmission to the fetus in utero (Congenital Rubella).
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 156 (Book Page): [The virus is transmitted directly from person to person by droplets... and droplet nuclei... The virus can cross the placenta (vertical transmission) and infect the foetus in utero.]

category: Describe the mode of transmission and the highly contagious nature of measles, mumps, and rubella
front: Q: How does the communicability of Rubella compare to Measles, and why?
back:
• Rubella is significantly less communicable than Measles.
• Reason: Absence of coughing in Rubella patients reduces aerosol production.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 156 (Book Page): [Rubella is much less communicable than measles, probably because of the absence of coughing in rubella.]

category: Describe the mode of transmission and the highly contagious nature of measles, mumps, and rubella
front: Q: What is the period of infectivity for Rubella relative to its symptoms?
back:
• From one week before symptoms appear.
• Until one week after the rash appears.
• Peak infectivity occurs during the eruption of the rash.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 156 (Book Page): [It probably extends from a week before symptoms to about a week after rash appears. Infectivity is greatest when the rash is erupting.]

category: Describe the mode of transmission and the highly contagious nature of measles, mumps, and rubella
front: Q: What are the primary mode of transmission and Secondary Attack Rate (SAR) for Mumps?
back:
• Mode: Droplet infection and direct contact with infected persons.
• SAR: Estimated at approximately 86%.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 158 (Book Page): [The disease is spread mainly by droplet infection and after direct contact with an infected person... Secondary attack rate: Estimated to be about 86 per cent.]

category: Describe the mode of transmission and the highly contagious nature of measles, mumps, and rubella
front: Q: When is a Mumps patient considered no longer infectious to others?
back:
• Once the swelling of the parotid/salivary glands has subsided.
• Maximum infectivity is just before and at the onset of parotitis.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 158 (Book Page): [The period of maximum infectivity is just before and at the onset of parotitis. Once the swelling of the glands has subsided, the case may be regarded as no longer infectious.]

category: Describe the mode of transmission and the highly contagious nature of measles, mumps, and rubella
front: Q: Why are subclinical cases significant in the transmission of Mumps?
back:
• Subclinical cases account for 30-40% of all infections.
• They maintain the cycle of infection as they remain undiagnosed and mobile.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 158 (Book Page): [Subclinical cases which account for 30-40 per cent of all cases (2) appear to be responsible for maintaining the cycle of infection.]

category: Describe the mode of transmission and the highly contagious nature of measles, mumps, and rubella
front: Q: Which infectious materials contain the Mumps virus during the communicable period?
back:
• Saliva and swabs from Stenson’s duct.
• Also found in blood, urine, human milk, and CSF.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 158 (Book Page): [The virus can be isolated from the saliva or from swabs taken from the surface of Stenson’s duct. Virus has also been found in the blood, urine, human milk and on occasion in the CSF.]

category: Describe the mode of transmission and the highly contagious nature of measles, mumps, and rubella
front: Q: What is the primary mode of transmission and portal of entry for Measles?
back:
* Mode: Droplet infection and droplet nuclei.
* Portal of entry: Respiratory tract and potentially the conjunctiva.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 154 (Book Page): Transmission occurs directly from person to person mainly by droplet infection and droplet nuclei... The portal of entry is the respiratory tract. Infection through conjunctiva is also considered likely.

category: Describe the mode of transmission and the highly contagious nature of measles, mumps, and rubella
front: Q: Define the 'highly contagious nature' of Measles in terms of the Secondary Attack Rate (SAR).
back:
* SAR: Exceeds 90% in virgin (susceptible) communities.
* Infectivity: One of the most infectious human diseases known.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 153 (Book Page): When the disease is introduced into a virgin community more than 90 per cent of that community will be infected.

category: Describe the mode of transmission and the highly contagious nature of measles, mumps, and rubella
front: Q: Contrast the transmissibility of Rubella with that of Measles.
back:
* Rubella is much less communicable than Measles.
* Reason: Absence of coughing in rubella, which reduces aerosol spread.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 157 (Book Page): Rubella is much less communicable than measles, probably because of the absence of coughing in rubella.

category: Describe the mode of transmission and the highly contagious nature of measles, mumps, and rubella
front: Q: A child with Measles has a rash that appeared yesterday. Determine the remaining period of communicability.
back:
* 3 days remaining.
* Total Period: 4 days before to 4 days after the appearance of the rash.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 154 (Book Page): Transmission occurs directly from person to person... from 4 days before onset of rash until 4 days thereafter.

category: Describe the mode of transmission and the highly contagious nature of measles, mumps, and rubella
front: Q: What are the two primary modes of transmission for the Mumps virus?
back:
* Droplet infection (respiratory droplets).
* Direct contact with an infected person.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 159 (Book Page): The disease is spread mainly by droplet infection and after direct contact with an infected person.

category: Describe the mode of transmission and the highly contagious nature of measles, mumps, and rubella
front: Q: Aside from droplet spread, what critical mode of transmission is unique to Rubella among the MMR group?
back: * Vertical Transmission: The virus crosses the placenta to infect the fetus in utero (Congenital Rubella).
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 157 (Book Page): The virus can cross the placenta (vertical transmission) and infect the foetus in utero, leading to congenital rubella in the newborn.

category: Describe the mode of transmission and the highly contagious nature of measles, mumps, and rubella
front: Q: At what specific clinical stage is a patient with Mumps most contagious?
back: * Period: Just before and at the onset of parotitis (glandular swelling).
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 159 (Book Page): The period of maximum infectivity is just before and at the onset of parotitis.

category: Describe the mode of transmission and the highly contagious nature of measles, mumps, and rubella
front: Q: How do Rubella and Measles differ regarding subclinical cases as a source of infection?
back:
* Rubella: Large number of subclinical cases (major source of spread).
* Measles: Subclinical cases are rare; infection is typically clinical.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 157 (Book Page): A large number of rubella infections are, in fact, subclinical. This represents one of the major differences between measles and rubella.

category: Describe the mode of transmission and the highly contagious nature of measles, mumps, and rubella
front: Q: What is the estimated Secondary Attack Rate (SAR) for Mumps in a susceptible household?
back: * SAR: Approximately 86%.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 159 (Book Page): SECONDARY ATTACK RATE : Estimated to be about 86 per cent.

category: Describe the mode of transmission and the highly contagious nature of measles, mumps, and rubella
front: Q: What is the causative agent and family for Rubella (German Measles)?
back:
* Agent: RNA virus.
* Family: Togavirus family.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 157 (Book Page): Rubella is caused by an RNA virus of the togavirus family.

category: Describe the mode of transmission and the highly contagious nature of measles, mumps, and rubella
front: Q: What are the primary modes of transmission for the measles (rubeola) virus?
back:
- Droplet infection and droplet nuclei.
- Portal of entry: Respiratory tract or conjunctiva.
- Highly contagious person-to-person spread.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 154 (Book Page): Transmission occurs directly from person to person mainly by droplet infection and droplet nuclei... The portal of entry is the respiratory tract. Infection through conjunctiva is also considered likely.

category: Describe the mode of transmission and the highly contagious nature of measles, mumps, and rubella
front: Q: Specify the period of communicability for measles relative to the appearance of the rash.
back:
- 4 days before to 4 days after rash onset.
- Maximum infectivity occurs during the prodromal stage and eruption.
- Isolation for 7 days post-rash is recommended.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 153 (Book Page): The period of communicability is approximately 4 days before and 4 days after the appearance of the rash. Isolation of the patient for a week from the onset of rash more than covers the period.

category: Describe the mode of transmission and the highly contagious nature of measles, mumps, and rubella
coreConcept: Rubella vs. Measles Pathophysiology of Spread
front: Q: Why is rubella clinically considered less communicable than measles?
back:
- Absence of coughing in rubella.
- Reduced aerosol/droplet generation compared to measles catarrhal symptoms.
- Measles involves intense coryza and cough which facilitates spread.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 156 (Book Page): Rubella is much less communicable than measles, probably because of the absence of coughing in rubella.

category: Describe the mode of transmission and the highly contagious nature of measles, mumps, and rubella
front: Q: Describe the expected infection rate when measles is introduced into a virgin community.
back:
- Over 90% of the community will be infected.
- Highly contagious nature leads to rapid outbreaks.
- Epidemics occur when susceptible children reach ~40%.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 152 (Book Page): When the disease is introduced into a virgin community more than 90 per cent of that community will be infected... It tends to occur in epidemics when the proportion of susceptible children reaches about 40 per cent.

category: Describe the mode of transmission and the highly contagious nature of measles, mumps, and rubella
front: Q: When is the period of maximum infectivity for a patient with Mumps?
back:
- Just before and at the onset of parotitis.
- Total period: 4-6 days before symptoms until swelling subsides.
- Secondary attack rate is approximately 86%.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 159 (Book Page): The period of maximum infectivity is just before and at the onset of parotitis. Once the swelling of the glands has subsided, the case may be regarded as no longer infectious.

category: Describe the mode of transmission and the highly contagious nature of measles, mumps, and rubella
front: Q: What are the two primary routes of transmission for the Rubella virus?
back:
- Horizontal: Droplets/aerosols via respiratory route (1 week before to 1 week after rash).
- Vertical: Transplacental transmission to the fetus (Congenital Rubella).
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 156 (Book Page): The virus is transmitted directly from person to person by droplets... The virus can cross the placenta (vertical transmission) and infect the foetus in utero, leading to congenital rubella.

category: Describe the mode of transmission and the highly contagious nature of measles, mumps, and rubella
front: Q: How do environmental factors like season and crowding impact measles transmission?
back:
- Temperate: Winter disease due to indoor crowding.
- Tropical: Dry season disease.
- Population density and movement significantly increase epidemicity.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 154 (Book Page): In temperate climates, measles is a winter disease, probably because people crowd together indoors. Epidemics of measles are common in India during winter and early spring.

category: Describe the mode of transmission and the highly contagious nature of measles, mumps, and rubella
front: Q: What is the significance of subclinical cases in the transmission of Mumps?
back:
- Account for 30-40% of all cases.
- Act as hidden reservoirs maintaining the infection cycle.
- Infectious despite lacking clinical parotid swelling.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 159 (Book Page): Both clinical and subclinical cases. Subclinical cases which account for 30-40 per cent of all cases appear to be responsible for maintaining the cycle of infection.

category: Describe the mode of transmission and the highly contagious nature of measles, mumps, and rubella
front: Q: Contrast viral shedding duration in postnatal rubella versus congenital rubella.
back:
- Postnatal: ~1 week before to 1 week after rash.
- Congenital: Infants may shed the virus for many months after birth.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 156 (Book Page): Infants born with congenital rubella may shed the virus for many months. [Postnatal] extends from a week before symptoms to about a week after rash appears.

category: Describe the mode of transmission and the highly contagious nature of measles, mumps, and rubella
front: Q: Which anatomical secretions contain the infective material for a measles case?
back:
- Secretions of the nose, throat, and respiratory tract.
- Highest during the prodromal period.
- Presence in droplets and droplet nuclei.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 153 (Book Page): Secretions of the nose, throat and respiratory tract of a case of measles during the prodromal period and the early stages of the rash.

category: Describe the mode of transmission and the highly contagious nature of measles, mumps, and rubella
front: Q: What are the primary modes of transmission for Measles, Mumps, and Rubella?
back: Droplet infection, droplet nuclei (aerosols), and direct contact with infected respiratory secretions.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 153 (Book Page), 156, 158: [Measles: Transmission occurs directly from person to person mainly by droplet infection and droplet nuclei... Rubella: The virus is transmitted directly from person to person by droplets... Mumps: The disease is spread mainly by droplet infection.]

category: Describe the mode of transmission and the highly contagious nature of measles, mumps, and rubella
front: Q: Explain why Measles is more contagious than Rubella regarding clinical symptoms.
back: Measles causes severe catarrhal symptoms (cough, coryza), producing more infected droplets; Rubella lacks coughing, reducing aerosol spread.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 156 (Book Page): [Rubella is much less communicable than measles, probably because of the absence of coughing in rubella.]

category: Describe the mode of transmission and the highly contagious nature of measles, mumps, and rubella
front: Q: Contrast the communicability periods of Measles and Rubella relative to the rash.
back: Measles: 4 days before to 4 days after rash onset. Rubella: 1 week before to 1 week after rash onset.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 153 (Book Page), 156: [Measles: Approximately 4 days before and 4 days after the appearance of the rash. Rubella: It probably extends from a week before symptoms to about a week after rash appears.]

category: Describe the mode of transmission and the highly contagious nature of measles, mumps, and rubella
front: Q: A non-immune community is exposed to Measles. What is the expected infection rate?
back: Over 90% of the community will be infected due to its highly contagious nature.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 152 (Book Page): [When the disease is introduced into a virgin community more than 90 per cent of that community will be infected.]

category: Describe the mode of transmission and the highly contagious nature of measles, mumps, and rubella
front: Q: What is the peak period of infectivity for Mumps virus transmission?
back: The period of maximum infectivity is just before and at the onset of parotitis (glandular swelling).
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 158 (Book Page): [The period of maximum infectivity is just before and at the onset of parotitis.]

category: Describe the mode of transmission and the highly contagious nature of measles, mumps, and rubella
front: Q: List the mandatory clinical reporting period for isolating a Measles case.
back: Isolation for 7 days after the onset of the rash covers the period of communicability.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 153 (Book Page): [Isolation of the patient for a week from the onset of rash more than covers the period of communicability.]

category: Describe the mode of transmission and the highly contagious nature of measles, mumps, and rubella
front: Q: Describe the risk of vertical transmission in Rubella.
back: The virus can cross the placenta (vertical transmission) to infect the fetus in utero, causing congenital rubella.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 156 (Book Page): [The virus can cross the placenta (vertical transmission) and infect the foetus in utero, leading to congenital rubella.]

category: Describe the mode of transmission and the highly contagious nature of measles, mumps, and rubella
front: Q: A 5-year-old in a household has Mumps. What is the expected Secondary Attack Rate (SAR)?
back: The SAR is estimated to be approximately 86%.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 158 (Book Page): [SECONDARY ATTACK RATE: Estimated to be about 86 per cent.]

category: Describe the mode of transmission and the highly contagious nature of measles, mumps, and rubella
front: Q: Besides the respiratory tract, which other portal of entry is likely for Measles?
back: The conjunctiva (infection occurs if virus is instilled into the eye).
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 153 (Book Page): [The portal of entry is the respiratory tract. Infection through conjunctiva is also considered likely.]

category: Describe the mode of transmission and the highly contagious nature of measles, mumps, and rubella
front: Q: At what percentage of susceptible children do Measles epidemics typically occur?
back: When the proportion of susceptible children reaches approximately 40%.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 152 (Book Page): [It tends to occur in epidemics when the proportion of susceptible children reaches about 40 per cent.]

category: Describe the mode of transmission and the highly contagious nature of measles, mumps, and rubella
front: Q: How is the measles virus primarily transmitted and what is its portal of entry?
back: 1. Mode: Direct person-to-person droplet infection or droplet nuclei (aerosols). 2. Portal: Respiratory tract or conjunctiva.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 154 (Book Page): Transmission occurs directly from person to person mainly by droplet infection and droplet nuclei... The portal of entry is the respiratory tract. Infection through conjunctiva is also considered likely.

category: Describe the mode of transmission and the highly contagious nature of measles, mumps, and rubella
front: Q: What defines the period of communicability for measles in relation to the clinical rash?
back: Approximately 4 days before and 4 days after the appearance of the rash. Communicability is highest during the prodromal period.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 153 (Book Page): The period of communicability is approximately 4 days before and 4 days after the appearance of the rash.

category: Describe the mode of transmission and the highly contagious nature of measles, mumps, and rubella
front: Q: Why is Rubella clinically characterized as being less communicable than Measles?
back: Due to the absence of coughing in Rubella, which significantly reduces the dispersal of infective respiratory droplets.
