back: When the country achieves ≥80% coverage of the first dose (MCV1) nationally for three consecutive years.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 155 (Book Page): [Second dose of measles vaccine may be added to the routine immunization schedule in countries that have achieved ≥80% coverage of the first dose of the vaccine at the national level for 3 consecutive years]

category: Analyze community-based vaccination campaigns
front: Q: Why must malnutrition not be used as a contraindication for community immunization?
back: Malnourished children have higher mortality from vaccine-preventable diseases and a greater need for protection.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 128 (Book Page): [In fact, it is particularly important to immunize children with malnutrition. ... These are the very children who are most in need of immunization. They are most likely to die should they acquire a vaccine—preventable disease]

category: Analyze community-based vaccination campaigns
front: Q: Why does the transition from high to intermediate HAV endemicity paradoxically increase clinically significant disease?
back: Children escape early (asymptomatic) infection; susceptibility shifts to adolescents/adults who develop symptomatic illness and outbreaks.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 217 (Book Page): [improved economic and sanitary conditions may lead to a higher susceptibility in older age groups and higher disease rates... paradoxically, with the transition from high to intermediate endemicity, the incidence of clinically significant hepatitis A increases.]

category: Analyze community-based vaccination campaigns
front: Q: What specific operational failure in mass Measles campaigns leads to Toxic Shock Syndrome (TSS)?
back: Using a single reconstituted vaccine vial for more than 4 hours or contamination of the vial.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 155 (Book Page): [Toxic shock syndrome (TSS) occurs when measles vaccine is contaminated or the same vial is used for more than one session on the same day or next day. The vaccine should not be used after 4 hours of opening the vial.]

category: Analyze community-based vaccination campaigns
front: Q: How is 'DOTS Coverage' defined within a community tuberculosis control framework?
back: Percentage of the national population residing in administrative units (districts/townships) that have officially adopted DOTS.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 182 (Book Page): [DOTS coverage is defined as the percentage of the national population living in areas where health services have adopted DOTS. "Areas" are the lowest administrative or management units...]

category: Analyze community-based vaccination campaigns
front: Q: Analyze the impact of BCG vaccination on the community-wide risk of Tuberculosis infection.
back: BCG provides individual protection against severe childhood TB but has minimal impact on overall community transmission.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 203 (Book Page): [BCG vaccination of uninfected individuals (usually children) can prevent tuberculosis in them, it can have only a relatively small epidemiological effect in that it will not contribute significantly to the reduction in the overall risk of infection in the community as a whole.]

category: Analyze community-based vaccination campaigns
front: Q: What are the three specific numerical thresholds required for a district to reach 'NT Elimination' status?
back:
1. Incidence <0.1/1000 live births. 
2. TT2 coverage >90%. 
3. Attended deliveries >75%.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 317 (Book Page): [NT elimination : - Rate < 0.1/1000 live births and - TT2 coverage > 90% and - attended deliveries > 75%]

category: Analyze community-based vaccination campaigns
front: Q: Define the 'Adequacy' criteria for stool specimens in AFP surveillance during polio eradication.
back: Two specimens collected 24–48 hours apart, within 14 days of paralysis onset, arriving via reverse cold chain.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 210 (Book Page): [‘Adequate’ stool specimens are two stool specimens ... collected at least 24 hours apart, within 14 days after the onset of paralysis, and arriving in the laboratory by reverse cold chain]

category: Analyze community-based vaccination campaigns
front: Q: What is the long-term incidence target for the global 'Stop TB Strategy' by 2050?
back: Less than or equal to 1 TB case per million population per year.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 206 (Book Page): [By 2050: The global incidence of TB disease will be less than or equal to 1 case per million population per year.]

category: Analyze community-based vaccination campaigns
front: Q: Why did Mission Indradhanush prioritize 201 specific districts in its initial phase?
back: These high-focus districts contained approximately 50% of all unvaccinated children in the country.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 448 (Book Page): [201 high focus districts will be covered in the first phase. ... These 201 districts have nearly 50 per cent of all unvaccinated children of the country.]

category: Identify the recommended vaccine schedule for children and adults
front: Q: When is the Japanese Encephalitis (JE) vaccine administered in the routine childhood schedule?
back: Administered between 16 and 24 months of age, concurrently with the first DPT and OPV booster doses in endemic areas.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 129 (Book Page): Japanese Encephalitis 16-24 months with DPT/OPV booster

category: Identify the recommended vaccine schedule for children and adults
front: Q: What is the minimum recommended interval between subsequent primary doses of DPT, OPV, and Hepatitis B?
back: The interval between two consecutive doses must not be less than one month (4 weeks).
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 129 (Book Page): (a) Interval between 2 doses of DPT, OPV and hepatitis B should not be less than one month.

category: Identify the recommended vaccine schedule for children and adults
front: Q: What is the maximum age limit for a child to receive the BCG vaccine if it was missed at birth?
back: BCG can be administered as early as possible after birth until the child reaches one year of age.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 129 (Book Page): BCG At birth or as early as possible till one year of age

category: Identify the recommended vaccine schedule for children and adults
coreConcept: Hepatitis B Protocol for Low Birth Weight
front: Q: How is the Hepatitis B birth dose managed for premature infants weighing less than 2000g?
back: The dose given at birth is not counted toward the primary series; three additional doses must be given starting at one month of chronological age.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 222 (Book Page): In such cases the vaccine dose given at birth should not be counted towards the primary series and 3 additional doses should be given according to the national immunization schedule

category: Identify the recommended vaccine schedule for children and adults
front: Q: Describe the primary and booster schedule for the adult-type (dT) diphtheria-tetanus vaccine.
back: 2 doses given 4 to 6 weeks apart, followed by a booster dose 6 to 12 months after the second dose.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 182 (Book Page): Administration of dT vaccine to adults is carried out in 2 doses at an interval of 4 to 6 weeks, followed by a booster 6 to 12 months after the second dose.

category: Identify the recommended vaccine schedule for children and adults
front: Q: Contrast the recommended administration ages for the first Measles dose and the MMR vaccine.
back: 1. Measles 1st dose: 9 months. 2. MMR vaccine: 15 months.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 128 (Book Page): Measles — 9 months, 16-24 months MMR — 15 months

category: Identify the recommended vaccine schedule for children and adults
front: Q: How should a healthcare worker handle a routine OPV dose for a child presenting with active diarrhea?
back: Administer the dose, but do not count it toward the schedule; request the child return in 4 weeks for the missing dose.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 129 (Book Page): (c) If the child has diarrhoea, give a dose of OPV, but do not count the dose and ask the mother to return in 4 weeks for the missing dose.

category: Identify the recommended vaccine schedule for children and adults
front: Q: According to IAP recommendations, at what specific ages should the Typhoid vaccine be administered?
back: Administered at age 2 years, with boosters at 5, 8, and 12 years of age.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 128 (Book Page): Typhoid — 2 years, 5 years, 8 years, 12 years

category: Identify the recommended vaccine schedule for children and adults
front: Q: State the exact dose, route, and anatomical site for the first Measles vaccine in infants.
back: 1. Dose: 0.5 ml. 2. Route: Sub-cutaneous. 3. Site: Right upper arm.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 129 (Book Page): Measles 9 completed months-12 months 0.5 ml Sub-cutaneous Right upper Arm

category: Identify the recommended vaccine schedule for children and adults
front: Q: What is the recommended gestational timing for Tetanus Toxoid (TT-2) or Booster doses in pregnancy?
back: Ideally before 36 weeks of pregnancy; however, it should be given even if more than 36 weeks have passed or during labor if missed.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 129 (Book Page): * Give TT-2 or Booster doses before 36 weeks of pregnancy. However, give these even if more than 36 weeks have passed. Give TT to a woman in labour, if she has not previously received TT.

category: Analyze community-based vaccination campaigns
front: What were the original six target diseases specified by the WHO Expanded Programme on Immunization (EPI)?
back:
1. Diphtheria
2. Pertussis
3. Tetanus
4. Polio
5. Tuberculosis
6. Measles
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 128 (Book Page): [EPI] to protect all children of the world against six vaccine-preventable diseases, namely - diphtheria, whooping cough, tetanus, polio, tuberculosis and measles by the year 2000.

category: Analyze community-based vaccination campaigns
front: Why is the first dose of Measles vaccine usually delayed until 9 months of age in community campaigns?
back: To avoid neutralization by transplacentally acquired maternal antibodies, which can render the vaccine ineffective if administered too early.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 155 (Book Page): immunization before the age of 9 months runs the risk of the vaccine being rendered ineffective by the natural antibodies acquired through the mother.

category: Analyze community-based vaccination campaigns
front: Contrast the community impact of OPV vs IPV regarding 'herd immunity' and intestinal protection.
back:
* OPV: Induces intestinal IgA, prevents wild-virus transmission, and provides herd immunity.
* IPV: Protects the individual from paralysis but allows intestinal virus shedding (no herd immunity).
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 213 (Book Page): Intestinal infection stimulates the production of IgA secretory antibodies which prevent subsequent infection... thus is effective in limiting virus transmission in the community.

category: Analyze community-based vaccination campaigns
front: A child presents with mild malnutrition and a low-grade fever during a campaign. What is the vaccination strategy?
back: Vaccinate immediately. Malnutrition and minor illnesses (fever, diarrhea) are NOT contraindications; these children are at the highest risk for disease mortality.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 128 (Book Page): In fact, it is particularly important to immunize children with malnutrition. Low grade fever, mild respiratory infections or diarrhoea... should not be considered as contraindications.

category: Analyze community-based vaccination campaigns
front: What handling requirements for reconstituted Measles vaccine prevent 'Toxic Shock Syndrome' in community sessions?
back:
1. Use within 4 hours of reconstitution.
2. Store in the dark at 2-8°C.
3. Discard any vial remainder after the session.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 155 (Book Page): Toxic shock syndrome (TSS) occurs when measles vaccine is contaminated or the same vial is used for more than one session... The vaccine should not be used after 4 hours of opening.

category: Analyze community-based vaccination campaigns
front: What is the incidence threshold for a district to be classified as having achieved 'Neonatal Tetanus (NT) elimination'?
back: A neonatal tetanus incidence rate of less than 0.1 cases per 1,000 live births.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 317 (Book Page): NT elimination : - Rate < 0.1/1000 live births

category: Analyze community-based vaccination campaigns
front: Under what specific epidemiological condition does WHO mandate a Hepatitis B 'birth dose' within 24 hours?
back: In countries where the prevalence of chronic HBV (HBsAg) in the general population is ≥ 8% (High Endemicity).
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 222 (Book Page): countries where the prevalence in the general population of chronic HBV infection is more than 8 per cent, the first dose... should be given within 24 hours.

category: Analyze community-based vaccination campaigns
front: How is Vaccine-Derived Poliovirus (VDPV) differentiated from Wild Poliovirus (WPV) in campaign surveillance?
back: Laboratory genetic sequencing identifies nucleotide substitutions indicating prolonged replication (>4-6 weeks) rather than the normal short-term vaccine replication.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 211 (Book Page): VDPVs resemble WPVs biologically... they have genetic properties consistent with prolonged replication or transmission, which is substantially longer than the normal period of vaccine virus replication.

category: Analyze community-based vaccination campaigns
front: How does increasing immunization coverage levels affect the 'Cyclical Peaks' of Measles in a community?
back: The intervals between cyclical peaks increase, and the intensity (case numbers) of the peaks is minimized.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 153 (Book Page): With the increase in immunization coverage levels, the intervals between cyclical peaks has increased and the intensity of the peak minimized.

category: Analyze community-based vaccination campaigns
front: What is the dose and interval for Vitamin A supplementation integrated with the National Immunization Schedule?
back:
* 1st Dose: 1 lakh IU at 9 months (with Measles).
* Subsequent: 2 lakh IU every 6 months until age 5 (Total 9 doses).
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 129 (Book Page): Vitamin A (1st dose) At 9 months with measles... (2nd to 9th dose) one dose every 6 months up to the age of 5 years.

category: Analyze community-based vaccination campaigns
front: Q: What are the two core indicators of 'Operational Feasibility' in a community vaccination schedule?
back:
1. Ability to achieve high percentage coverage.
2. Minimizing visits via simultaneous vaccine administration.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 128 (Book Page): operationally feasible : this includes cost and ability to achieve a high percentage of coverage which is a key factor in an effective immunization programme. The schedule must minimize the number of visits, by simultaneous administration of vaccines

category: Analyze community-based vaccination campaigns
front: Q: Why is the average age of measles incidence shifting to older cohorts in highly vaccinated communities?
back: Widespread vaccination provides vaccine-induced immunity in children, reducing natural transmission and creating an immunity gap in older susceptible cohorts.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 129 (Book Page): traditional epidemiological patterns of major infectious diseases, often raising the average age of incidence... now majority of individuals have vaccine induced immunity, which may or may not have the same long-term stability.

category: Analyze community-based vaccination campaigns
front: Q: Contrast the community-level impact of IPV versus OPV regarding wild virus transmission.
back:
1. IPV: No intestinal immunity; wild virus can still multiply and spread.
2. OPV: Induces intestinal immunity; prevents transmission and provides 'herd immunity'.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 213 (Book Page): IPV... does not induce intestinal or local immunity... wild viruses can still multiply in the gut and be a source of infection to others. ... OPV induces both local and systemic immunity

category: Analyze community-based vaccination campaigns
front: Q: In high-risk Polio districts, what specific implementation strategy is used to vaccinate migratory children?
back: Deployment of mobile teams at transit points, including railway stations, bus stops, and moving trains.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 216 (Book Page): use of mobile teams to vaccinate children at transit points (e.g. railway and bus stations) and on moving trains

category: Analyze community-based vaccination campaigns
front: Q: Define the 'Mopping Up' strategy in the final stages of Polio eradication.
back: Intensive door-to-door immunization campaigns targeting high-risk districts where wild poliovirus circulation is suspected.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 216 (Book Page): The strategy of “mopping up” involves door-to-door immunization in high-risk districts, where wild polio virus is known or suspected to be still circulating.

category: Analyze community-based vaccination campaigns
front: Q: What is the primary sensitivity indicator used to evaluate a community's AFP surveillance system performance?
back: The detection of at least one non-polio AFP case per 100,000 children under 15 years annually.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 210 (Book Page): A country's surveillance system needs to be sensitive enough to detect at least one case of AFP for every 100,000 children under 15 — even in the absence of polio.

category: Analyze community-based vaccination campaigns
front: Q: Define 'Epidemiologically Relevant' in the context of community-based vaccination planning.
back: Inclusion of vaccines only against diseases that represent significant public health problems and have effective vaccines available.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 128 (Book Page): (a) epidemiologically relevant, that is, vaccinations should be included only against diseases which are public health problems and against which an effective vaccine exists

category: Analyze community-based vaccination campaigns
front: Q: Compare the 'Attended Delivery' requirements for NT Control versus NT Elimination district classification.
back:
1. NT Control: >50% attended deliveries.
2. NT Elimination: >75% attended deliveries.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 317 (Book Page): NT control : ... and - Attended deliveries > 50%... NT elimination : ... and - attended deliveries > 75%

category: Analyze community-based vaccination campaigns
front: Q: How must a campaign address 'Social Acceptability' to ensure high community participation?
back: Account for local customs, beliefs, seasonal/climatic factors (harvesting), work patterns, and minimizing clinic waiting times.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 128 (Book Page): socially acceptable : the schedule must take into account the local customs, beliefs and practices, seasonal and climatic factors and daily work pattern of the community.

category: Analyze community-based vaccination campaigns
front: Q: What was the specific objective of the 'Technology Mission on Vaccination' in the national program?
back: To streamline immunization activities from research and development to the actual delivery of services to vulnerable populations.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 447 (Book Page): A “Technology Mission on Vaccination and Immunization of Vulnerable Population, specially Children” was set up to cover all aspects of the immunization activity from research and development to actual delivery of services

category: Analyze community-based vaccination campaigns
front: Q: What is the specific goal and target year of Mission Indradhanush?
back: To vaccinate all children under five who are unvaccinated or partially vaccinated against seven diseases (DPT, Polio, TB, Measles, Hep-B) by the year 2020.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 448 (Book Page): [The goal is to vaccinate all under-fives by the year 2020... against seven vaccine preventable diseases, i.e., diphtheria, whooping cough, tetanus, polio, tuberculosis, measles and hepatitis B.]

category: Analyze community-based vaccination campaigns
front: Q: Name the components of the Pentavalent vaccine and its primary operational advantage.
back: Components: DPT, Hepatitis B, and Hib. Advantage: Reduces required injections from 6 to 3, enhancing compliance and coverage.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 448 (Book Page): [Pentavalent vaccine containing DPT, hepatitis B and Hib vaccines... DPT and hepatitis B vaccination require 6 injections... the number of injections are reduced to 3.]

category: Analyze community-based vaccination campaigns
front: Q: Distinguish between NIDs and SNIDs in polio campaigns regarding scale.
back: NIDs (National Immunization Days): Cover approximately 172 million children nationwide. SNIDs (Sub National): Cover 40-80 million children in high-risk areas.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 448 (Book Page): [The NIDs rounds cover approximately 172 million children and SNIDs rounds cover 40-80 million children.]

category: Analyze community-based vaccination campaigns
front: Q: What are the two immediate community actions required upon detecting a single case of polio?
back: 1. Immediate epidemiological investigation. 2. "Mopping up" (door-to-door immunization in high-risk districts) within 48 hours.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 215 (Book Page): [The occurrence of a single case of polio is now considered as an epidemic, and should prompt an immediate epidemiological investigation... Mopping up involves door-to-door immunization in high-risk districts.]

category: Analyze community-based vaccination campaigns
front: Q: How does vaccine coverage determine implementation of the 2nd Measles dose opportunity?
back: Coverage <80%: Via Supplementary Immunization Activity (SIA) for ages 9 months–10 years. Coverage >80%: Integrated into routine immunization at 16–24 months.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 448 (Book Page): [evaluated coverage of first dose of measles vaccination is less than 80 per cent... through supplementary immunization activity (SIA)... coverage more than 80 per cent, the second dose... given through routine immunization at 16-24 months.]

category: Analyze community-based vaccination campaigns
front: Q: What defines the administration criteria for the "OPV-0" dose?
back: Given at birth or as early as possible strictly within the first 15 days, usually before hospital discharge.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 129 (Book Page): [OPV-0: At birth or as early as possible within the first 15 days... given to all children delivered in health institutions before their discharge.]

category: Analyze community-based vaccination campaigns
front: Q: List the two community-empowerment components of the "Stop TB" strategy.
back: 1. Advocacy, communication, and social mobilization. 2. Community participation in TB care (Patients’ charter).
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 208 (Book Page): [5. Empowering people with TB; and communities: Advocacy, communication and social mobilization; Community participation in TB care; Patients’ charter for tuberculosis care.]

category: Analyze community-based vaccination campaigns
front: Q: What is the minimum certification standard for "Completeness of reporting" in AFP surveillance?
back: At least 80% of expected routine reports (weekly/monthly) must be received on time, including "zero reports."
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 211 (Book Page): [At least 80% of expected routine (weekly or monthly) AFP surveillance reports should be received on time, including zero reports where no AFP cases are seen.]

category: Analyze community-based vaccination campaigns
front: Q: Rank the Sabin strains (1, 2, 3) by their frequency of association with VAPP.
back: Highest: Sabin 3 (60% of cases), followed by Sabin 2 and Sabin 1.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 212 (Book Page): [Vaccine-associated paralytic poliomyelitis (VAPP)... frequently associated with Sabin 3 (60% of cases), followed by Sabin 2 and Sabin 1.]

category: Analyze community-based vaccination campaigns
front: Q: What defines environmental surveillance in the context of polio campaigns?
back: Testing sewage or environmental water samples to detect poliovirus circulation in the absence of clinical AFP cases.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 211 (Book Page): [Environmental surveillance involves testing sewage or other environmental samples for the presence of poliovirus... often confirms wild poliovirus infections in the absence of cases of paralysis.]

category: Analyze community-based vaccination campaigns
front: Q: What criteria define a vaccination schedule as 'Operationally Feasible' in a community health setting?
back:
1. Minimum cost.
2. Ability to achieve high percentage coverage.
3. Reduction of visits through simultaneous administration of multiple vaccines.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 128 (Book Page): [operationally feasible : this includes cost and ability to achieve a high percentage of coverage... The schedule must minimize the number of visits, by simultaneous administration of vaccines]

category: Analyze community-based vaccination campaigns
front: Q: What coverage targets are set for the first dose of Measles Containing Vaccine (MCV1) nationally and per district?
back:
1. National level: ≥ 90% coverage.
2. District/Administrative unit: ≥ 80% coverage in every unit.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 152 (Book Page): [raise routine coverage with the first dose of MCV (MCV1) to ≥ 90 per cent nationally, and ≥ 80 per cent in every district or equivalent administrative unit]

category: Analyze community-based vaccination campaigns
front: Q: Define 'Mopping up' activities as a specific strategy for the final stages of poliovirus eradication.
back: Mopping up involves door-to-door immunization in high-risk districts where wild poliovirus transmission is known or suspected to be still circulating.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 215 (Book Page): [The strategy of “mopping up” involves door—to-door immunization in high-risk districts, where wild polio virus is known or suspected to be still circulating.]

category: Analyze community-based vaccination campaigns
front: Q: Why do measles epidemics typically recur in cycles despite ongoing community immunization efforts?
back: Epidemics occur when the proportion of susceptible children in the community reaches approximately 40%. Elimination requires achieving over 95% coverage across all generations.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 152 (Book Page): [It tends to occur in epidemics when the proportion of susceptible children reaches about 40 per cent... achieving an immunization rate of over 95 per cent]

category: Analyze community-based vaccination campaigns
front: Q: How does 'Environmental Surveillance' detect poliovirus circulation in areas with no reported clinical cases?
back: It involves systematic testing of sewage samples. This identifies the virus's presence in the environment, confirming circulation even in the absence of symptomatic paralysis cases.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 210 (Book Page): [Environmental surveillance involves testing sewage or other environmental samples... confirms wild poliovirus infections in the absence of cases of paralysis.]

category: Analyze community-based vaccination campaigns
front: Q: At what community coverage percentage is disease transmission disrupted via Herd Immunity according to the UIP?
back: Transmission patterns are severely disrupted at 80% coverage or more, providing protection to unimmunized individuals within the community.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 447 (Book Page): [generally agreed that when immunization coverage reaches a figure of 80 per cent or more... provide a degree of protection even for the remaining children who have not been immunized, because of “herd immunity”]

category: Analyze community-based vaccination campaigns
front: Q: Which implementation strategy is adopted for Neonatal Tetanus (NT) in high-risk districts with low antenatal care?
back: The primary two-dose Tetanus Toxoid (TT) series is extended to all women of child-bearing age (WCBA) to ensure coverage before pregnancy.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 319 (Book Page): [In areas where the incidence of neonatal tetanus is high, the primary 2—dose course can be extended to all women of child-bearing age]

category: Analyze community-based vaccination campaigns
front: Q: During a PPI campaign, how should a health worker manage an infant with diarrhea presenting for OPV?
back:
1. Administer the OPV dose immediately.
2. Do not count this dose as a scheduled dose.
3. Instruct the mother to return in 4 weeks.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 129 (Book Page): [(c) If the child has diarrhoea, give a dose of OPV, but do not count the dose and ask the mother to return in 4 weeks for the missing dose.]

category: Analyze community-based vaccination campaigns
front: Q: What is the epidemiological rationale for scheduling PPI rounds between November and February?
back: These months represent the 'low transmission season' for polio in South Asia, maximizing the effectiveness of mass administration before the June-September peak.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 215 (Book Page): [PPIs occur as two rounds about 4 to 6 weeks apart during low transmission season of polio, i.e. between November to February.]

category: Analyze community-based vaccination campaigns
front: Q: Name the three key components of the accelerated measles mortality reduction strategy.
back:
1. Two-dose MCV delivery through routine services.
2. Supplementary Immunizing Activities (SIAs).
3. Improved disease surveillance.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 152 (Book Page): [accelerated measles mortality reduction strategy of delivering 2 doses of measles containing vaccine (MCV)... through routine services and supplementary immunizing activities (SIAs), and improving disease surveillance.]

category: Analyze community-based vaccination campaigns
front: What constitutes the 'epidemiologically relevant' component of a community-based immunization schedule?
back: Vaccinations should strictly target diseases that represent significant public health problems for which an effective vaccine is available.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 128 (Book Page): epidemiologically relevant, that is, vaccinations should be included only against diseases which are public health problems and against which an effective vaccine exists

category: Analyze community-based vaccination campaigns
front: How is 'Universal' immunization interpreted regarding population protection and transmission disruption?
back: It implies every child has access. When coverage reaches 80%+, transmission patterns are severely disrupted, providing herd immunity to unimmunized children.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 447 (Book Page): ‘Universal’ immunization is, therefore, best interpreted as implying the ideal that no child should be denied... coverage reaches a figure of 80 per cent or more, then disease transmission patterns are so severely disrupted as to provide a degree of protection even for the remaining children... because of ‘herd immunity’

category: Analyze community-based vaccination campaigns
front: Identify the three 2015 milestones for global measles eradication established at the 2010 World Health Assembly.
back:
1. MCV1 coverage ≥90% nationally (≥80% per district).
2. Incidence <5 cases per million.
3. Mortality reduction ≥95% from year 2000 levels.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 152 (Book Page): (1) raise routine coverage with the first dose of MCV (MCV1) to ≥ 90 per cent nationally, and ≥ 80 per cent in every district... (2) reduce and maintain annual measles incidence to < 5 cases per million; and (3) reduce measles mortality by ≥ 95 per cent

category: Analyze community-based vaccination campaigns
front: What is the primary objective of 'Legacy Planning' in the Polio Eradication Strategic Plan?
back: Mainstreaming essential polio functions into existing public health programs and transitioning assets/infrastructure to benefit other global health priorities.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 209 (Book Page): successful legacy planning will include the mainstreaming of essential polio functions into on-going public health programmes... and the transition of assets and infrastructure to benefit other development goals

category: Analyze community-based vaccination campaigns
front: Contrast the diagnostic role of environmental surveillance with AFP surveillance in polio eradication.
back: Environmental surveillance involves sewage testing to detect poliovirus circulation in the absence of paralytic cases or to track international spread.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 210 (Book Page): Environmental surveillance often confirms wild poliovirus infections in the absence of cases of paralysis. Systematic environmental sampling... provides important supplementary surveillance data.

category: Analyze community-based vaccination campaigns
front: In the context of endgame strategies, what does 'mopping up' immunization involve?
back: Door-to-door vaccination campaigns conducted in high-risk districts where wild poliovirus is known or suspected to still circulate.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 215 (Book Page): The strategy of “mopping up” involves door-to-door immunization in high-risk districts, where wild polio virus is known or suspected to be still circulating.

category: Analyze community-based vaccination campaigns
front: Differentiate Japanese Encephalitis (JE) vaccine strategies for initial campaigns versus routine integration.
back: Initial campaigns target all children aged 1–15 years; routine integration subsequently targets new cohorts at 9–12 months and 16–24 months.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 448 (Book Page): Single dose of JE vaccine was given to all children between 1 to 15 years of age through campaigns... integrated into routine immunization... vaccinating with two doses at 9-12 months and 16-24 months

category: Analyze community-based vaccination campaigns
front: A district planner evaluates the 'Pentavalent' vaccine. What specific administrative benefit does it offer over separate DPT and Hep-B?
back: It reduces the number of injections required to deliver the primary series from six down to three.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 448 (Book Page): DPT and hepatitis B vaccination require 6 injections to deliver primary doses. With the introduction of pentavalent vaccine... the number of injections are reduced to 3.

category: Analyze community-based vaccination campaigns
front: What is the epidemiological significance of July, August, and September for Neonatal Tetanus (NT) in India?
back: These months represent peak seasonal incidence, accounting for over 50% of all annual NT cases in India.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 317 (Book Page): NT has a marked seasonal incidence in India. More than 50 per cent of the total annual cases of NT occur in the month of July, August and September.

category: Analyze community-based vaccination campaigns
front: What was the selection rationale for the 201 districts targeted in Phase 1 of Mission Indradhanush?
back: These high-focus districts contained approximately 50% of all unvaccinated children in the country.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 448 (Book Page): 201 high focus districts will be covered in the first phase... These 201 districts have nearly 50 per cent of all unvaccinated children of the country.

category: Analyze community-based vaccination campaigns
front: Q: What are the two primary coverage targets of India's Universal Immunization Programme (UIP)?
back:
1. 100% coverage of pregnant women with 2 doses of Tetanus Toxoid.
2. At least 85% coverage of infants with primary vaccines (BCG, DPT, OPV, Measles) by age one.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 447 (Book Page): [Universal Immunization Programme was started in India in 1985. It has two vital components: immunization of pregnant women against tetanus, and immunization of children in their first year of life... achieve 100 per cent coverage of pregnant women... and at least 85 per cent coverage of infants.]

category: Analyze community-based vaccination campaigns
front: Q: How does the Pentavalent vaccine optimize the operational feasibility of community-based vaccination?
back: It integrates DPT, Hep-B, and Hib into one injection, reducing the total number of required injections for primary immunization from six down to three.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 448 (Book Page): [DPT and hepatitis B vaccination require 6 injections to deliver primary doses. With the introduction of pentavalent vaccine... the number of injections are reduced to 3.]

category: Analyze community-based vaccination campaigns
front: Q: Distinguish between NIDs and SNIDs in the context of Pulse Polio campaigns.
back: NIDs (National Immunization Days) are nationwide rounds covering ~172 million children. SNIDs (Sub-National Immunization Days) are targeted rounds covering 40–80 million in specific high-risk areas.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 448 (Book Page): [The NIDs rounds cover approximately 172 million children and SNIDs rounds cover 40-80 million children.]

category: Analyze community-based vaccination campaigns
front: Q: What specific tracking strategy is used for newborns in high-risk polio blocks of UP and Bihar?
back: Every newborn is identified at birth, vaccinated during campaigns, and systematically tracked for eight subsequent immunization rounds to ensure no doses are missed.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 215 (Book Page): [In the states of UP and Bihar every new born child is being identified and vaccinated during the polio immunization campaigns and is being tracked for 8 subsequent rounds.]

category: Analyze community-based vaccination campaigns
front: Q: What role does 'Mission Indradhanush' play in the national immunization strategy?
back: It functions as a 'catch-up' campaign specifically targeting children who are either completely unvaccinated or partially vaccinated against seven major preventable diseases.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 448 (Book Page): [The Government of India launched Mission Indradhanush... to cover children who are either unvaccinated or partially vaccinated... The drive will be through a “catch-up” campaign mode.]

category: Analyze community-based vaccination campaigns
front: Q: Identify the three criteria for a district to be classified under 'Neonatal Tetanus (NT) Elimination'.
back:
1. NT Rate: <0.1 per 1000 live births.
2. TT2 Coverage: >90%.
3. Attended Deliveries: >75% by trained personnel.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 317 (Book Page): [NT elimination : - Rate < 0.1/1000 live births and - TT2 coverage > 90% and - attended deliveries > 75%]

category: Analyze community-based vaccination campaigns
front: Q: Why is the 'Pulse' strategy used in supplemental campaigns for Polio eradication?
back: To achieve sudden, simultaneous mass administration of OPV to all children (0-5 years) in a single day, regardless of their previous routine immunization history.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 215 (Book Page): [The term "pulse" has been used to describe this sudden, simultaneous, mass administration of OPV on a single day to all children 0-5 years of age, regardless to previous immunization.]

category: Analyze community-based vaccination campaigns
front: Q: How is 'Social Mobilization' implemented to improve campaign participation in resistant communities?
back: By engaging local influencers, community leaders, and religious figures to build public confidence, improve acceptance, and reduce vaccine refusal rates.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 216 (Book Page): [Social mobilization activities are being intensified by involving the local influencers, community and religious leaders to improve community participation and acceptance of polio vaccine.]

category: Analyze community-based vaccination campaigns
front: Q: What does the 'Mopping Up' strategy involve during the final stages of Polio campaigns?
back: High-intensity, door-to-door immunization within high-risk districts where the wild poliovirus is still suspected or known to be circulating.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 215 (Book Page): [The strategy of “mopping up” involves door-to-door immunization in high-risk districts, where wild polio virus is known or suspected to be still circulating.]

category: Analyze community-based vaccination campaigns
front: Q: Define 'Operational Feasibility' as a principle for designing a community immunization schedule.
back: The ability to achieve high coverage at a sustainable cost while minimizing the number of clinic visits through simultaneous vaccine administration.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 128 (Book Page): [operationally feasible : this includes cost and ability to achieve a high percentage of coverage... The schedule must minimize the number of visits, by simultaneous administration of vaccines.]

category: Analyze community-based vaccination campaigns
front: Q: What are the four essential criteria for a well-designed community immunization schedule?
back:
1. Epidemiologically relevant (target health problems).
2. Immunologically effective (correct age/timing).
3. Operationally feasible (cost/coverage).
4. Socially acceptable (cultural/local customs).
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 128 (Book Page): [A well thought-out immunization schedule must be (a) epidemiologically relevant (b) immunologically effective (c) operationally feasible (d) socially acceptable.]

category: Analyze community-based vaccination campaigns
front: Q: Define the 'Pulse' strategy in community-based mass immunization campaigns.
back: Sudden, simultaneous, mass administration of a vaccine (e.g., OPV) on a single day to all children in a target age group (e.g., 0-5 years), regardless of prior history.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 215 (Book Page): [The term "pulse" has been used to describe this sudden, simultaneous, mass administration of OPV on a single day to all children 0-5 years of age, regardless to previous immunization.]

category: Analyze community-based vaccination campaigns
front: Q: Differentiate between routine MCV1 and MCV2/SIA strategies for measles reduction.
back:
MCV1: Aim is ≥90% national routine coverage.
MCV2/SIA: Supplementary activities to provide a 'second opportunity' and cover gaps in routine coverage.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 152 (Book Page): [WHO and UNICEF developed an accelerated measles mortality reduction strategy of delivering 2 doses of measles containing vaccine (MCV) to all children through routine services and supplementary immunizing activities (SIAs).]

category: Analyze community-based vaccination campaigns
front: Q: A child with diarrhea presents during a campaign. How is OPV administration managed?
back: Administer the dose, but do not count it toward the primary schedule. The mother must return in 4 weeks for a repeat dose.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 129 (Book Page): [If the child has diarrhoea, give a dose of OPV, but do not count the dose and ask the mother to return in 4 weeks for the missing dose.]

category: Analyze community-based vaccination campaigns
front: Q: Describe the mechanism of 'Two-phase' chemotherapy in TB community control programs.
back:
1. Intensive Phase (1-3 months): Kills rapidly multiplying bacilli to prevent persistence.
2. Continuation Phase: Sterilizes remaining dormant or persisting bacilli to prevent relapse.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 194 (Book Page): [(i) the first is a short, aggressive or intense phase... to kill off as many bacilli as possible. (ii) the second or “continuation” phase is aimed at sterilizing the smaller number of dormant or persisting bacilli.]

category: Analyze community-based vaccination campaigns
front: Q: What is the clinical case definition for Mumps in community surveillance?
back: Acute onset of unilateral or bilateral tender, self-limited swelling of the parotid or other salivary glands, lasting 2 or more days without other apparent cause.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 159 (Book Page): [Clinical mumps : acute onset of unilateral or bilateral tender, self-limited swelling of the parotid or other salivary gland, lasting 2 or more days and without other apparent cause.]

category: Analyze community-based vaccination campaigns
front: Q: How is 'Alternate Vaccine Delivery' (AVD) implemented to strengthen community coverage?
back: Support for transporting vaccines from the Primary Health Centre (PHC) directly to sub-centers or outreach session sites where services are deficient.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 448 (Book Page): [Support for alternate vaccine delivery from PHC to sub-centre and outreach sessions; Deploying retired manpower to carry out immunization activities in urban slums.]

category: Analyze community-based vaccination campaigns
front: Q: Contrast 'cVDPV' from 'WPV' in the context of community health threat.
back: Circulating Vaccine-Derived Poliovirus (cVDPV) results from prolonged replication of OPV strains; it poses the same public health threat and requires the same control measures as Wild Poliovirus (WPV).
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 212 (Book Page): [cVDPVs pose the same public health threat as WPVs and require the same control measures.]

category: Analyze community-based vaccination campaigns
front: Q: Why is 'Herd Immunity' achieved at 80-85% coverage in community programs?
back: Disease transmission patterns are severely disrupted, providing protection to non-immunized individuals because the pathogen cannot find enough susceptible hosts.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 447 (Book Page): [generally agreed that when immunization coverage reaches a figure of 80 per cent or more, then disease transmission patterns are so severely disrupted as to provide a degree of protection even for the remaining children.]

category: Analyze community-based vaccination campaigns
front: Q: What defines a district under 'Neonatal Tetanus (NT) Elimination' status?
back:
1. Incidence <0.1/1000 live births.
2. TT2 coverage >90%.
3. Attended deliveries >75%.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 317 (Book Page): [NT elimination : - Rate < 0.1/1000 live births and - TT2 coverage > 90% and - attended deliveries > 75%]

category: Analyze public awareness programs & school health initiatives to control its transmission
front: Q: Which specific setting provides a unique opportunity for delivering vaccines like MR and HPV to adolescents?
back: Educational institutions (schools and colleges) are key settings for adolescent vaccine delivery.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 129 (Book Page): [Adolescence... offering special opportunities, such as a vaccine delivery in the setting of educational institutions. The vaccines of interest are MR and MMR... hepatitis B, influenza, varicella and HPV vaccines etc.]

category: Analyze public awareness programs & school health initiatives to control its transmission
front: Q: What is the fourth component of the 2012-2020 Global Measles and Rubella Strategic Plan regarding the public?
back: Communicate and engage to build public confidence in, and demand for, vaccination.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 153 (Book Page): [(4) communicate and engage to build public confidence in, and demand for vaccination;]

category: Analyze public awareness programs & school health initiatives to control its transmission
front: Q: What socio-environmental factors must be considered to make an immunization schedule 'socially acceptable'?
back: Local customs, beliefs, practices, seasonal/climatic factors, and the daily work pattern of the community.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 128 (Book Page): [(d) socially acceptable : the schedule must take into account the local customs, beliefs and practices, seasonal and climatic factors and daily work pattern of the community.]

category: Analyze public awareness programs & school health initiatives to control its transmission
coreConcept: Crisis Communication in Vaccine Adverse Events
front: Q: How should awareness programs address a cluster of Toxic Shock Syndrome (TSS) deaths following measles vaccination?
back: Explain that TSS results from contaminated vials or poor injection quality, not the vaccine itself, to prevent panic.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 155 (Book Page): [Toxic shock syndrome (TSS) occurs when measles vaccine is contaminated... TSS is totally preventable and reflects poor quality of immunization services.]

category: Analyze public awareness programs & school health initiatives to control its transmission
front: Q: How does the 'Janani Suraksha Yojana' contribute to controlling neonatal tetanus transmission through awareness?
back: It encourages institutional deliveries, which ensures clean cord care and sterile birth practices by trained personnel.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 317 (Book Page): [The mission also actively encourages institutional deliveries through interventions such as the ‘Janani Suraksha Yojana’. These measures have contributed to reducing the burden of neonatal tetanus (NT)]

category: Analyze public awareness programs & school health initiatives to control its transmission
front: Q: Which age group was the target for Japanese Encephalitis (JE) awareness and vaccination campaigns in endemic districts?
back: Children between 1 to 15 years of age.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 448 (Book Page): [Single dose of JE vaccine was given to all children between 1 to 15 years of age through campaigns]

category: Analyze public awareness programs & school health initiatives to control its transmission
front: Q: In the Stop TB Strategy, what is the role of 'Advocacy, Communication, and Social Mobilization' (ACSM)?
back: Empowering people with TB and the community to improve case detection and treatment adherence.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 206 (Book Page): [5. Empowering people with TB; and communities — Advocacy, communication and social mobilization — Community participation in TB care]

category: Analyze public awareness programs & school health initiatives to control its transmission
front: Q: Why do public health planners now focus on the 10-19 year age group for booster immunizations?
back: Because vaccine-induced immunity in adults may lack the long-term stability of natural disease-induced immunity.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 129 (Book Page): [the adolescent age group of 10-19 years represent an important additional target group... now majority of individuals have vaccine induced immunity, which may or may not have the same long-term stability.]

category: Analyze public awareness programs & school health initiatives to control its transmission
front: Q: What strategy is used to find and vaccinate neonates in high-risk Polio areas like Uttar Pradesh?
back: Targeting neonates with a specific 'birth dose' of mOPV1 to ensure immunity from the start.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 215 (Book Page): [to identify and target all neonates in high-risk areas of UP with a "birth dose" of mOPV1]

category: Analyze public awareness programs & school health initiatives to control its transmission
front: Q: What is the primary role of international partners like Rotary International in Mission Indradhanush?
back: Providing technical support for intensive planning and monitoring of vaccination campaigns.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 448 (Book Page): [The mission will be technically supported by WHO, UNICEF, Rotary International and other donor partners.]

category: Analyze public awareness programs & school health initiatives to control its transmission
front: Q: What four social factors must a 'socially acceptable' immunization schedule accommodate?
back:
1. Local customs, beliefs, and practices.
2. Seasonal and climatic factors.
3. Community daily work patterns.
4. Reduction of long clinic waiting times.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 128 (Book Page): [the schedule must take into account the local customs, beliefs and practices, seasonal and climatic factors and daily work pattern of the community. One important factor is to reduce long waiting time]

category: Analyze public awareness programs & school health initiatives to control its transmission
front: Q: Why is the adolescent age group (10-19) now a target for school-based immunization programs?
back:
1. Average age of disease incidence is rising due to successful infant EPI.
2. Vaccine-induced immunity may lack the long-term stability of naturally acquired immunity.
3. Schools offer centralized delivery for MR, MMR, Td, and HPV.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 129 (Book Page): [the adolescent age group of 10-19 years represent an important additional target group for immunization... offering special opportunities, such as a vaccine delivery in the setting of educational institutions.]

category: Analyze public awareness programs & school health initiatives to control its transmission
front: Q: What is the fourth core objective of the 2012-2020 Global Measles and Rubella Strategic Plan regarding public awareness?
back: To communicate and engage with the community to build public confidence in vaccines and generate demand for vaccination services.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 153 (Book Page): [(4) communicate and engage to build public confidence in, and demand for vaccination; and (5) conduct research and development]

category: Analyze public awareness programs & school health initiatives to control its transmission
front: Q: In a school health setting, how are Diphtheria contacts managed if their last booster was >2 years ago?
back:
1. Administer an immediate booster dose of Diphtheria toxoid.
2. Place under daily medical surveillance for at least one week.
3. Conduct bacteriological surveillance with repeated throat swabs.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 167 (Book Page): [where primary course or booster dose of diphtheria toxoid was received more than 2 years before, only a booster dose of diphtheria toxoid need be given. ... Contacts should be placed under medical surveillance ... for at least a week]

category: Analyze public awareness programs & school health initiatives to control its transmission
front: Q: How does social mobilization improve Polio vaccine acceptance in high-risk communities?
back: By actively involving local influencers, community leaders, and religious leaders to build trust and counter vaccine refusal or hesitation.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 216 (Book Page): [Social mobilization activities are being intensified by involving the local influencers, community and religious leaders to improve community participation and acceptance of polio vaccine.]

category: Analyze public awareness programs & school health initiatives to control its transmission
front: Q: Why is public awareness of chest symptoms critical for TB case-finding programs?
back: Because over 60% of pulmonary TB patients develop symptoms early (cough/fever) and seek medical advice voluntarily; awareness ensures they report before reaching advanced stages.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 192 (Book Page): [many of them (over 60 per cent) seek medical advice on their own initiative. The chest symptoms often develop early, that is before the disease has gone on to an advanced stage. This is the most fertile group for case-finding.]

category: Analyze public awareness programs & school health initiatives to control its transmission
front: Q: What is the 'catch-up' strategy utilized by Mission Indradhanush for unvaccinated children?
back: Conducting four special vaccination campaigns in high-focus districts using the intensive planning and monitoring experience derived from the Pulse Polio program.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 448 (Book Page): [The drive will be through a “catch-up” campaign mode. ... Intensive planning and monitoring experience of pulse polio immunization programme will be used.]

category: Analyze public awareness programs & school health initiatives to control its transmission
front: Q: Beyond protecting women, what is the second priority of the Rubella vaccination strategy to stop transmission?
back: To interrupt transmission by vaccinating all children aged 1-14 years, followed by routine universal immunization at age one.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 157 (Book Page): [priorities being first to protect women of child-bearing age ... and then to interrupt transmission of rubella by vaccinating all children currently aged 1-14 years, and subsequently all children at one year of age.]

category: Analyze public awareness programs & school health initiatives to control its transmission
front: Q: For TB control, why is it said that 'tuberculosis is a social disease with medical aspects'?
back: Because transmission is heavily influenced by quality of life, overcrowding, education level, and lack of awareness, which act as a 'barometer' of social welfare.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 188 (Book Page): [Tuberculosis is a social disease with medical aspects. It has also been described as a barometer of social welfare. ... lack of education, large families, early marriages, lack of awareness of causes of illness, etc.]

category: Analyze public awareness programs & school health initiatives to control its transmission
front: Q: What unique delivery advantage does the 'school setting' offer for Td, Hepatitis B, and HPV vaccines?
back: It provides a structured, high-coverage environment for 'endgame' strategies and disease elimination/eradication measures in adolescents beyond the infancy schedule.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 129 (Book Page): [Adolescence presents certain challenges ... while also offering special opportunities, such as a vaccine delivery in the setting of educational institutions. The vaccines of interest are ... Td as booster dose for neonatal tetanus elimination, hepatitis B, influenza, varicella and HPV vaccines]

category: Analyze community-based vaccination campaigns
front: Q: Under what specific epidemiological condition is a 'birth dose' of Hepatitis B vaccine mandatory?
back: A: It is required in countries where the chronic HBV prevalence in the general population exceeds 8 percent to prevent perinatal transmission.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 222 (Book Page): [In countries where a high proportion of HBV infection is acquired perinatally, specifically in countries where the prevalence in the general population of chronic HBV infection is more than 8 per cent, the first dose of hepatitis B vaccine should be given within 24 hours after birth.]

category: Analyze community-based vaccination campaigns
front: Q: What is the operational purpose of the 'Zero-dose' OPV in maternity wards?
back: A: To provide early intestinal immunity and ensure infants are protected before potential exposure, avoiding the risks of community infection at regular clinics.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 212 (Book Page): [It is recommended that a dose of OPV (zero-dose) is required to be given to all children delivered in health institutions before their discharge from the hospital... to avoid infection.]

category: Analyze community-based vaccination campaigns
front: Q: What are the specific cold chain requirements for transporting AFP stool specimens to the laboratory?
back:
1. Stored at 4-8°C.
2. Packed between frozen ice packs in a cold box.
3. Must arrive at the laboratory within 72 hours.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 209 (Book Page): [Stool specimens have to be sealed in containers and stored immediately inside a refrigerator or packed between frozen ice packs at 4-8°C in a cold box... Specimens should arrive at the laboratory within 72 hours of collection.]

category: Analyze community-based vaccination campaigns
front: Q: Why is the Measles vaccine stored in colored glass vials during community campaigns?
back: A: The vaccine is highly sensitive to sunlight; colored glass protects it from losing potency due to light exposure.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 154 (Book Page): [The vaccine is also sensitive to sunlight, hence it is kept in coloured glass vials.]

category: Analyze community-based vaccination campaigns
front: Q: What is the significance of 'Environmental Surveillance' in regions with zero clinical polio cases?
back: A: It involves testing sewage to detect wild poliovirus circulation that may occur without causing symptoms or paralysis in the community.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 210 (Book Page): [Environmental surveillance often confirms wild poliovirus infections in the absence of cases of paralysis. Systematic environmental sampling (e.g. in Egypt and Mumbai, India) provides important supplementary surveillance data.]

category: Analyze community-based vaccination campaigns
front: Q: How rapidly does reconstituted Measles vaccine lose potency at 37°C?
back: A: It loses almost all potency within 1 hour; therefore, it must be used within 4 hours of opening.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 154 (Book Page): [Reconstituted measles vaccine... loses almost all potency after 1 hour at 37°C. After reconstitution, the vaccine must be stored in the dark at 2-8°C and used within 4 hours.]

category: Analyze community-based vaccination campaigns
front: Q: What is the 'Golden Rule' for Tetanus Toxoid (TT) administration in late-visit pregnant women?
back: A: No mother should be denied even a single dose of TT, even if she presents very late in pregnancy.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 319 (Book Page): [The golden rule is that no pregnant mother should be denied even one dose of tetanus toxoid if she is seen late in pregnancy.]

category: Analyze community-based vaccination campaigns
front: Q: Describe the community integration of Vitamin A supplementation with the Measles vaccine.
back: A: The first dose of Vitamin A (1 lakh IU) is administered orally at 9 completed months concurrently with the measles vaccine.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 129 (Book Page): [Vitamin A (1st dose) At 9 months with measles. 1 ml Oral (1 lakh IU).]

category: Analyze community-based vaccination campaigns
front: Q: How does the strategy for Hepatitis A vaccination change during a community outbreak?
back: A: Use single-dose inactivated vaccines for pre-exposure (travelers) and post-exposure (close contacts) prophylaxis within 14 days of exposure.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 218 (Book Page): [Use of hepatitis A vaccine... should be considered for pre-exposure prophylaxis (e.g. for travellers) and post-exposure prophylaxis (e.g. for close contacts of acute cases of hepatitis A).]

category: Analyze community-based vaccination campaigns
front: Q: What numerical threshold defines the 'Elimination' of Neonatal Tetanus (NT) in a district?
back:
1. Incidence rate < 0.1 per 1,000 live births.
2. TT2 coverage > 90%.
3. Attended deliveries > 75%.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 317 (Book Page): [NT elimination : - Rate < 0.1/1000 live births and - TT2 coverage > 90% and - attended deliveries > 75%]

category: Analyze public awareness programs & school health initiatives to control its transmission
front: Q: Which two age intervals are targeted for Tetanus Toxoid (TT) boosters in school-age children?
back:
1. 10 years
2. 16 years
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 129 (Book Page): [TT 10 years & 16 years 0.5 ml. Intra-muscular Upper Arm]

category: Analyze public awareness programs & school health initiatives to control its transmission
front: Q: Why is the adolescent age group (10-19 years) a strategic target for school health initiatives?
back:
1. Educational institutions offer efficient vaccine delivery settings.
2. Provides opportunity for boosters (Td) and new vaccines (HPV, HBV).
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 129 (Book Page): [adolescence... offering special opportunities, such as a vaccine delivery in the setting of educational institutions.]

category: Analyze public awareness programs & school health initiatives to control its transmission
front: Q: What is the primary objective of 'Mission Indradhanush' regarding public outreach and awareness?
back:
1. Conduct intensive 'catch-up' campaigns.
2. Target unvaccinated or partially vaccinated children under five.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 448 (Book Page): [Mission Indradhanush... to cover children who are either unvaccinated or partially vaccinated... drive will be through a ‘catch-up’ campaign mode.]

category: Analyze public awareness programs & school health initiatives to control its transmission
front: Q: How do public awareness programs address 'social acceptability' in immunization schedules?
back:
1. Account for local customs/beliefs.
2. Adjust for seasonal/climatic factors.
3. Minimize clinic waiting times.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 128 (Book Page): [socially acceptable : the schedule must take into account the local customs, beliefs and practices, seasonal and climatic factors and daily work pattern of the community.]

category: Analyze public awareness programs & school health initiatives to control its transmission
front: Q: What specific social mobilization strategy is used to improve Polio vaccine acceptance in high-risk blocks?
back: Involvement of local influencers, community leaders, and religious leaders to build trust and participation.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 216 (Book Page): [Social mobilization activities are being intensified by involving the local influencers, community and religious leaders to improve community participation and acceptance of polio vaccine.]

category: Analyze public awareness programs & school health initiatives to control its transmission
front: Q: Which pillar of the 2012-2020 Global Measles and Rubella Strategic Plan focuses on public demand?
back: Communicating and engaging to build public confidence in, and demand for, vaccination.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 153 (Book Page): [(4) communicate and engage to build public confidence in, and demand for vaccination;]

category: Analyze public awareness programs & school health initiatives to control its transmission
front: Q: In the 'Stop TB Strategy,' which component focuses on empowering patients and communities?
back: Advocacy, Communication, and Social Mobilization (ACSM), and the implementation of the Patients' Charter.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 208 (Book Page): [5. Empowering people with TB; and communities — Advocacy, communication and social mobilization... Patients’ charter for tuberculosis care]

category: Analyze public awareness programs & school health initiatives to control its transmission
front: Q: What is the recommended school entry age for the second DPT booster in the National Schedule?
back: 5 to 6 years of age.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 168 (Book Page): [followed by another booster (DT only) at the age of 5 to 6 years... at school entry.]

category: Analyze public awareness programs & school health initiatives to control its transmission
front: Q: A school health program targets Td vaccination for adolescent girls. What specific public health goal does this address?
back: Elimination of neonatal tetanus by providing a booster dose for future maternal protection.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 129 (Book Page): [Td as booster dose for neonatal tetanus elimination, hepatitis B, influenza, varicella and HPV vaccines etc.]

category: Analyze public awareness programs & school health initiatives to control its transmission
front: Q: According to the Indian Academy of Paediatrics (IAP), what is the recommended schedule for Typhoid vaccination in school children?
back: Administered at 2 years, 5 years, 8 years, and 12 years of age.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 129 (Book Page): [Typhoid — 2 years, 5 years, 8 years, 12 years]

category: Analyze public awareness programs & school health initiatives to control its transmission
front: Q: What are the four fundamental requirements of a well-designed immunization schedule?
back:
1. Epidemiologically relevant (public health priority).
2. Immunologically effective (correct timing/age).
3. Operationally feasible (cost and high coverage).
4. Socially acceptable (matching local customs/beliefs).
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 128 (Book Page): [A well thought-out immunization schedule must be (a) epidemiologically relevant... (b) immunologically effective... (c) operationally feasible... (d) socially acceptable.]

category: Analyze public awareness programs & school health initiatives to control its transmission
front: Q: How is 'Social Acceptability' achieved in public health awareness programs?
back: By tailoring schedules to local customs, beliefs, seasonal/climatic factors, and community work patterns. A critical focus is reducing long clinic waiting times to ensure patient compliance.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 128 (Book Page): [the schedule must take into account the local customs, beliefs and practices, seasonal and climatic factors and daily work pattern of the community... to reduce long waiting time.]

category: Analyze public awareness programs & school health initiatives to control its transmission
front: Q: Why are educational institutions identified as strategic sites for adolescent immunization?
back: Schools provide a centralized setting to reach the 10-19 age group. Targeted vaccines include MR/MMR for outbreak prevention, Td boosters, Hepatitis B, and HPV.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 152 (Book Page): [Adolescence presents... special opportunities, such as a vaccine delivery in the setting of educational institutions... vaccines of interest are MR and MMR... Td as booster... hepatitis B, influenza, varicella and HPV.]

category: Analyze public awareness programs & school health initiatives to control its transmission
front: Q: What public awareness pillar is used to counter 'vaccine refusal' in the Global Measles Strategy?
back: The 'Communication and Engagement' pillar. It builds public confidence and generates demand for vaccination through community involvement and advocacy.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 153 (Book Page): [(4) communicate and engage to build public confidence in, and demand for vaccination... (4) the increasing refusal of immunization by some populations.]

category: Analyze public awareness programs & school health initiatives to control its transmission
front: Q: A mother refuses vaccination due to a minor child cold. How does public awareness address this misconception?
back: Programs must educate that low-grade fever, mild respiratory infections, and diarrhea are NOT contraindications. Malnourished children are most in need of protection.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 128 (Book Page): [Low grade fever, mild respiratory infections or diarrhoea and other minor illnesses should not be considered as contraindications to immunization.]

category: Analyze public awareness programs & school health initiatives to control its transmission
front: Q: What is the primary 'catch-up' mode utilized by Mission Indradhanush?
back: It conducts intensive vaccination campaigns for children missed during routine sessions. It targets unvaccinated or partially vaccinated under-fives in high-focus districts.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 448 (Book Page): [The drive will be through a “catch-up” campaign mode... Mission Indradhanush on 25th December 2014, to cover children who are either unvaccinated or partially vaccinated.]

category: Analyze public awareness programs & school health initiatives to control its transmission
front: Q: How do Pulse Polio initiatives target high-risk 'migratory' populations?
back: Using mobile teams at transit points (railways, bus stations, trains) and border crossing booths. This ensures children on the move are not missed during SIAs.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 216 (Book Page): [use of mobile teams to vaccinate children at transit points (e.g. railway and bus stations) and on moving trains... special booths are established in areas bordering neighbouring countries.]

category: Analyze public awareness programs & school health initiatives to control its transmission
front: Q: How does the Stop TB Strategy empower communities and patients?
back: Through Advocacy, Communication, and Social Mobilization (ACSM). It promotes community participation in care and utilizes the Patients' Charter to reduce stigma.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 206 (Book Page): [5. Empowering people with TB; and communities — Advocacy, communication and social mobilization — Community participation in TB care — Patients’ charter.]

category: Analyze public awareness programs & school health initiatives to control its transmission
front: Q: What role do 'local influencers' play in ensuring successful vaccine uptake?
back: Local, community, and religious leaders are engaged to improve participation and overcome socio-cultural barriers, especially in resistant or hesitant pockets.
citation: In book "Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine", Page 216 (Book Page): [Social mobilization activities are being intensified by involving the local influencers, community and religious leaders to improve community participation and acceptance.]

category: Analyze public awareness programs & school health initiatives to control its transmission
front: Q: Which two 'social factors' are primary targets for TB public awareness campaigns?
back:
1. Lack of education/awareness about the causes of illness.
2. Social stigma associated with the disease. Both contribute to transmission and delayed diagnosis.
